$comment: Metals, ores and industrial minerals for the C64 tree. 'shared' maps an id to a full node object; other subsystem files should link to those ids with the "ref" children form ("children": ["metal.alumina"]). Nodes that are not in `shared` are still defined once inside the root.children branches and can be referenced by id the same way.

metal.rosin.activator.name: The halide activator in the flux core
metal.rosin.activator.description: Plain rosin is a weak flux. The electronics industry improved it by adding a small amount of acid activator - in 1982 almost always zinc chloride, or in the more aggressive grades a zinc chloride-ammonium chloride mixture - so the flux can remove oxides that rosin alone would leave. The trade is real: more activator means a better joint and a corrosive residue that, if it is not washed off, eats the copper. This is why the flux grade is a specification on the wire, and why the electronics-grade rosin wire of 1982 was normally a mildly activated (MA) or activated (A) flux rather than pure RMA.

facts.label: Activator
facts.value: zinc chloride at 0.1-2%, or zinc-ammonium chloride

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: RA (rosin-ammonia), RMA (rosin mildly activated), MA, A

facts.label: The trade
facts.value: more activator means better oxide removal and worse corrosion of copper if residues remain

metal.rosin.activator.note: Flux grade nomenclature and the activator levels are standard; medium confidence on which grade Commodore specified in 1982.

metal.pine-resin.name: Pine resin from a plantation or a pulp mill
metal.pine-resin.description: The leaf: resin bled from the trunks of Pinus species in managed plantations in the American Southeast, Brazil, India, Malaysia, Portugal and China. In the 1980s most rosin came not from tapping but from distilling pine stumps and pulping residues left over from the paper industry - a pulp-mill residue. So the flux in a C64 solder joint is, quite literally, a by-product of making pulp, which makes it a convergence point with the paper and pulp side of the organics chain.
places: Kraft pulp mill, southeastern United States

facts.label: Rosin yield
facts.value: roughly 1-3% of softwood pulp-mill residue

metal.pine-resin.note: By the 1980s the pulp-mill (wood rosin) route supplied the majority of industrial rosin; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split between gum and wood rosin.

metal.quartzite.name: High-grade quartzite (97-99% SiO2)
metal.quartzite.description: A metamorphosed, recrystallised quartz sandstone that is quarried rather than deep-mined. The chemical silicon industry does not use beach sand at all - it uses very low iron, very low aluminium quartzite, because Al and Fe are the impurities that survive the entire chain into the crystal. Two regions have essentially all of it. Note this is a DIFFERENT rock from the industrial silica sand used for glass, foundry moulds and copper-smelter flux, which is a much more common material.

facts.label: Main sources
facts.value: Norway (The Quartz Corp, JOlster and Tana), Brazil, and the Spruce Pine district of North Carolina

facts.label: Why not ordinary sand
facts.value: iron and aluminium in silica sand carry straight through to the crystal

children.name: Quartzite quarry, ~100,000 t/year
children.description: The Norwegian quartzite quarry is a bench mine in metamorphosed sandstone: drilling, blasting, a primary jaw crusher, and a sorting step where workers - and, later, optical sorters - remove the visibly iron-stained lumps by hand. The rock is then crushed, washed on a sluice or in a scrubber, dried and size-graded, because a single grain of iron left in the batch makes a bad day of the whole furnace.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open-pit bench quarry, drill and blast, ~15-25 m benches

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 100,000 t/year for the largest suppliers

children.note: Site-specific tonnages vary; this is a representative figure for a world-scale supplier rather than a cited figure for one named quarry.

metal.silica.mgsi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
metal.silica.mgsi.description: The commodity-grade output of a submerged arc furnace: a grey-black brittle lump material about the density of bone. In 1982 a Japanese or Taiwanese silicon plant bought it as if it were ore. The specification that matters is not the silicon but the boron - anything above roughly 20 ppm boron cannot reach electronics grade, which is why the silicon furnace takes a low-ash petroleum coke and not the 10-12% ash coke the steel industry uses.

facts.label: Why not steel coke
facts.value: coke ash carries boron and phosphorus above the electronics budget

metal.silica.polysilicon.name: Polysilicon ingot and rod, 9N
metal.silica.polysilicon.description: Shiny grey metalloid deposited as a polycrystalline boule on electrically heated silicon seed rods and then sawn into chunks. The chunks are the cathode-grade feedstock that the crystal puller charges. In 1982 the world outside Japan consumed polysilicon as an expensive specialty chemical, not as a commodity. The 6510 is an NMOS part, so its 1982 die uses aluminium gate metal and thermally grown oxide rather than a polysilicon gate; this branch is the industry feedstock route behind that, and it is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

facts.label: Typical purity
facts.value: 9N (99.9999999%); 6N-7N was typical of the 1982 era

facts.label: Form
facts.value: sawn rod segments, 5-30 kg per chunk in 1980s practice

facts.label: Energy for the whole route
facts.value: 100-200 kWh per kg of polysilicon

metal.caustic-soda.name: Caustic soda (NaOH), 50% solution
metal.caustic-soda.description: Two entirely different consumers in this tree. The Bayer process digestion liquor, where a caustic grade tanker holds roughly 300-400 t of 50% solution and a refinery's caustic and steam costs dominate its operating cost. And the chlor-alkali industry, where the same product comes out of the same cell as the chlorine and hydrogen that make the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Cost accounting in aluminium is dominated by caustic and steam; every tonne of caustic lost to red mud is recovered by lime in the causticisation circuit or bought.

facts.label: Bayer consumption
facts.value: order 100-200 kg of Na2O-equivalent per tonne of alumina, plus process losses

facts.label: Concentration sold
facts.value: 50% w/w membrane-grade solution

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, done with lime

metal.caustic-soda.note: Documented: sodium hydroxide is produced by variations of the electrolytic chloralkali process, first as a 32% solution and then evaporated to a 50% solution, with chlorine as the main by-product. Not established: the 100-200 kg of Na2O equivalent per tonne of alumina, the 300-400 t tanker size, and the lime causticisation reaction as written.

metal.chlorine.name: Chlorine gas (Cl2)
metal.chlorine.description: A pale yellow-green gas denser than air, made in the chlor-alkali plant and piped or tanker-shipped to the hydrochloric acid synthesis unit. Around 1982 much of it went to solvent makers and to water treatment as chlorinated organics; only a fraction ever reached a silicon plant, and silicon-grade chlorine must be bone dry, because water plus trichlorosilane gives hydrochloric acid and hexasiloxane gel that plugs the fluidised bed.

facts.label: Water content spec
facts.value: <40 ppm H2O for electronic-grade silicon plants

facts.label: Liquefaction
facts.value: shipped as liquid at about -34 C, or as dry gas in tube trailers

metal.chlorine.note: Documented: the chloralkali process is the technology that produces chlorine together with sodium hydroxide and hydrogen, and chlorine is a yellow-green gas at room temperature. Not established: the below-40 ppm water specification for electronic-grade silicon plants and the liquefaction point of about -34 C.

metal.hydrogen.name: Electrolysis hydrogen from the chlor-alkali cathode
metal.hydrogen.description: The wet hydrogen off the cathode goes to acid synthesis, and in a silicon plant it also goes to the Siemens reactor as the carrier that carries trichlorosilane to the rod and strips the chlorine off. The purification train is a caustic scrubber, then a drying tower, and the carbon monoxide has to be taken below a few ppm or the polysilicon comes out with carbon in it. The same hydrogen, purified a stage further, is what a stainless bright-annealing line uses.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: chlor-alkali cathode gas

facts.label: Purishment
facts.value: caustic scrub, molecular-sieve dry, CO below 5-10 ppm

metal.hydrogen.note: The CO limit is my recollection of silicon-grade hydrogen specifications; medium confidence.

metal.hydrochloric-acid.name: Hydrochloric acid (commercial 32-37%)
metal.hydrochloric-acid.description: The hydrochloric acid that chlorinates metallurgical silicon. Industrial acid is made by burning hydrogen in chlorine, both products of the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the silicon plant's feedstock chain runs back through a 1970s chlor-alkali plant and, behind that, a salt mine or a solar salt pan. The same acid is used for galvanising pickling, for the stainless pickling line, for the tinplate line, and for regenerating ferric chloride etchant at the board fab.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl

facts.label: Commercial strength
facts.value: commercial acid is sold at about 32-37% w/w; that is a sale grade, NOT the azeotrope. The HCl-water azeotrope is 20.2% HCl, constant-boiling at 108.6 C.

facts.label: Typical silicon-plant demand
facts.value: order 10-30 t of acid per tonne of polysilicon plant output

metal.hydrochloric-acid.note: Contradicted on the azeotrope. Hydrochloric acid as a binary mixture of HCl and water has a constant-boiling azeotrope at 20.2% HCl and 108.6 C, so the 32-37% figure is a commercial sale concentration, not the azeotrope this node calls it. The route is documented - hydrogen and chlorine are combined in an HCl burner and the gas absorbed in deionised water, and the acid is also obtained by absorbing by-product hydrogen chloride. Not established: the 10-30 t of acid per tonne of polysilicon plant output.

metal.salt-brine.name: Rock salt and solar salt brine
metal.salt-brine.description: Two very different-looking things that are the same feedstock. Rock salt is a bed of halite pushed up by evaporation of a restricted sea and then mined; solar salt is the same chemistry done in the sun, in shallow evaporation ponds that turn a square mile of bay into a crystalliser. The chlor-alkali cell does not care which it gets: what matters is a saturated brine with the calcium and magnesium removed, because both precipitate as scale in the diaphragm cell and would otherwise carry oxygen into the chlorine.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: rock salt (halite) mined at Wieliczka, Michigan and along the saltbelt; solar salt evaporated in the San Francisco Bay and the Great Salt Lake

facts.label: Purity to the chlor-alkali cell
facts.value: brine made up to saturated, about 310 g/L NaCl before it enters the cell

facts.label: Per tonne of chlorine
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.1 t of NaCl, plus about 1 t of electrical energy

metal.salt-brine.note: Not established: the saturated-brine figure of about 310 g/L NaCl, the 1.0-1.1 t of NaCl per tonne of chlorine, and the calcium/magnesium scale argument, which no general reference states. What the references do support is that the cell runs on concentrated NaCl brine and that rock salt forms as evaporite beds from restricted seas.

metal.limestone.name: Limestone (CaCO3) quarry
metal.limestone.description: High-calcium limestone for the Solvay towers, the blast furnaces, the Bayer plant, the lead sinter and the lime kilns. Quarried by bench mining with a face shovel or a chain dragline, crushed, and graded; a blast furnace wants roughly a third of a tonne of limestone per tonne of hot metal. The same rock is the flux in the copper flash furnace, the causticisation reagent in alumina refining, and the neutraliser at the board fab.

facts.label: Use rate
facts.value: order 0.2-0.35 t per tonne of hot metal in the blast furnace

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: surface quarry, 5-15 m benches, crushed to 10-50 mm

children.name: Limestone quarry and crushing plant
children.description: A 5-15 m bench taken out of a 10-40 m face with a face shovel or a chain dragline, drilled and blasted where the rock is competent, then a primary jaw or gyratory crusher to 50-150 mm and a crushing and screening plant that produces three fractions: 0.5-5 cm for the sinter plant, 5-40 mm for the blast furnace and the kilns, and a fines fraction that goes back. A limestone quarry is one of the least complicated mines there is, which is why lime is cheap everywhere and why the Bayer process's caustic and lime costs are the alumina industry's real cost base.

facts.label: Product sizes
facts.value: 0.5-5 cm sinter feed, 5-40 mm furnace and kiln feed, plus fines

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 0.2-5 Mt/year for a chemical-grade supplier

children.note: Not established: the 5-15 m bench height, the 10-40 m face, the 50-150 mm primary product, the three product fractions and the 0.2-5 Mt/year output. No reference fetched describes limestone quarrying practice at this level of detail.

metal.limestone.note: Documented: limestone is mostly calcite and aragonite, and in the blast furnace it binds with silica and other impurities to remove them from the iron. Not established: the CaCO3 92-98% / SiO2 0.5-2% assay, the 0.2-0.35 t per tonne of hot metal consumption rate, and the bench and crushing detail.

metal.quartz.name: Natural vein quartz
metal.quartz.description: Vein and pegmatite quartz, of which Brazil's Minas Gerais was the world source for the resonator industry. In 1982 it had two jobs: the seed for hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz, and, in small volume, high-stability resonators for frequency standards where natural material genuinely beat synthetic on Q. A computer clock did not need that. The industrial silica sand and the silicon-grade quartzite elsewhere in this file are processed rocks; this is crystal-grade rock.

facts.label: Occurrence
facts.value: vein quartz in a granitic pegmatite or a hydrothermal vein

facts.label: Use
facts.value: resonator-grade seed and, for high-Q parts, natural crystal

metal.quartz.note: Not established: that Minas Gerais was the world source for the resonator industry in 1982, the seed-for-hydrothermal-growth use, or that natural crystal beat synthetic on Q for high-stability resonators.

metal.graphite.electrode.name: Graphite and carbon electrodes
metal.graphite.electrode.description: The EAF electrodes, the submerged arc furnace electrodes of the ferrosilicon, ferrochrome and ferromanganese industries, the aluminium pot anodes, the silicon furnace electrodes and the large carbon blocks of a blast furnace hearth all consume the same two feedstocks: calcined petroleum or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as the binder. A 'graphite' electrode is green-milled from petroleum coke, extruded, and baked above 2500 C; a 'carbon' electrode stops at 800-1200 C. Pitch coke dominates for the graphite grades because it gives the higher density and the lower ash.

facts.label: Graphite grade
facts.value: baked at 2500-3000 C, ash <1%, density ~2.2 g/cm3

facts.label: Carbon grade
facts.value: baked at 800-1200 C, ash 2-5%, density ~1.6-1.8 g/cm3

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 20-30% coal-tar pitch

facts.label: Diameters in 1982
facts.value: 75-350 mm for electrodes; 400-1000 mm for pot anodes and hearth blocks

metal.graphite.electrode.note: Pitch coke is the highest-grade carbon feedstock and is itself a coke-oven by-product; see metal.coke in this file for the oven that makes the tar.

metal.carbon.anode.name: Carbon anode for the Hall-Heroult cell
metal.carbon.anode.description: Calcined petroleum coke at 90-95% carbon, ground to 1-20 mm, mixed with 25-30% of crushed and baked coke returns and 25-30% coal-tar pitch as the binder, extruded through a die with a threaded stud on the end, and roasted at 1000-1100 C for 20-30 hours. The point of roasting rather than baking is to drive the volatiles out before the anode goes into the cell, because an anode that gases in the pot poisons the metal. Consumption is 0.45-0.55 t of anode per tonne of aluminium, and the anode is consumed continuously - which is what makes aluminium smelting a carbon business as much as an electrochemical one.

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 90-95% C, 1-20 mm, from petroleum coke

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 25-30% by mass of the green anode

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: 1000-1100 C for 20-30 h in a ring or tunnel kiln

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 0.45-0.55 t of anode per tonne of aluminium

facts.label: Anode effect
facts.value: the carbon dioxide from the anode that is not captured at the plant, plus the periodic anode effect, is the smelter's main CO2 and fluoride emission

metal.carbon.anode.note: The anode effect was not well understood until the 1980s-90s and was the subject of active investigation precisely in this period.

metal.cryolite.name: Cryolite (Na3AlF6), the electrolyte solvent
metal.cryolite.description: The white, insoluble, water-repellent mineral that makes aluminium electrolysis possible at all. Pure alumina melts at 2072 C; a bath of cryolite with excess aluminium fluoride and some calcium fluoride is liquid at 950-970 C, and the alumina dissolves in it at 6-10%. The other crucial property is that cryolite is not consumed stoichiometrically - it is a solvent - and only the fluorine lost as HF and in the fume has to be replaced. Correcting the brief: consumption was roughly 0.5-1.0 t of cryolite per tonne of aluminium in 1980s practice (theoretical about 0.5 t, higher in practice because of fluoride loss), not 'four tonnes of aluminium per tonne of cryolite'.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: Na3AlF6; natural cryolite is 3NaF.AlF3

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 1012 C pure; the bath runs at 950-970 C because of the excess AlF3 and CaF2

facts.label: Alumina solubility
facts.value: 6-10 wt% in the cryolite melt

facts.label: Bath composition
facts.value: cryolite 75-80%, excess AlF3 6-13%, CaF2 3-5%

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.5-1.0 t per tonne of aluminium

facts.label: Natural source
facts.value: Ivittuut, Greenland - the only commercial natural cryolite deposit - was still being mined in 1982 and closed in 1987; every other tonne was synthetic

metal.cryolite.note: Explicit correction of the 4 t Al per t cryolite figure in the brief: cryolite is a solvent, not a stoichiometric reactant, so consumption is roughly a tonne per tonne of metal, not a quarter of that. High confidence on the mechanism; medium on the exact consumption range, which varies with the fluorine recovery practice.

metal.fluorspar.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) ore
metal.fluorspar.description: Calcium fluoride rock, the only commercial source of fluorine. A 1982 hydrofluoric acid plant buys 97-98% acid made by treating acid-grade fluorspar (97%+ CaF2) with sulphuric acid in a kiln, and the acid then goes into the aluminium fluoride and cryolite that the Hall-Heroult bath needs and into the fluoride digestion that turns coltan into soluble tantalum fluoride. The ore is mined in open pits and underground, in hydrothermal veins in limestone and as replacement bodies in dolomite.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 60-95% CaF2 after flotation

facts.label: End use
facts.value: ~90% to aluminium smelting for cryolite and bath flux; the rest to HF and to steelmaking

children.name: Fluorite open-pit and underground mine
children.description: Fluorite fills the cavities and fracture zones of limestone, so it is mined either as a replacement body in a working limestone quarry or as a vein. Mexican fluorite was mined underground at Naica and in open pits in Chihuahua. (Not Naica's famous giant crystals: those are selenite gypsum, up to 11.4 m, in a cave in the mine's limestone host rock — not fluorite.) The South African deposits are in the carbonate sequences of the Transvaal Group, and the Chinese and Mongolian ones, which became dominant in the late 1980s, are in greisen and vein systems related to granite.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: epigenetic fill in limestone cavities, and veins in greisen

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit and underground, with flotation to 60-95% CaF2

children.note: Not established: the mine-level geography (Naica, Chihuahua, Transvaal Group) and the limestone-replacement versus greisen-vein settings as stated for these workings. The limestone-hosted vein occurrence and the South Africa/Mexico/China reserve pattern are as sourced.

metal.sulphuric-acid.name: Sulphuric acid, 93-99%, from smelter SO2
metal.sulphuric-acid.description: The most-produced inorganic chemical in the world, and about half to three fifths of it was made not from burning sulphur but from the offgas of the copper, zinc and lead smelters in this file. The plants are the same: gas cleaning, drying, 10-14% SO2, 400-450 C over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst, absorption in 98-99% acid in the first absorber, and then a second absorber with fresher acid - the double contact, double absorption process that was the industry standard by 1982. This node is the deliberate convergence point: the copper flash furnace, the zinc sinter plant, the lead sinter plant, the copper tankhouse and the zinc leach all feed or draw from the same acid plant.

facts.label: Inlet SO2
facts.value: 8-14% from a flash furnace, roaster or sinter plant

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: V2O5 on silica, 400-450 C

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: double contact / double absorption, the 1980s standard

facts.label: Acid per tonne
facts.value: roughly 3-6 t of 100% acid per tonne of copper

children.name: Where the smelter acid goes
children.description: Roughly half of world sulfuric acid production is made from smelter offgas. In 1982 the biggest single use was fertiliser: phosphoric acid from Florida apatite, then superphosphate. The second was metal refining - the copper tankhouse electrolyte, the zinc plant leach circuit and the iron and steel pickling line, all of which are in this tree. The third was hydrofluoric acid. So a great deal of the world's phosphate rock was fertilised with acid made from the sulphur in somebody else's copper ore.

facts.label: Global split
facts.value: ~50-60% of sulfuric acid capacity was smelter-based in the early 1980s

facts.label: End uses
facts.value: phosphoric acid and fertiliser, metal pickling, hydrofluoric acid, oil refining

metal.phosphate-ore.name: Apatite ore for phosphoric acid
metal.phosphate-ore.description: The Florida pebble phosphate - a marine sedimentary phosphorite of fossil bones and excreta - is the classic source, and it is the end consumer of most of the sulfuric acid made in the copper and zinc branches of this file. It is mined by dragline or bucket-wheel stripping of 5-15 m of overburden over a 3-6 m ore layer, then crushed and slurry-piped to a beneficiation plant. Almost no phosphate rock in 1982 came from a chemical process: the whole fertiliser industry downstream of the copper and zinc smelters is a sedimentary rock mined out of a swampy coastal plain.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 28-32% P2O5, often dolomitic in Florida

facts.label: Method
facts.value: strip mining with a dragline or bucket-wheel, 3-6 m of ore under 5-15 m of overburden

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: crushing to 2-3 cm, washing in a sluice, and gravity or flotation upgrading

metal.red-mud.name: Red mud (bauxite residue)
metal.red-mud.description: A caustic, red, kaolin-rich sludge, typically 2.5-6 mol/L free NaOH, containing essentially all the iron, titanium and silica from the ore. A large refinery produces 100-150 tonnes of it per tonne of alumina. In 1982 the industry standard for handling it was to build a dam and pump it in; the search for a use was real academic work with no commercial outcome. Successful commercial red-mud use at scale did not arrive until the 2000s and later, so nothing in a 1982 C64 contains it.

facts.label: Free NaOH
facts.value: 2.5-6 mol/L

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 100-150 t per tonne of Al2O3

facts.label: 1980s handling
facts.value: thickened to a dry-stack dam; clay-dry-lining of the dam floor became common in the 1990s-2000s

metal.bayer-liquor.name: Bayer liquor (pregnant sodium aluminate solution)
metal.bayer-liquor.description: The hot, caustic, green-black liquid at the heart of the Bayer process: bauxite digested in sodium hydroxide at 150-200 C goes into solution as sodium aluminate, NaAlO2 (hydrated: NaAl(OH)4), while the iron, titanium and most silica stay behind as red mud and are filtered off. Cooling the clarified liquor and seeding it with gibbsite crystals precipitates aluminium hydroxide, and the spent liquor is recycled to digestion. Recycling is what makes the liquor more than a solvent: gallium and vanadium build up in it to the point where they can be extracted profitably, which is why the Bayer process is the main source of gallium even though the yield is low.

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: Al2O3.2H2O + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + 3H2O; aluminium carried as Al(OH)4-

facts.label: Digestion
facts.value: 150-200 C in NaOH pressure vessels; gibbsitic ore digests low, diasporic ore needs 240-280 C

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: seeded with gibbsite crystals on cooling: 2H2O + NaAlO2 -> Al(OH)3 + NaOH; takes days unseeded

facts.label: Gallium
facts.value: builds up in recycled liquor with vanadium and is extracted upstream of precipitation; the rest reports to alumina and red mud

metal.bayer-liquor.note: Documented: the digestion and precipitation reactions, the seeding practice, and the gallium/vanadium accumulation in recycled liquor. Not established: liquor concentrations and residence times for any specific 1982 refinery. Gallium metal itself is unmodelled in this tree (no gallium node); the extraction route is recorded here so the branch is not lost.

metal.aluminium-hydroxide.name: Aluminium hydroxide (gibbsite precipitate)
metal.aluminium-hydroxide.description: The white crystalline precipitate seeded out of cooled Bayer liquor: Al(OH)3, mineralogically gibbsite with rarer bayerite, doyleite and nordstrandite polymorphs. It is the fork in the aluminium road: some 90% of it is calcined at about 1200 C to smelter-grade alumina, and the rest is sold as-is - as a flame-retardant filler in rubber and plastics, and as the feed for water-treatment chemicals such as aluminium sulfate and polyaluminium chloride. Like the alumina it becomes, it is amphoteric, dissolving in both acid and caustic.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: Al(OH)3; gibbsite is the Bayer precipitate polymorph

facts.label: Calcination
facts.value: 2Al(OH)3 -> Al2O3 + 3H2O at about 1200 C in rotary kilns or flash calciners; some 90% of gibbsite goes this way

facts.label: Other uses
facts.value: flame-retardant filler in rubber and plastics; feed for aluminium sulfate, PAC and sodium aluminate water-treatment chemicals

metal.aluminium-hydroxide.note: Documented: the polymorphs, the amphoteric chemistry, the calcination reaction and temperature, the 90% split to alumina, and the filler and water-chemical uses. Not established: which 1982 refineries sold hydrate versus calcining everything on site.

metal.alumina.name: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5% Al2O3
metal.alumina.description: A white, sandy, hygroscopic powder delivered to the smelter in railcars or 1-2 t bags. The contract is brutal: 99.5% Al2O3 minimum, loss on ignition below about 1%, total iron below 0.02%, because every gram of iron that reaches the cell ends up in the metal and the ingot stops being 99.7%. In 1982 this was a global commodity with about a dozen producers - Alcoa, Alcan, Kaiser, Norsk Hydro, Sumitomo, and the Australian and Jamaican national producers. This is the deliberate convergence point for the bauxite and the pot branch: both hang off it.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: free-flowing sandy powder, 0.05-0.5 mm, bulk density ~1 t/m3

facts.label: Physical
facts.value: hygroscopic - shipped and stored sealed, and preheated to avoid steam spalling in the pot feed

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~1.5-2 t bauxite -> 1 t alumina -> 0.50-0.52 t aluminium

metal.alumina.note: Documented: smelter-grade alumina is the feedstock for the Hall-Heroult cell, is distinguished from refractory and abrasive grades, and is a mixture of transition aluminas and alpha-alumina whose phase composition depends on the calcination conditions. Not established: the 99.5% Al2O3 minimum with Fe2O3 and SiO2 below 0.02% and LOI below 1%, the 0.05-0.5 mm particle size and 1 t/m3 bulk density, and the 1.5-2 t bauxite to 1 t alumina ratio.

metal.aluminum.ingot.name: Primary aluminium ingot, 99.7%
metal.aluminum.ingot.description: The metal itself, and the deliberate convergence point of the electrolysis branch and the rolling branch. Tapped from the pot every 24-48 hours, brought up to about 720 C, filtered to remove the entrained alumina and metal droplets, alloyed if the customer wants it, and cast. In 1982 the standard product was the 20-25 kg P1020 ingot, or the 500 kg or 1.5 t minimum-content ingot that newer smelters preferred, 99.70% minimum aluminium with iron and silicon the main impurities. Rolling ingots for the foil mills were a different shape entirely - see the foil branch.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.70% Al minimum (P1020 / grade A7)

facts.label: Impurities
facts.value: Fe 0.1-0.25%, Si 0.05-0.2%, plus Ga, Ti and Zn traces

facts.label: Ingot forms
facts.value: 20-25 kg stackable ingot, 500 kg minimum-content ingot, or 1.5 t

facts.label: Pour temperature
facts.value: about 710-730 C

metal.aluminum.foil.name: Aluminium foil, 6-25 um, for capacitors
metal.aluminum.foil.description: The C64's power supply is full of electrolytic capacitors, and every one of them is an aluminium foil sandwich: a thin cathode foil wound with a thicker anode foil and a paper separator soaked in electrolyte. Making 6 um foil is a genuinely hard rolling problem - at that gauge the metal is thinner than the oxide skin that forms on it, so the rolls and the housekeeping are the whole technology. This is a deliberate convergence node: the foil branch, the anode-foil etch branch and the rolling-mill branch all hang off it.

facts.label: Gauges
facts.value: 6-9 um cathode foil, 8-16 um anode foil

facts.label: Roll gauge count
facts.value: of the order of 20-30 um rolled per pass to reach foil

metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.name: Aluminium rolling oil and the degreaser
metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.description: Cold rolling of aluminium would tear without a lubricant: a water-in-oil emulsion or a neat mineral oil with fatty-acid esters, applied by nozzles at order 0.1-1 g/m2. The oil is what lets the gauge get down without the surface tearing, and it has to be removed afterwards - a few grams of oil left on capacitor foil ruin the capacitor, because the electrolyte chemistry and the oxide interface are that sensitive. Foil mills ran a dedicated degreasing line with naphtha or trichloroethane and a 200-300 C bake.

facts.label: Oil application
facts.value: order 0.1-1.0 g per m2 of strip

facts.label: Residual after degrease
facts.value: below about 50 mg/m2, lower for capacitor foil

facts.label: Degrease solvent
facts.value: naphtha, perchloroethylene or trichloroethane, plus a 200-300 C bake

metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.note: Solvent choice varied with local regulation; perchloroethylene was being phased out in Europe and North America through the 1980s. Medium confidence.

metal.aluminum.sheet.name: Aluminium sheet: the case and the shields
metal.aluminum.sheet.description: Two uses in a C64: the heat-sink and shield material, and the case itself. The Commodore breadbin case is an aluminium extrusion with a stove-enamel finish, and the internal shields and the modulator compartment are plain sheet. Cold-rolled 1050A or 3003 sheet at 0.3-1.5 mm goes into drawing and stamping; the anodising or powder coating is the plastics-and-paint agent's business, but the substrate starts here. Also the convergence point for the die-casting branch: a 1982 C64 has several kilograms of aluminium foundry alloy in its key plungers and the joystick and case-bracket castings.

facts.label: Alloys
facts.value: 1050A (pure, for foil and case), 3003 (Al-Mn, general sheet), 6063 (extrusion), A13 (Al-Si casting alloy, for die castings)

facts.label: Typical gauge
facts.value: 0.3-1.5 mm for a case or shield

metal.aluminum.sheet.note: Not established: that the breadbin case was an aluminium extrusion, which conflicts with the ABS case chain, and the 1050A/3003/6063/A13 assignments and 0.3-1.5 mm gauge for C64 parts. The alloy chemistries are as sourced.

metal.aluminum.extrusion.name: Aluminium extrusion: the case and the heat sinks
metal.aluminum.extrusion.description: A hot billet is forced through a steel die by a ram at 420-500 C, at 20-100 MN of pressure, at several metres a second, and the profile that comes out is straight and, if the die is good, dimensionally within a fraction of a millimetre. The Commodore case is a complicated extrusion: the cooling fins, the rail and the case walls are all one profile, and the visible finish is a consequence of the die geometry. The rectifier and regulator heat sinks are separate small extrusions or machined blocks.

facts.label: Extrusion pressure
facts.value: 20-100 MN, of order 500-1500 t of force

facts.label: Extrusion speed
facts.value: up to about 100 m/min for a light 6063 section

facts.label: Die material
facts.value: hot-work tool steel; 600-1000 roughing holes and 1000-1500 h of die life in order

facts.label: Case profile
facts.value: 6063 with a 0.2-0.4 mm wall and integral cooling fins

children.name: Hydraulic extrusion press, 500-2500 t
children.description: The industry standard was the 2300-2500 t class press with a 200-500 mm container, driven by a hydraulic intensifier that gave a hard step change in speed at the start of the stroke. A heated soak furnace beside the press holds the billets, a shear cuts them to length, and the runout bench stretches the profile while it is still hot. A C64 case would have been pressed at a Taiwanese or Hong Kong extrusion shop on a machine of exactly this size.

facts.label: Press size
facts.value: 2300-2500 t in the largest class, 500-1500 t for smaller sections

facts.label: Straightening
facts.value: in-line stretcher on the runout bench

children.name: The soak furnace and the billet's temperature history
children.description: Billet quality is set before the press ever sees it. The billets are heated in a gas- or oil-fired pit furnace to 420-500 C and held for 3-24 hours so that the temperature is uniform through the section, because a billet with a hot core and a cold skin extrudes with a surface tear and a soft interior. The furnace is a 3-5 m long box with a hot zone and a transition zone, and the entire extrusion industry's reputation for inconsistent profiles is mostly the reputation of its furnaces. A C64's case extrusion depended on the profile being within a fraction of a millimetre, because it had to fit a plastic moulding and a painted finish.

facts.label: Why so long
facts.value: a 25 t billet needs hours for the core to reach temperature

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: gas or oil fired pit furnace with hot and transition zones

children.note: Medium confidence; the soak practice is standard but the times depend entirely on the section size.

Not established: the 2300-2500 t and 500-1500 t press classes, the 200-500 mm container, the hydraulic intensifier, the 3-24 h soak at 420-500 C and the in-line stretcher. The extrusion reference reached in this pass is the general Extrusion article; there is no separate Wikipedia article on aluminium extrusion, so the specific press and soak figures have no encyclopaedic source.

children.name: Steel extrusion die and its forging
children.description: The die is a disc of hot-work tool steel with a cavity machined into it, and it has to be made before it can be used: drilled, rough-machined, heat-treated, then finish-machined and nitrided. A case profile takes a lot of steel and a lot of hours, which is why the extrusion industry is full of small specialist shops rather than a few giants. The same die steel family, SKD61 and H13, is the tooling steel of the plastics agent's injection-moulding branch.

facts.label: Die life
facts.value: order 1000-1500 h, then repair

facts.label: Steel per die
facts.value: 100-600 t, machined over days

children.note: Die lives vary enormously with profile complexity and alloy; medium confidence.

metal.copper.cathode.name: Electrolytic copper cathode, 99.99%
metal.copper.cathode.description: The end product of the mine-to-metal chain and the shape in which essentially all world copper trades. A flat plate grown on a stainless steel or copper starter sheet, with a characteristic slightly rough surface because too many nucleation sites make a soft, dull deposit. Cathode mass is 45-125 kg depending on the refinery. Weighed, sampled, stamped and shipped. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tankhouse branch, the foil branch and the wire branch.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99%, LME Grade A at 99.9935% minimum

facts.label: Typical impurities
facts.value: Fe 3-8 ppm, S 1-10 ppm, Pb 1-10 ppm, O 10-50 ppm

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 45-125 kg per plate

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: 40-60 g/L free Cu2+, 180-230 g/L free H2SO4, 10-25 ppm Fe/As/Bi

metal.copper.wire.name: Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings
metal.copper.wire.description: The switch-mode transformer in a C64's power supply - and any small mains-frequency transformer - is a coil of enamelled copper wire. The wire starts as 6-8 mm rod, is patented (heated to 200-350 C so the work-hardening from drawing anneals out), then drawn through a series of diamond dies to 0.15-0.5 mm, then enamelled and baked. 1982's magnet wire was overwhelmingly polyurethane enamel, sometimes with a nylon or polyester overcoat; polyurethane is the classic because it strips cleanly from the copper and does not need a flame to remove. This is a deliberate convergence node: the transformer winding, the ferrite core and the soldered joint all come off it.

facts.label: Gauge
facts.value: AWG 24-34 (0.5 down to 0.2 mm) for a small transformer; AWG 38-42 for fine coils

facts.label: Enamel
facts.value: polyurethane, thermal class 130-155, sometimes with a polyester or nylon overcoat

facts.label: Film build
facts.value: 15-40 um total for a class 155 wire

metal.copper.foil.name: Copper foil: 35 um PCB and 6-18 um capacitor foil
metal.copper.foil.description: Two completely different foils with the same name, and this is a deliberate convergence node. The PCB foil is 35 um copper (70 um on very old boards) electrolytically deposited or rolled; the C64's board is single-sided, so it is one sheet of foil laminated to 1.6 mm FR-4. The capacitor foil is electro-deposited drum foil, deposited 6-18 um onto a rotating stainless or titanium drum from a copper sulphate bath, stripped and wound, then roughened again for etching just like aluminium foil.

facts.label: PCB foil
facts.value: 35 um (2 oz/sq ft) standard, 70 um on very early boards

facts.label: Capacitor foil
facts.value: 6-18 um electro-deposited, with base copper under the etched layer

facts.label: Thickness tolerance
facts.value: +/-10% on 35 um foil

metal.anode-slime.name: Anode slime: the real reason to smelt copper
metal.anode-slime.description: The sludge on the tankhouse cell floor, 5-20 kg per tonne of copper refined, containing gold, silver, platinum, palladium, selenium and tellurium. It is dried and shipped to precious-metals refineries, where the gold is separated by cupellation, the selenium by roasting to SeO2 and volatilising, and the platinum group metals by solvent extraction and precipitation. By 1982 the anode slime was typically worth more per tonne than the copper in the anode, and a copper mine with good gold credits could be a gold mine that happened to have copper in it. This is a deliberate convergence node: the copper, gold and silver branches all meet in it.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 5-20 kg of dry slime per tonne of copper

facts.label: Value in 1982
facts.value: typically 30-100% of the value of the contained copper

metal.tin.ingot.name: Refined tin ingot or tin powder, 99.9-99.97%
metal.tin.ingot.description: Shipped as a 25-50 kg or 250 kg ingot at 99.9-99.97%, or - for the electronics industry - atomised into a fine powder. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tin smelting branch and the solder branch: the solder manufacturer needs the ingot, and the solder-paste manufacturer needs the powder. Iron is the impurity that matters, because iron is a solder poison that wets badly and raises the liquidus.

facts.label: Powder
facts.value: atomised, 10-25 um, for solder paste and for making solder alloy powder

facts.label: 1982 context
facts.value: most electronics soldering was still a hand or wave-solder pot of solid-core wire; paste was a minority

metal.tin.plating.name: Tin plating of steel and of copper alloys
metal.tin.plating.description: Tinplate - a 1.1-11.2 g/m2 tin coating on 0.15-0.3 mm of steel - is made by electrolytic tinning of a continuous steel strip on a horizontal passivating line: the strip is degreased, pickled in acid, tinned in a sulphate or fluoroborate bath, rinsed, and then either passivated in chromic acid (food can) or - through the 1980s - given an electrolytic chromate or tin-oxide passivation to stop the tin growing dendrites during storage. Food can was the dominant market by mass. A C64 uses tinplate only incidentally, in a switch body or a shield; tin plating of copper-alloy contacts uses a different chemistry altogether and is the node that matters for the machine.

facts.label: Coating mass
facts.value: 1.1-11.2 g/m2 (2.8-28.2 g per 100 cm2); 5-6 g/m2 typical for electronics sheet

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: chromic acid for food can, or an electrolytic chromate or oxide passivation in the 1980s

facts.label: Tinplate market
facts.value: food can was about 90% of production

children.name: Tin plating of copper-alloy contacts
children.description: Not tinplate on steel, but tin on brass or phosphor bronze - the plating on the contacts of a C64 switch or a keyboard connector. The 1980s chemistry was an acid stannate or an alkaline stannate bath: SnSO4 with sulfuric acid, or sodium stannate with caustic soda and a puller such as sodium gluconate. Tin is on a connector contact because it forms a soft, low-resistance, non-tarnishing intermetallic with the copper. The reason it fails is the tin whisker - a single-crystal filament of tin that grows out of the plating under compressive stress in humid storage and can bridge a 0.1 mm gap. Tin whiskers were the reliability nemesis of exactly this kind of contact.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: acid sulphate (SnSO4/H2SO4) or alkaline stannate (Na2SnO3/NaOH)

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: 2-5 um of tin on a Cu-Sn alloy or brass

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: tin whisker growth, and on tin-plated copper under high stress, copper-tin intermetallic embrittlement

children.note: The specific plating system used on Commodore's connectors is not something I can confirm; both chemistries were in use in 1982. Medium confidence.

metal.lead.ingot.name: Refined lead ingot, 99.99%
metal.lead.ingot.description: Cast into 25 kg pigs or into 500 kg slabs. About two thirds of all the lead refined in the world was never made into a product in the refinery - it went straight into an alloy, most of it lead-acid battery plate and cable sheath. The solder industry took a small fraction, on the order of five to ten percent, and in 1982 that fraction was the entire basis of the electronics solder business. This is a deliberate convergence node: the blast furnace branch, the Parkes desilverisation branch and the solder branch all meet here.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) standard; 99.999% 'five nines' was available for special applications

facts.label: End use split
facts.value: batteries about 60%, cable sheath about 15%, solder about 5-10%

metal.solder.wire.name: 63/37 solder wire with a rosin core
metal.solder.wire.description: The wire that went through a C64 assembly line: a solid 63/37 core inside a flux core inside a tin-lead sheath, made by the cored-wire method and drawn on the same kind of multiwire machine the copper industry uses, in a smaller and more delicate setup. This is a deliberate convergence node: the solder alloy branch, the rosin branch and the wave-solder branch all meet here, and it is the single most identifiable material in the whole tree - it is why the C64 is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

facts.label: Gauge
facts.value: 0.5-0.8 mm for through-hole boards; 0.3 mm for fine work

facts.label: Flux core
facts.value: 10-25% of the diameter by volume

facts.label: Spool
facts.value: 100 g to 2 kg retail, 5-10 kg industrial spools for wave solder

facts.label: Consumption in a C64
facts.value: roughly 3500 through-hole joints at about 30 mg each, so order 100 g per machine

metal.zinc.ingot.name: Special high grade zinc ingot, 99.995%
metal.zinc.ingot.description: Twenty-five kilogram ingots, or the 500 kg minimum-content ingot that the bigger plants preferred by 1982. Special high grade at 99.995% was the grade specified by the galvanising industry and by die-casters, because both are very sensitive to lead, cadmium and iron. Two thirds of world zinc goes into galvanising and roughly a sixth into die casting. The four markets below are the whole of the demand: galvanising, die casting, electroplating with a chromate passivate, and brass. An ingot that misses any of the four impurity limits is unsellable, which is why the smelter spends its margin on the assay rather than on the metal.

facts.label: End use
facts.value: ~65% galvanising, ~15-20% die casting, ~10% brass, rest chemicals

metal.zinc.electrowinning.name: Electrowinning of zinc on aluminium cathodes
metal.zinc.electrowinning.description: Zinc is one of the few metals won by electrolysis out of an aqueous solution at industrial scale. The reason is that zinc is more negative than hydrogen and would just deposit hydrogen from water if it were not for the high hydrogen overvoltage on aluminium; each cathode is an aluminium plate of 1-2 m2 and 10-25 mm thick, and the scraper at the top of the cycle knocks off a 5-25 kg slab. The slabs are melted in a small induction furnace and cast into 25 kg ingots at 99.995%. The energy is 3,000-3,500 kWh per tonne of zinc - high, but the purity and the by-product recovery make the route worth it for ores that cannot be smelted. This is the convergence point of the roast, leach, purification and ingot branches.

facts.label: Current density
facts.value: 500-1200 A/m2 of cathode

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: 1-2 m2 of aluminium plate, 10-25 mm thick

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 24-72 h, then strip; plates weigh 5-25 kg of zinc each

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 3000-3500 kWh per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.992-99.995% zinc, cast into 25 kg ingots

metal.zinc.electrowinning.note: The zinc-iron plant was the dominant new-build technology through the 1980s; the Imperial Smelting zinc-iron process and the roast-leach-electrowin are the same family.

children.name: Lead-silver anode in the tankhouse
children.description: The insoluble anode is a lead alloy - 99% Pb with 0.5-1% Ag, cast as 10-40 mm thick plates - which works because when it does corrode slowly, the lead dioxide layer that forms is a perfectly good anode surface. Silver is added because it slows the corrosion. So the zinc tankhouse is structurally a lead operation: it consumes lead anodes at a rate of a few kilograms per tonne of zinc, which is one of the more elegant hidden cross-links between the lead and zinc branches in this file.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 2-5 kg of lead alloy anode per tonne of zinc

children.name: The single-deck electrolysis cell
children.description: The 1980s zinc tankhouse cell was a plain open-top concrete or rubber-lined steel box, 3-6 m long, 1.5-2.5 m wide, 2-3 m deep, with an aluminium cathode every 15-25 mm and a lead anode between them. The electrolyte is fed in at one end and pulled out at the other; the plates go in, run for 24-72 hours, come out, get scraped, and go to the melting furnace. A modern plant with 300,000-400,000 m2 of cathode area is a building the size of a football pitch. This is one of the least mechanised and most manually-intensive electrolysis plants in the industry, because the plate handling has never lent itself to automation.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: 3-6 m long, 1.5-2.5 m wide, 2-3 m deep, 2-5 V

facts.label: Electrode pitch
facts.value: 15-25 mm between an anode and a cathode

children.note: Medium confidence; the cell layout is standard but varies between plants.

metal.sodium-dichromate.name: Sodium dichromate (Na2Cr2O7)
metal.sodium-dichromate.description: The bright-orange salt through which virtually all chromium ore passes: chromite is roasted with soda ash at order 1000 C in air to water-soluble sodium chromate, leached in hot water, and acidified with sulfuric acid (or carbon dioxide) to the dichromate, which is crystallised as the dihydrate. Virtually every chromium compound and material starts here - the chromic acid of the hard-chrome plating bath, the dichromate of the chromate conversion coating, leather tanning, pigments. Like all hexavalent chromium compounds it is carcinogenic, which is why the refineries that make it work under stringent effluent rules.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: Na2Cr2O7, handled as the dihydrate Na2Cr2O7.2H2O; molar mass 262 g/mol anhydrous

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 2Cr2O3 + 4Na2CO3 + 3O2 -> 4Na2CrO4 + 4CO2 at order 1000 C in air

facts.label: Acidification
facts.value: 2Na2CrO4 + H2SO4 -> Na2Cr2O7 + Na2SO4 + H2O; crystallised at 30-35 C

facts.label: Solubility
facts.value: 73 g/100 mL at 25 C, about twenty times the potassium salt - the reason industry prefers it

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: hexavalent chromium: carcinogenic and corrosive; refinery effluent reduced back to Cr(III) before discharge

metal.sodium-dichromate.note: Documented: the roast and acidification reactions, the dihydrate handling, the solubility, and the central-intermediate role. Roast temperature varies with ore and furnace practice; the sibling electrolytic-chromium node in this file records 500-700 C for its soda-ash roast, a lower-temperature variant of the same chemistry. Not established: annual tonnages for any single 1982 refinery.

metal.chromate-passivation.name: Chromate conversion coating
metal.chromate-passivation.description: A nitric acid or chromic acid bath - most often a sodium dichromate bath in 1982 - converts a zinc, tin or cadmium surface to a chromium oxide-hydroxide film a few hundred nanometres thick. Yellow is dichromate, olive is chromic acid, and the black 'iridium' used on some zinc die castings is a different chromate chemistry altogether. This is where the electronics industry met hexavalent chromium: not only in the plating baths but on every chromate-passivated steel part, on every tin-plated part that went through a passivation tank, and in the anode foil formation treatment. It is the reason the OSHA hexavalent chromium standard, published in 1971, was one of the first such rules in the United States, and it is a deliberate convergence point of the zinc, tin, aluminium-foil and chromium branches.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: sodium dichromate plus nitric acid, 5-30 s at room temperature

facts.label: Film
facts.value: ~0.1-0.5 um of mixed chromium oxide-hydroxide

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) in the film, which is why the dried chromate coating itself is not toxic

facts.label: Applicable to
facts.value: zinc electroplate, tinplate, cadmium, and aluminium anode foil formation treatments

metal.chromate-passivation.note: This node is the third of chromium's three markets - ferrochrome into stainless steel, electrolytic metal into the plating bath, and chromate conversion on the plated surface - so it is deliberately given two parents, the chromium branch and metal.zinc.electroplate.

metal.hex-chrome-plating.name: Hexavalent chromium electroplating bath
metal.hex-chrome-plating.description: The classic chromiumic acid bath: CrO3 at 50-250 g/L in dilute sulfuric acid at 100-250 g/L, run at 45-60 C, 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2, with a lead-lead dioxide anode. A special steel anode is used and the bath is extremely hard to waste-treat: the chromium has to get from Cr(VI) down to Cr(III) before it can be precipitated. Cr(VI) is acutely and cumulatively toxic with a demonstrated carcinogenicity, and the 1971 OSHA standard for airborne hexavalent chromium was one of the first such rules in the United States. A C64's hard chrome on the switch contacts, the case hinges and the shield-contact points would have been plated in a plant subject to it.

facts.label: Voltage and current
facts.value: 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2 for hard chrome

facts.label: Anode
facts.value: lead-lead dioxide; 5-15% Sn-Pb alloy

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: an automatic catalyst based on sulphate, in the 1980s

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: OSHA standard on airborne hexavalent chromium, 1971

metal.hex-chrome-plating.note: Hexavalent chromium plating is essentially unchanged since the 1980s except for the trivalent and hex-free alternatives developed after 2000; high confidence on the chemistry.

metal.nickel.ingot.name: Electrolytic or cathode nickel, 99.9%
metal.nickel.ingot.description: Nickel metal arrives at the user as a cathode or a briquette: 99.8% for ferronickel-grade stainless, 99.9% for stainless and for plating. For a plating line the metal arrives as matte or as a soluble anode, but in 1982 the majority of nickel plating anodes were still the insoluble carbon steel anode, with the nickel actually coming from the electrolyte as nickel sulphate made from nickel oxide. This is a deliberate convergence node: the laterite branch, the Mond branch, the plating branch and the stainless branch all meet here.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.8% cathode, 99.9% for plating and stainless

facts.label: 1982 supply route
facts.value: mostly ferronickel-derived; electrolytic and carbonyl nickel were the premium products

metal.stainless.304.name: AISI 304 and 430 stainless steel
metal.stainless.304.description: The iron-chromium-nickel family, and a deliberate convergence point of three branches in this file. 304 is 18% chromium, 8% nickel, the balance iron - austenitic, non-magnetic, non-hardenable. 430 is 16-18% chromium with no nickel - ferritic, magnetic, and cheap. Both are made the way any steel is made: blast furnace for the iron, then a stainless steelmaking step that decarburises in an argon-oxygen decarburisation vessel, and the key is that the melt must not pick up more than about 0.05% carbon or the chromium goes into carbide and the metal loses its corrosion resistance. Stainless is the audio jack shell, the shield cans, some of the chassis and any fastener. Its cost is driven almost entirely by the chromium and the nickel, which is why the nickel price crash of 1982-83 directly cheapened stainless.

facts.value: 18% Cr, 8% Ni, C below 0.08%, austenitic
16-18% Cr, C below 0.12%, ferritic, magnetic

facts.label: Decarburisation
facts.value: AOD or VOD down to 0.02-0.05% C

facts.label: Nickel share of cost
facts.value: 8% of 304 by mass but roughly half the alloy cost

facts.label: 1982 supply note
facts.value: a lot of consumer-electronics 'stainless' was actually nickel-chromium plated or tin-plated mild steel

metal.stainless.304.note: The point about plated versus solid stainless is a genuine and important ambiguity for a consumer case: both were used in 1982 consumer goods and I cannot tell which is in a specific C64 without the part.

children.name: Where a 1982 C64's stainless actually is
children.description: Not much: the outer shell of the composite or RCA connector, the shield cans over the analogue sections, some of the tuner and modulator housings, the hinge hardware, and any stainless fastener. In practice much of what looks like stainless in 1982 consumer electronics was nickel-chrome electroplated or tin-plated mild steel, because solid 304 in a thin stamping cost several times what a plating operation cost. The distinction matters and cannot be settled without the part.

facts.label: Mass in a C64
facts.value: order 50-200 g of solid stainless at most

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: nickel-chrome or tin-plated mild steel sheet, which looks identical from outside

children.note: Low confidence on which specific Commodore parts are solid stainless versus plated; this needs the actual hardware or the parts drawings.

metal.ferrochrome.name: High-carbon ferrochrome, 60-70% Cr
metal.ferrochrome.description: Chromite ore and coke are charged into a submerged arc furnace at 1400-1600 C with a chromite self-fluxing slag, and the result is an alloy of 60-70% chromium, 1-3% silicon and 5-8% carbon. It consumes about 500-700 kWh per tonne of ferrochrome - a fifth of aluminium's energy per tonne but on a much smaller tonnage. In the 1980s the industry was the classic vertically integrated single-industry town: the chromite mine, the power station with its 400 MW supply contract, and the smelter were all owned by the same company in the same town. The 1982-85 US and European voluntary export restraints on ferrochrome were aimed squarely at the market power of one country, and it is why ferrochrome is one of the very few metals where the 1982 price environment is a real story.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-105 MVA, three electrodes, 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 60-70% Cr, 1-3% Si, 5-8% C, balance iron

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 500-700 kWh per tonne of ferrochrome

facts.label: 1982-85 trade measure
facts.value: the United States and the European Community imposed voluntary export restraints on ferrochrome

metal.ferrochrome.note: Explicit correction of the brief's framing of chromium: the chromite-to-ferrochrome branch is dominated by South Africa, not by any American or European mine, and the 1982-85 export restraint is the period's defining event in it.

metal.ferromanganese.name: High-carbon ferromanganese, Mn 65-80%, C 6-8%
metal.ferromanganese.description: Made in a submerged arc furnace, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, at 1400-1600 C with the electrode tips submerged in the slag. The charge is sintered manganese ore, coke, limestone and often a good deal of iron ore, because the aim is an alloy of about 70% manganese at 6-8% carbon, and manganese is expensive enough that the industry buys more ore than stoichiometry requires in order to reach the assay. The manganese comes out as a carbide, Mn7C3, not as the metal, which is why the alloy has a carbon content at all. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: high-carbon ferromanganese is 6-8% C, not 13-15%; medium-carbon is 1-4% and low-carbon is under 0.5%, so 13-15% is not a real grade.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Medium and low carbon
facts.value: C 1-4% and C below 0.5%

facts.label: Phase
facts.value: manganese is present as carbide, mostly Mn7C3

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.5 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel made

metal.ferromanganese.note: Correction to the brief: 6-8% C for high-carbon ferromanganese, not 13-15%. Confidence high on the grades; the furnace size range is a class figure.

children.name: Why a ferroalloy smelter is built beside its power station
children.description: A 100 MVA submerged arc furnace draws about 80-90 MW continuously and cannot be stopped without destroying the furnace. So it needs a long-term supply contract and, in most cases, its own generating plant or a dedicated hydro or coal share. In the 1980s several ferroalloy industries - Norway's ferrochrome and ferrosilicon, South Africa's ferrochrome, Norway and Quebec's ferrosilicon - were built around cheap hydropower, and the industry's geography is essentially a map of where the cheap electricity was. It is the same fact as the aluminium smelter's, and the reason the same two or three countries dominated both.

facts.label: Furnace load
facts.value: 80-90 MW continuous for a 100 MVA unit

facts.label: Energy per tonne
facts.value: 3,000-6,000 kWh for ferromanganese; 8,000-11,000 for ferrosilicon; 500-700 for ferrochrome

children.note: The energy figures are consistent across the ferroalloy literature; medium confidence on the exact values by product.

metal.manganese.ore.name: Pyrolusite and manganiferous ore, 25-50% Mn
metal.manganese.ore.description: Manganese ore is almost never a clean manganese mineral. The Groote Eylandt and South African supergene ores are a hard, black, sooty mass of MnO2 cryptocrystalline material - wad and psilomelane - interbedded with iron formation. Grade is 25-50% Mn, and low-grade ore needs beneficiation: the South African ores were washed and jigged to reject the iron, and Groote Eylandt is washed in a scrubber and on a sluice. Silica and phosphorus are the two impurities that destroy value. This is a convergence node: the ferromanganese furnace, the ferrite branch's manganese carbonate and the steel deoxidiser all hang off it.

facts.label: Forms
facts.value: hard lumps (metallurgical), fines, sinter feed, and nodule fines

facts.label: Supply 1982
facts.value: South Africa and Australia were the dominant sources; the Groote Eylandt mine had been shipping since 1969

children.name: Supergene manganese mining in the Kalahari
children.description: The Transvaal and the northern Cape were the world's largest producers in 1982 by a wide margin, and the operation was surface mining on a 5-20 m ore layer over a 100 m thick band of black manganese-bearing sandstone. Drag hoists, belt conveyors, and a scrubber-and-jig beneficiation plant, then a sinter belt. The ore is a black, hard, siliceous rock and it is dug out of a 30 m face.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit, shovel and dragline, 5-20 m ore benches

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: scrub and jig to reject iron; 30-40% Mn product

children.note: The Kalahari field was opened in the 1970s and by 1982 was the dominant world source of metallurgical manganese ore; medium confidence on bench details.

metal.chromite.name: Chromite ore (FeCr2O4), 38-46% Cr2O3
metal.chromite.description: A hard, black, opaque spinel - FeO plus chromium oxide in a cubic lattice - that occurs not as veins but as layer after layer in the lower part of the Bushveld Complex and the Transvaal Group. It is unusually resistant to both chemical attack and heat, which is why chromite is also found in beach placer sands in Oregon and California, and it is effectively the only chromium ore of commercial scale. The Bushveld chromite pits run 200 m deep on a 1-6 m seam, which is one of the more extreme geometries in mining. This is a convergence node for the ferrochrome furnace, the AOD vessel and the chromium metal plant.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 38-46% Cr2O3 for smelter-grade chromite

facts.label: Occurrence
facts.value: layered in the Lower Zone of the Bushveld Complex and the Transvaal Group

facts.label: Other sources
facts.value: Kemi in Finland, the Appalachian and Oregon beach sands, Kazakhstan and Zimbabwe

children.name: Layer-seam chromite open pit, 200 m deep
children.description: The Bushveld chromite mines are among the deepest and most geometrically awkward open pits in the world. A 1-6 m chromitite layer is covered by 100-200 m of layered norite, and the pit must be advanced strip by strip along the seam, so the benches are narrow and the truck travels a long way for every tonne. The waste is platinum-group ore, so the chromite mines and the platinum mines are the same mines, and their combined revenue is what made the region what it is. The ore is crushed to about 100 mm and shipped to a smelter, sometimes 400 km away.

facts.label: Seam thickness
facts.value: 0.5-6 m chromitite layer

facts.label: Cover
facts.value: 100-200 m of layered norite and pyroxenite

facts.label: Co-product
facts.value: the waste rock is platinum-group ore

children.note: Documented: chromite forms in layered intrusions as layers from 1 cm to 1 m thick, laterally up to 70 km, and the Bushveld is the type example with chromitite layers and PGM reefs. Not established: the 0.5-6 m seam, the 100-200 m norite cover, the 150-300 m pit depth, the crushing to about 100 mm and the 400 km haul - so the claim that these are among the deepest and most awkward open pits in the world is unsupported.

metal.chromium.aod.name: Argon-oxygen decarburisation and the stainless vessel
metal.chromium.aod.description: The step that makes stainless steel possible. A 300-450 tonne ladle is fitted with a lance that injects a mixture of argon and oxygen under the steel surface. The argon stirs the melt and dilutes the carbon, the oxygen burns carbon to carbon monoxide, and because the gas is argon rather than air the melt does not pick up nitrogen - and nitrogen is exactly what stops 304 from being fully austenitic. At the end the gas is switched to pure oxygen and then back to argon to dilute the carbon without oxidising the chromium. The whole cycle takes 40-90 minutes and takes carbon from about 0.6% down to 0.03%, and it is why a stainless melt shop looks like nothing else in the steel industry. A deliberate convergence point of the chromium, nickel, ferrochrome and steel branches.

facts.label: Ladle
facts.value: 300-450 t, with a submerged lance

facts.label: Gas
facts.value: ~78% Ar / 22% O2 initially, rising to pure O2, then back to Ar

facts.label: Chromium loss
facts.value: some chromia goes to the bath, recovered from ferrochrome dust

children.name: Where the chromium ends up in a 1982 C64
children.description: AISI 304 in the audio jack shell, the shield cans and any stainless fastener or bracket; 430 where a magnetic ferritic grade was wanted. Chromium at 18% is above the roughly 11% needed for the surface to passivate, which is the whole trick: chromium forms a self-healing chromium oxide film about 2 nm thick, and that film is why stainless does not corrode. The passivation step in nitric acid is what removes the free iron that welding and machining leave on the surface, and without it the stainless rusts.

facts.label: Cr in 304
facts.value: 18%, well above the ~11% passivation threshold

facts.label: Passive film
facts.value: ~1-5 nm of chromium(III) oxide

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: 20-30% nitric acid, room temperature or 50 C, 30 min

children.note: The passivation chemistry is standard; whether Commodore's specific parts were passivated in manufacture is medium confidence.

children.name: The AOD lance and its tuyere block
children.description: The lance is a 10-25 cm carbon-molybdenum or refractory tube lowered into the metal on a mast, and it carries both the argon and the oxygen. Around it sits a refractory tuyere block in the ladle lining with a single small hole through which the gas is injected into the melt, so the gas is introduced a few hundred millimetres below the surface and the stirring is far more effective than a surface lance. The lance itself is a consumable: the oxygen attacks the tip, and a lance lasts one heat or a few hours, so there is a pile of spent lances outside every AOD vessel.

facts.label: Lance
facts.value: 10-25 cm diameter, carbon-molybdenum, a consumable

facts.label: Injection depth
facts.value: 200-500 mm below the metal surface

facts.label: Argon flow
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 Nm3 per minute per tonne of steel

children.note: Medium confidence; the lance geometry and injection depth are standard practice.

metal.chromium.metal.name: Electrolytic chromium metal from chrome alum
metal.chromium.metal.description: Pure chromium metal - for the chromium plating chemistry and for chromium sputtering targets - is made the opposite way to ferrochrome: hydrometallurgically. Chromite is roasted with soda ash to a water-soluble sodium chromate, the chromate is leached, the hexavalent chromium is reduced to trivalent in an acid solution, and the metal is electrowon onto a lead cathode to 99.9%. It is a short, small industry - a few thousand tonnes a year of a metal worth a great deal. The chrome alum the world consumed came largely from chemical processing plants, and the sulphur dioxide from the roast was a nuisance that pre-1950 plants simply released. The same hydrometallurgical route also produced the sodium chromate that went into the chromate conversion coatings of the zinc and tin plating branches.

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 500-700 C with soda ash, to water-soluble sodium chromate

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: sodium metabisulphite to Cr(III) as chrome alum

facts.label: Electrowinning
facts.value: lead cathode, low voltage, to 99.9% Cr

metal.chromium.metal.note: The hydrometallurgical chromium route is well documented; medium confidence on the exact 1982 process parameters.

children.name: Chromium electrowinning cell and the diaphragm
children.description: Chromium is electrowon from a trivalent chromium sulphate solution at 5-8 V with a lead or lead-alloy cathode, in cells separated by a diaphragm - traditionally asbestos cloth, later a synthetic fibre - because the anodic chlorine would otherwise oxidise the trivalent chromium back and the two would meet and precipitate. The product is 99.9% chromium at 80-90% current efficiency. The cell room is the most noxious part of the whole chromium industry: hexavalent chromium in the feed, acidic mist, and an operator who must be in a respirator.

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: lead or lead alloy

facts.label: Diaphragm
facts.value: asbestos cloth, later synthetic fibre

children.note: Low confidence on the cellroom details; this part of the industry is poorly documented outside the chrome plating literature, where the figures for chromium metal electrowinning are not commonly given.

metal.cassiterite.name: Cassiterite concentrate (SnO2)
metal.cassiterite.description: Cassiterite is a very heavy, very hard, brown-to-black mineral - the specific gravity of 7 makes gravity separation unusually effective on it, which is why tin mining has always had a placer tradition. The concentrates bought by an smelter in 1982 came from four very different operations: alluvial and offshore dredging in Malaysia and Indonesia, hard-rock lodes in the Bolivian and Brazilian Precambrian shields, hard-rock in Cornwall and the Pan, and shallow residual deposits in Thailand and Nigeria. Concentrates assayed 40-80% Sn with arsenic, iron, tungsten and fluorine as the problem impurities - fluorine in particular is the reason the Bolivian smelter needed a roast.

facts.label: Smelting route
facts.value: 70% of world tin was smelted in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Bolivia; China emerged in the 1990s

facts.label: Problem impurities
facts.value: As, Fe, W, and F (fluorine in Bolivian concentrates)

metal.galena.name: Galena (PbS) concentrate
metal.galena.description: Galena is cubic, bright grey when fresh and dull grey when oxidised, extremely heavy at 7.6 g/cm3, and it is one of the few common ores that a prospector could identify by eye. The great mining districts in 1982 were the Tri-State district of Missouri, Oklahoma and Kansas (which supplied most of the United States' lead and is a fossil limestone-hosted deposit), the Broken Hill and Mount Isa districts of Australia, Cerro de Pasco and Huancavelica in Peru, and the Iberian and Atlas belts. Concentrates assay 40-75% Pb and are always accompanied by enough silver and zinc to make a good deal of the mine's revenue.

facts.label: Concentrate assay
facts.value: 40-75% Pb, typically 0.5-3% Ag, 2-8% Zn

facts.label: Host
facts.value: carbonate-hosted replacement bodies (Tri-State) and metamorphosed massive sulphide (Broken Hill)

children.name: Underground lead-zinc mine
children.description: The Tri-State district's galena bodies sit as veins and bedding replacements in Mississippian limestone only a few metres thick, and they were worked by room-and-pillar mining - essentially taking the limestone out and leaving the lead in place, because the ore grade at 3-6% Pb did not pay for selective mining. The mineral was hand-picked off the back of the working face and off the cars. This is a soft-rock, shallow, cheap mining operation, and its day had largely gone by 1982 as the deeper and lower-grade Missouri deposits took over.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: room-and-pillar in limestone, ore bodies 3-15 m thick

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 3-6% Pb, and a lot of hand sorting

children.note: Documented: galena was a major mineral of the Tri-State district around Joplin, and occurs in low-temperature lead-zinc deposits within limestone beds. Not established: the room-and-pillar mining method, the 3-15 m ore bodies, the 3-6% Pb grade and the extent of hand sorting; none of these appear in the galena or lead smelting references.

metal.sphalerite.name: Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate, 50-60% Zn
metal.sphalerite.description: Sphalerite is one of the few ores that is not visually recognisable: it is a black to honey-brown cubic crystal whose colour depends on the iron substituting in the lattice, so the industry grades it in grades of iron - a 4% iron concentrate looks black and a 12% iron concentrate looks ruby red-brown. Concentration is by flotation with an amine or xanthate collector. The great districts were the Red Dog and the Sullivan mine in British Columbia, Broken Hill, the Cerro Rico of Potosi, the Rammelsberg of Goslar, and the Appalachian and Midwestern US zinc districts such as the Bartlesville and the Tennessee mines.

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: usually underground room-and-pillar or long-hole stoping in a stratiform or replacement body

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: differential flotation or bulk float with amine collectors

children.name: Underground zinc-lead mine
children.description: The Red Dog and Sullivan type deposit: a massive sulphide body in a sedimentary basin, mined underground from a ramp or a shaft, with the ore hoisted in a friction hoist or a skip, and the mill right at the portal. Broken Hill's Broken Hill Proprietary was the other archetype, an open pit above a very large primary orebody that was mined for sixty years. Where the zinc and lead are in separate veins, gravity and flotation split them: galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 do separate well on a dense-medium separator.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: underground room-and-pillar or long-hole stoping; open pit for large primary bodies

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: dense-media / differential gravity for galena vs sphalerite, then flotation

children.note: Documented: roughly half the world's sphalerite lead and zinc comes from sediment-hosted massive sulphide deposits - stratiform Pb-Zn sulphides hosted by shales, carbonates and siltstones - with combined grades typically 10-20%, and Red Dog, Sullivan, Mount Isa and Broken Hill are the named mines. Not established: galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 specific gravity, the dense-media or differential gravity split between them, and the friction-hoist and mill-at-the-portal detail.

metal.nickel.laterite.name: Nickel laterite (garnierite ore)
metal.nickel.laterite.description: A soft, earthy, red-brown clay-and-laterite ore, really a weathering product of ultramafic rock: olivine and pyroxene in a serpentinised peridotite are altered from scratch, and nickel substitutes for magnesium in the clay lattice, giving garnierite. There is no nickel mineral to concentrate; the whole ore body is the ore. The great deposits in 1982 were the Cuban Moa and Nicaro operations - where the ore was shipped to the United States and Japan for the nickel limit of the United States Defense Production Act of 1981 made government stockpiling a political event - the Philippines' Surigao and Bacojo operations, the New Caledonian laterite, and the Queensland laterite. Laterite is mined in the open pit in soft, wet ground with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline, and often leached in place.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 1.5-3.0% Ni, 15-40% Fe, low silica (<2%) for the best, high-silica (>20%) for the Chinese and Indonesian shales

facts.label: Ore type
facts.value: limonite (high-Fe, low-Mg), saprolite, or smectitic (high-silica) - only the limonite-rich low-silica ore is worth the pressure leach

facts.label: Depth of weathering
facts.value: 5-100 m of overburden before reaching the saprolite

children.name: Bucket-wheel excavator laterite mine
children.description: The soft, wet, deeply weathered ore is the ideal bucket-wheel material. A walking or rail-mounted bucket-wheel excavator with a 20-40 m boom cuts the overburden and the ore bench itself, dropping it onto a belt conveyor, and the ore goes to a long washing and screening plant rather than to a crusher. The Philippine and Cuban operations had bucket-wheel excavators with booms over 50 m by the early 1980s. The ore arrives at the plant as a slurry, which is why the pressure leach of the 1980s was designed for a pumped pulp and not for a dry concentrate.

facts.label: Boom length
facts.value: 20-60 m; the largest bucket-wheel excavators of the era

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 0.3-0.6 m3 per bucket at 0.6-1.5 s cycle

facts.label: Conveying
facts.value: belt conveyor from the excavator directly to the washing plant

children.note: Boom lengths and bucket volumes are machine-class figures, not specific to any named mine; medium confidence.

metal.gold.ingot.name: Refined gold anode, 99.99%, and the plated flash
metal.gold.ingot.description: The gold that reaches the electronics industry is 99.99% minimum, as a rolled sheet or an anode, and it is used in three ways. Flash plating for connector fingers and IC leads: the gold is dissolved in a cyanide gold bath - typically a gold cyanide, potassium cyanide, gold hydroxide bath at 0.5-2 g/L gold - and deposited on the nickel underplate at 0.1-1 A/dm2 for a few seconds, giving 0.05-0.25 um. Wire bonding: 15-50 um pure gold wire, drawn through diamond dies like copper, is welded from the die pad to the package lead with a thermosonic bonder. And sputtering: thin film resistors and the gold metallisation on some hybrid ICs were gold, sputtered from a cathode.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99% (4N); bonding wire is 99.999% (5N)

facts.label: Flash thickness
facts.value: 0.05-0.25 um on connector fingers and leads

facts.label: Wire gauge
facts.value: 15-50 um (0.6-2 mil) gold bonding wire

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: gold cyanide / potassium cyanide with a gold hydroxide addition, 0.5-2 g/L Au

metal.gold.ingot.note: The thickness and bath figures are textbook ranges; I cannot confirm the specific plating specification on Commodore's connectors in 1982.

metal.silver.ingot.name: Silver ingot, 99.9%, and silver contact material
metal.silver.ingot.description: A 99.9% ingot is the standard commodity grade, cast as 0.5-1 kg bars or as a 15-30 kg or 1000 troy ounce bar.
