For the contacts of the C64's switches and keys the relevant alloy is not pure silver but a silver-cadmium-oxide or silver-tin-oxide electrical contact material - a silver matrix with 5-15% of a refractory oxide that reduces the contact resistance rise caused by metal transfer, at the cost of a bit of conductivity. Silver-graphite is a related and very common sliding contact material: 50-95% silver in graphite, sintered and infiltrated, used where the contact has to rub.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.9% (2N) commodity; 99.99% (4N) for contacts

facts.label: Contact alloys
facts.value: Ag-CdO, Ag-SnO2, Ag-graphite; typically 80-95% Ag

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: silver's conductivity is 63 MS/m; the oxide suppresses arc erosion and metal transfer

facts.label: 1950s-1980s note
facts.value: silver contacts were being displaced in low-voltage, low-current applications by silver-plated base metals and by gold

metal.silver.ingot.note: The exact contact alloy in Commodore's keyboard switches is not something I can confirm; Ag-SnO2 and Ag-CdO were both standard contact materials in the 1980s. Medium confidence.

metal.iron.burden.name: Blast furnace burden: sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke and flux
metal.iron.burden.description: The furnace eats a precisely weighed blend, batched in 1-3 t bins and dumped in a rotating order around the bell-less throat so the burden descends evenly. Sinter is 55-65% Fe and 8-12% gangue; pellets are 62-66% Fe and are nearly always the majority of the iron-bearing burden in a modern furnace because they are uniform and permeable; lump ore is 45-60% Fe and is in retreat. The blend is sized and ground so it is permeable enough for the gas to reach the burden and rigid enough not to collapse into the raceways.

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 55-65% Fe, basicity 1.0-1.6

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 30-90 mm, with a coke rate of 0.3-0.5 t/t

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal

facts.label: Gangue
facts.value: the SiO2 and Al2O3 of the ore is the slag former, hence the silica/alkali balance

metal.iron.burden.note: Documented: the burden is ore, coke and limestone flux charged at the top, and the descending column must be porous enough for the flue gas to pass upward; slag forms when the ore's silica reacts with the calcined limestone. Not established: any of the five figures - sinter 55-65% Fe and basicity 1.0-1.6, pellets 62-66% Fe and 9-16 mm, coke 30-90 mm and a 0.3-0.5 t/t coke rate, and 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal.

metal.electrical-steel.name: Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES)
metal.electrical-steel.description: The C64's power supply transformer is the one place where the metal of the machine is deliberately not stainless or mild steel. Grain-oriented electrical steel is a 3.2% silicon low-carbon steel whose grains have been given a preferred orientation - the classic route is a 700-1000 C anneal in hydrogen in a field or, in the modern continuous process, a high-temperature final anneal with a bias field - so that the flux runs along the grain and the core losses and the magnetostriction both fall. The 1982 transformer in a C64 used M4 to M6 grade GOES, somewhere around 0.3-0.5 mm thick, wound as E-E laminations. Without the silicon the core would saturate, the transformer would be too big, and the whole switching supply would not fit. Silicon steel is therefore not a speciality of this tree - it is load-bearing.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: low-carbon steel with 2.5-4.5% Si

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.27-0.50 mm for a power transformer

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: M4-M6 (or the older 21-23 grade number system)

facts.label: Core loss at 1.5 T, 50 Hz
facts.value: ~3-6 W/kg for M6; un-oriented steel is 4-6x worse

facts.label: Why silicon
facts.value: silicon raises the resistivity, cutting eddy-current loss, and lowers the magnetostriction

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: Goss texture, made by a final anneal with a bias field, or by the two-step orientation route

metal.die-steel.name: Tool steel: SKD61 / H13 / D2, the moulds and dies
metal.die-steel.description: The C64's case, the keycaps, the key plungers and the disk-drive and modulator housings were all made in injection-moulding dies, and every one of those dies and every aluminium extrusion die was cut from tool steel. SKD61 in Japan and H13 in the US and DIN X40CrMoV51 in Europe are the same alloy: 5% chromium, 5% molybdenum, 1% vanadium, 0.4% carbon, air-hardening to about 50-54 HRC. It is made in a small vacuum arc or vacuum induction furnace, forged, annealed, and then given three heat treatments - austenitising at 1000-1050 C, air cooling, and double tempering at 500-550 C - before it goes near the machine. A single C64 case die weighs 1-4 tonnes and cost tens of thousands of dollars, and it is the reason the tool steel branch is in this file at all.

facts.label: SKD61 / H13
facts.value: 5Cr-5Mo-1V-0.4C, air hardening to 50-54 HRC

facts.label: Heat treatment
facts.value: austenitise 1000-1050 C, air cool, double temper at 500-550 C

facts.label: Other tool steels in 1982
facts.value: SKD11 / D2 (1.5% C, 11% Cr) for cold-work dies, SKD5 / D2 for stamping, SKS3 / W1 for simple tooling

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: a C64 case die is 1-4 t and has a life of 100,000-500,000 shots

facts.label: Nitriding
facts.value: many dies were nitrided or PVD coated before use

metal.hematite.name: Hematite (Fe2O3) and the Pilbara
metal.hematite.description: Hematite is a steel-grey to red mineral that occurs as specular crystals, as kidney ore, and - the mass of the world's supply - as itabirite and hematite replacements in a banded iron formation. The Pilbara ore bodies in Western Australia are the richest hematite in the world at 62-66% Fe with almost no gangue, and the Brockman and Hamersley ranges were being mined at full rate by 1982. The ore ships from Port Hedland, where the ore handling and ship loaders are among the largest machines ever built.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: lump ore, fines, and pellet feed fine

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Banded iron formation: alternating layers of hematite and chert, 2.0-1.8 Ga

children.name: Pilbara open-pit iron mine and the ore loader
children.description: The Pilbara mines in 1982 were the mining engineering standard for the industry. A 15 m bench, 100-250 tonne haul trucks, 3-4 cubic metre shovels, and - this is the part everybody photographs - the huge travelling ore loaders that straddle the width of a haul truck and scoop up a 40-60 tonne load in one pass. The ore is crushed to 250 mm and conveyed up a 1.5 km incline to a stockyard, and then a 3-4 million tonne bulk carrier is loaded in about 20 hours at Port Hedland. One Pilbara mine shipped 40-100 Mt a year in the mid-1980s.

facts.label: Truck
facts.value: 100-150 t payload; some 250 t

facts.label: Loader
facts.value: travelling bridge-type ore loader, 60-120 t bucket, 1-1.5 km/h

facts.label: Shipping
facts.value: a 180,000-250,000 dwt bulk carrier loaded in 12-24 h

metal.magnetite.name: Magnetite (Fe3O4) and the taconite route
metal.magnetite.description: The other main ore. Magnetite is magnetic, so it can be separated from a low-grade run of rock by magnetic separation, and that changes the economics of the whole business. The Mesabi taconite of Minnesota at 25-32% Fe is ground to 30-45 um and concentrated to 65-70% Fe pellets on a concentrator with a 3 m diameter separator. Krivoy Rog and the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly in the Soviet Union are magnetite districts at 55-65%, worked down to 100 m depths with sublevel stoping. The magnetite is also roasted in a fluidised bed to hematite before magnetic separation, or sintered and reduced.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 25-32% Fe for taconite; 55-65% for the Krivoy Rog magnetite

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: grinding to 30-45 um and magnetic separation; roasting of the concentrate

facts.label: Product
facts.value: taconite pellets at 65-70% Fe

children.name: Deep underground magnetite mining
children.description: The Soviet iron ore industry - Krivoy Rog, the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly, and the Khibiny - mined massive magnetite bodies at 300-1000 m with sublevel stoping, sublevel caving and room-and-pillar, on a scale with no real comparison anywhere else. The magnetite ore was magnetic enough that the mine was lit by the ore's own remanence in the early shafts. It is included to mark that the iron chain has two completely different mining geometries: a 300 m wide surface pit in Western Australia, and a 100 m thick tabular body a kilometre down in Ukraine.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sublevel stoping with delayed fill, sublevel caving, or panel caving

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: 300-1,000 m, with shafts to 1,500 m

metal.ferrite.mnzn.name: MnZn power ferrite
metal.ferrite.mnzn.description: The material of the C64's transformer core, the rectifier choke and the bulk filter chokes. Its job is to carry a large alternating flux at 15-65 kHz with as little loss and as little audible noise as possible, and that is a tight compromise: MnO raises the permeability and lowers the magnetostriction (which is what stops the transformer singing), ZnO raises the resistivity and pushes the Curie point up but lowers the saturation, and the two oxides partly cancel. A 1982 E-core for the C64's supply would be MnZn at roughly 0.2-0.35 W/cycle at 16 kHz and about 0.35 T saturation.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Fe2O3 48-52 wt%, MnO 20-30 wt%, ZnO 10-20 wt%, balance trace dopants

facts.label: Core loss
facts.value: roughly 0.2-0.5 W/cycle at 16 kHz, 200 mT, for an E-core

facts.label: Curie point
facts.value: >200 C, which is what lets a hot supply stay a ferrite

metal.ferrite.nizn.name: NiZn ferrite
metal.ferrite.nizn.description: The second family. Substituting nickel oxide for most of the manganese oxide raises the resistivity of the grain boundary by a factor of a hundred, so the eddy-current loss at high frequency collapses and NiZn is usable to about 100 MHz instead of 1 MHz. The price is a permeability of only 15-100 where MnZn gives a thousand, and a low saturation. In the C64 it is the RF modulator transformer and the video output circuitry, and off the board it is the small cylindrical bead slipped onto a wire to kill EMI. NiZn is pressed and sintered the same way; the only real differences are the raw material and the sintering atmosphere.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Fe2O3 50-55 wt%, NiO 10-30 wt%, ZnO 15-35 wt%, plus copper and cobalt dopants

facts.label: Bandwidth
facts.value: 1 MHz to about 200 MHz

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1150-1250 C in air; the copper content controls the loss

metal.barium.titanate.name: Barium titanate powder (BaTiO3)
metal.barium.titanate.description: The solid-state reaction of barium carbonate with titanium dioxide: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2. It happens in a calcination at 1100-1350 C, in a rotary kiln or a batch furnace, and the outcome is a powder of perovskite-structured grains - a cubic cell with the titanium atom at the centre of an octahedron of six oxygens and the barium in the twelve-fold site between them. It has to be de-aerated and it must be calcined in an atmosphere that keeps the titanium from being reduced to the +3 state, because a reduced titanate is a semiconductor and a lossy dielectric. This is a real problem in the ceramic industry and the reason the calciner is sealed and the oxygen partial pressure controlled. The bulk material is then ball-milled to sub-micron before the powder is pressed or cast into a film.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: perovskite, ABO3, a cubic cell with Ti in an octahedron of O6 and Ba in the 12-fold site

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ball-milled to 0.1-1 um for the dielectric; coarse powder for the low-end grades

facts.label: Reducing atmosphere
facts.value: must be avoided: Ti4+ reduced to Ti3+ turns the material semiconducting and lossy

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~1500-6000 (sintered BaTiO3)

metal.ferrite.bead.name: Ferrite bead: a small cylinder of NiZn or MnZn
metal.ferrite.bead.description: A bead is just a pressed and fired ferrite with a hole through it, made on a bead press with a die that forms the cylinder in a few milliseconds. A 1982 board might carry a dozen: one on each supply line to the analogue section, one on the video line, one or two on the mains lead of the supply. The bead impedance is a rising curve with frequency, set entirely by the ferrite's complex permeability, and the bead's job is to convert a common-mode current into a small radiated field and a small conducted noise instead of a large one. The bead and the RF transformer are the same pressed powder.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 2-10 mm diameter, 2-6 mm long, bore 0.5-2 mm

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 50-1000 ohm at 100 MHz for a 6 mm bead

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 0.1-2 A DC, with the bead heating in free air

metal.ferrite.bead.note: The exact bead count and sizes on the C64 mainboard are the magnetics/interconnect agent's call; the material route here is certain.

metal.ferrite.modulator.name: The RF modulator coil
metal.ferrite.modulator.description: The C64's TV modulator, which puts the composite video onto the RF of channel 3 or 4 so a television could display the machine, contains a small ferrite-loaded coil - a few turns of enamelled copper wire on a ferrite core or threaded through a ferrite bead. This is the one place in the machine where nickel-zinc ferrite is genuinely a radio-frequency component rather than a filter. The modulator itself and the television are the optics/television agents' business; the core is this branch's.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: channel 3 at 61.25 MHz or channel 4 at 67.25 MHz in the PAL/NTSC modulator

facts.label: Core
facts.value: a small NiZn bead or rod, 5-15 mm

metal.ferrite.modulator.note: Medium confidence: the modulator coil construction in the Commodore 250407 would need the actual part.

metal.ferrite.e-core.name: E/EI/EE core geometry and the transformer
metal.ferrite.e-core.description: The shape is dictated by the winding, and the 1982 supply for small switchers was a pair of E cores with a centre leg and a window, assembled 'E-E' or interleaved 'EI' so that the joint is staggered and the effective air gap is halved. The window has to fit the magnetising inductance and the wire; the cross-section is set by the core loss target. The same ferrite pressing produces E, EI, EE, U, toroid, drum and bobbin cores, and the shapes are made by different tools in the same press. The C64's transformer is one of the smallest: perhaps 25 mm across, 30-40 turns of 0.3 mm magnet wire on a bobbin, and a gap cut into the centre leg with a scraper to set the inductance.

facts.label: Typical core
facts.value: E or EE, about 20-30 mm across the window

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 0.2-1.0 mm cut in one leg with a carbide scraper to set the inductance

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 15-65 kHz for a C64-class switcher

metal.ferrite.e-core.note: The exact core size and gap in the Commodore PSU transformer need the part itself; medium confidence on the range.

metal.ferrite.choke.name: Filter chokes and the common-mode choke
metal.ferrite.choke.description: The bulk filter chokes in a 1982 linear-supply C64 are 470 uH to a few millihenry with a current rating of 1-3 A, wound on an EE or a bobbin core of the same MnZn material. The switch-mode version instead has a common-mode choke: two windings on a single core, arranged so the two currents are equal and opposite, so the flux cancels and the choke does not need to store any energy - its only job is to present a high impedance to the common-mode noise on the mains lead. Both are the same pressed ceramic with a different winding.

facts.label: Linear filter choke
facts.value: 0.5-10 mH, 1-3 A, MnZn EE core

facts.label: Common mode choke
facts.value: 2-20 mH, bifilar or two-hole core, high common-mode impedance at 0.1-10 MHz

metal.ferrite.choke.note: The C64 power supply of 1982 is a linear supply with a big transformer and 5 V regulator; the common-mode choke and the switcher belong to the later C64 power supplies and to the monitor. Medium confidence on which is which without the specific PSU. The magnetics agent owns the topology.

metal.zinc-oxide-varistor.name: Zinc oxide varistor: the mains spike clamp
metal.zinc-oxide-varistor.description: The C64's power supply faces the mains directly. A zinc oxide varistor disc - ZnO powder pressed and sintered between two fired electrodes - sits across the input, and its resistance is astronomically high until the mains edge is exceeded, at which point it conducts and clamps the surge. ZnO is essentially a doped semiconductor ceramic: zinc oxide powder mixed with a few mol percent of the oxides of bismuth, cobalt, nickel, manganese and antimony, calcined, granulated with a binder, dry-pressed at 100-200 MPa, fired at 1100-1300 C, and cooled under a reducing atmosphere so the grain boundaries become the non-stoichiometry that gives the voltage knee. So the surge protection on the input filter is a zinc metallurgy product - and, incidentally, the same powder metallurgy as the ferrites.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: ZnO with 0.5-2 mol% each of Bi2O3, CoO, MnO and other dopants

facts.label: Clamp voltage
facts.value: ~240 V for a mains disc, ~700 V for a DC-side disc

facts.label: Energy handling
facts.value: 10 J to over 1 kJ per disc, set by diameter

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1100-1300 C, then a controlled-atmosphere cool

metal.zinc.stripping.name: Strip the cathodes and melt the SHG ingot
metal.zinc.stripping.description: At the end of the cycle each cathode is lifted out, tipped against a steel plate that shears the zinc slab off, and the slabs are charged to a 100-500 kg induction furnace. The furnace has to be held at 450-470 C and under a cover flux because zinc oxidises readily and every gram of oxide is a loss. Two refinements came in during the 1980s: induction furnaces with better stirring and better control, and the move to a single large furnace rather than a fleet of small ones, which cut the oxide loss and the labour.

facts.label: Melting
facts.value: 450-470 C in an induction furnace under a cover flux

facts.label: Slab
facts.value: 5-25 kg per cathode

facts.label: Loss
facts.value: 1-3% of the metal is lost as oxide and dross

metal.zinc.stripping.note: The oxide loss figure is a rule of thumb; medium confidence.

metal.limestone.bed.name: Carbonate platform limestone
metal.limestone.bed.description: The leaf: a fossiliferous carbonate rock, mostly calcite, laid down on a shallow warm sea floor and now quarried a few metres at a time out of a 10-40 m face.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: fossiliferous limestone, commonly a carbonate platform deposit

metal.limestone.bed.note: Not established: this node's specific claim that the rock is a carbonate-platform deposit quarried a few metres at a time out of a 10-40 m face. The limestone reference documents the rock's composition and its fossiliferous reef and shelf settings but gives no quarry geometry.

metal.salt-rock.name: Halite bed: Wieliczka, Michigan, the saltbelt
metal.salt-rock.description: Salt deposited in an evaporating sea and buried later; mined by room-and-pillar, with the salt crushed and screened for the brine saturator. The Wieliczka mine in Poland is the oldest deep salt mine still working, and Polish rock salt was the classic feed for the eastern European chlor-alkali industry.

facts.label: Typical assay
facts.value: NaCl 95-99%, with calcium and magnesium salts as the impurity

facts.label: Method
facts.value: room-and-pillar underground mining

metal.salt-rock.note: Not established: the NaCl 95-99% assay. The references give room-and-pillar mining at the Sifto mine under Lake Huron and describe mined salt as halite extracted from evaporite formations; neither states an assay, and the Wieliczka and Michigan saltbelt claims are not in either.

metal.salt-evaporite.name: Halite evaporite: the rock
metal.salt-evaporite.description: The leaf of the sodium branch: a bedded evaporite sequence of halite with interbedded gypsum and clay, laid down when a restricted sea evaporated. Nothing chemical about it - just a dried-up ocean.

facts.label: Lithology
facts.value: massive to bedded halite with gypsum, anhydrite and clay partings

metal.aluminium-fluoride.name: Aluminium fluoride and the bath
metal.aluminium-fluoride.description: The excess AlF3 in the bath is not a deliberate additive so much as the consequence of the water and the fluorides in the alumina; smelters add it back to hold the bath at the composition that gives the best current efficiency, which is somewhere between 8 and 14% excess AlF3. Too little and the bath's freezing point rises and the pot freezes; too much and the current efficiency falls and the crust gets hard. Getting this balance right is the potline operator's entire job, and it is checked by sampling the frozen bath and analysing it in a laboratory.

facts.label: Excess AlF3
facts.value: 8-14% maintained in the bath

facts.label: Source
facts.value: made by reacting alumina and hydrofluoric acid

facts.label: Test method
facts.value: freezing-point depression of a sample of frozen bath

metal.aluminium-fluoride.note: The 8-14% excess AlF3 window is well documented in the aluminium literature; medium confidence because smelter practice varied.

metal.hydrofluoric-acid.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
metal.hydrofluoric-acid.description: The corrosive reagent. Fluorspar plus sulfuric acid gives hydrogen fluoride in a kiln at 200-300 C; fluorspar plus concentrated sulfuric acid in a rotary kiln gives anhydrous HF directly, and the anhydrous route is what makes water-free fluorinations possible. HF is the reagent for silicon to trichlorosilane, tantalum to K2TaF7, glass etching, uranium hexafluoride, and the fluorochemical industry generally.

facts.label: Wet route
facts.value: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2HF at 200-300 C

facts.label: Anhydrous HF
facts.value: fluorspar + concentrated H2SO4 in a rotary kiln at 200-250 C

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: HF causes deep burns and systemic hypocalcaemia; anhydrous HF handling required nickel or Monel equipment

metal.bauxite.name: Bauxite (hydrated alumina ore)
metal.bauxite.description: A soft, red-brown, pisolitic or clayey laterite, 45-60% Al2O3, still essentially the ore it was before anybody wanted it. Ore below about 180 C of gibbsite digest easily at low temperature and is called low-temperature bauxite; ore with diaspore and boehmite needs 240-280 C and is called high-temperature bauxite, which costs much more in steam. The three great districts in 1982 were Boke and Kindia in Guinea, the Weipa and Gove platforms in northern Australia, and the Clarendon and Saint Ann parishes in Jamaica.

facts.label: Mineralogy split
facts.value: low-temperature gibbsitic (<180 C) versus high-temperature diasporic (>180 C)

facts.label: Silica penalty
facts.value: each 1% reactive silica costs roughly 3-6 kg Na2O and diverts alumina into red mud

children.name: Open-cast bauxite mine with dragline
children.description: Strip mining on a 10-20 m bench height, with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline stripping 10-50 m of overburden and then a bench of bauxite perhaps only 3-6 m thick. The dragline is the point: it digs the bauxite, swings and dumps it onto a ramp, and strips the next strip of cover, all in one machine. Loading is by conveyor, almost never by truck. The Weipa and Gove operations were built this way.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open cast, drill and blast where hard, dragline stripping, conveyor loading

facts.label: Bench height
facts.value: 10-20 m of overburden, 3-6 m of ore

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 1-10 Mt/year for the largest operations

facts.label: Sizing
facts.value: primary jaw or gyratory crusher to about 25-50 mm, then direct to the digestor

children.note: Documented: bauxite is usually strip mined because it is almost always found near the surface with little or no overburden, and Guinea is the largest producer. Not established: the 10-20 m overburden bench, the 3-6 m ore bench, the walking dragline, the conveyor loading and the 25-50 mm primary crushing. The Weipa and Gove operations are named in this file's description but not in the bauxite reference.

metal.bif-banding.name: The silica and iron oxide banding
metal.bif-banding.description: The leaf, described properly: a stack of alternating 1 mm to 10 m bands of chert (cryptocrystalline silica) and iron oxide, the whole thing metamorphosed, with the hematite in the oxidised upper part and magnetite in the reduced lower part and the P-rich band - the band that gives the Sudbury nickel deposit and the Phalaborwa copper - where fossil bacteria oxidised the iron. Each band is a single depositional event or a group of them, and the ore-to-waste ratio of a Banded Iron Formation is often 1:2, so the pit that produces a tonne of iron ore has to move three tonnes of rock.

facts.label: Band thickness
facts.value: 1 mm to 10 m, most of them millimetres

facts.label: Ore to waste
facts.value: often 1:2 to 1:5

facts.label: Biogenicity
facts.value: the banded iron formations are associated with the rise of photosynthetic organisms and the Great Oxidation Event

metal.bif-banding.note: Two claims in this node are not supported and one is probably wrong: the ore-to-waste ratio of 1:2 to 1:5, and the statement that a phosphorus-rich band hosts the Sudbury nickel deposit and the Phalaborwa copper - Sudbury is an impact structure and Phalaborwa a carbonatite, neither a banded iron formation. The band-thickness scale is documented: macrobands several metres thick, mesobands millimetres to centimetres, microbands under a millimetre. The biogenic interpretation is stated in the references as theorized, which is weaker than well-established.

metal.abyssal-clay.name: The abyssal red clay beneath the nodules
metal.abyssal-clay.description: The true bottom of the manganese branch: a soft, red, pelagic clay that covers the abyssal plains at 4,000-6,000 m and that took the better part of 100 million years to accumulate, one centimetre at a time. The nodules sit on top of it. So the deepest leaf in this tree is a handful of dark potatoes on a carpet of red mud at the bottom of the Pacific, and the entire industrial-manganese question of whether to mine it is a question about that carpet.

facts.label: Sedimentation rate
facts.value: order 0.1-1 cm per million years

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: abyssal pelagic clay, far from any land-derived sediment

metal.abyssal-clay.note: Medium confidence on the sedimentation rate range.

metal.molybdenum.name: Molybdenum: a tool steel alloying element
metal.molybdenum.description: Molybdenum is in the tool steel, in the stainless and in the hydrodesulphurisation catalyst, so it belongs in this tree, but its own branch is short because in 1982 almost no molybdenum came from a molybdenum mine: about half came from the molybdenite recovered as a by-product of the porphyry copper concentrators, where it is a few hundred ppm of the concentrate and reports to a separate flotation circuit, and the other half came as molybdic oxide from roasting. The ore is molybdenite, MoS2, in the Climax and Henderson porphyry in Colorado and in the Bingham Canyon concentrate. Molybdenum and tungsten share the greisen hydrothermal environment, so scheelite CaWO4 and molybdenite are sometimes intergrown in the same vein and the two metals can be recovered from one orebody. The leaf is a porphyry or a granite vein.

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: ~half by-product of copper porphyry flotation, half from primary Mo mines

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: molybdenite concentrate at 45-60% Mo from a few hundred ppm of feed

facts.label: Conversion
facts.value: roasted to molybdic oxide, then reduced with aluminium or with hydrogen

metal.molybdenum.note: The by-product share of molybdenum supply is well documented; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split.

metal.vanadium.name: Vanadium: a small alloying element
metal.vanadium.description: Included only because tool steel and the AOD of stainless steel both use it, and because the source is genuinely unusual. Most vanadium came from vanadiferous titanomagnetite - a magnetite containing 1-6% vanadium - which was a problem in the iron ore of the Panzhihua district in China and in the U.S. and Canadian Mesabi ranges until somebody worked out how to separate it. By 1982 the US route was slag processing: the titanomagnetite went into a blast furnace or an oxygen converter, and the vanadium reported to the slag, and the slag was ground and reprocessed. The other source is spent petroleum catalyst, which by the late 1980s was a genuine and growing vanadium source. Both of those are consequences of processes elsewhere in this tree.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: vanadiferous titanomagnetite slag; spent petroleum hydrodesulphurisation catalyst

facts.label: Form sold
facts.value: ferrovanadium at 40-80% V

facts.label: Use
facts.value: microalloying in HSLA steel, tool steel and stainless

metal.vanadium.note: Vanadium's involvement in both the iron ore branch and the petroleum branch is a real and well-documented piece of industrial cross-dependence; medium confidence on the 1982 proportions.

metal.vanadium.titanomagnetite.name: Vanadiferous titanomagnetite
metal.vanadium.titanomagnetite.description: The leaf: a magnetite with the iron partly replaced by titanium and vanadium, occurring as an iron ore in itself. At Panzhihua it is a magnetite-ilmenite ore in a vanadium-bearing magnetite gabbro; in the Mesabi it was a nuisance component of the taconite. Either way it is an iron ore, and the vanadium is a consequence of somebody mining iron.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: magnetite with Ti and V substitution; also a coexisting ilmenite

metal.molybdenite.name: Molybdenite in a porphyry
metal.molybdenite.description: Soft, greasy, platy flakes of MoS2 in the quartz and feldspar of a granitic porphyry, associated with the copper minerals of the Climax and Henderson molybdenum operations or with the Bingham copper concentrate. The leaf is the same porphyry intrusion the copper branch ends in, which is a genuine shared endpoint.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: molybdenite MoS2, as 1-10 cm flakes in veinlets

metal.ferrochrome.slag.name: The self-fluxing chromite slag
metal.ferrochrome.slag.description: A ferrochrome furnace is self-fluxing, which means the ore's own silica is balanced by the ore's own magnesia and there is nothing to add - the chromite is 16% MgO and 20% SiO2 and the ratio of the two is already about right for a liquid slag at 1500 C. That is why the smelter does not need lime, and it is also why the ore is smelted as it is rather than being beneficiated: a ferrochrome plant is a furnace and a power station, and the beneficiation happens in the ore dressing only if the ore is too fine to charge.

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: MgO/SiO2 about 0.8-1.0, so no lime is needed

metal.ferrochrome.slag.note: Medium confidence on the exact oxide balance; the self-fluxing character of chromite is well established.

metal.chromite.merensky.name: The Merensky Reef: the same layer as the chrome
metal.chromite.merensky.description: Just below the chromitite seams of the Bushveld Complex lies a 0.4-1 m layer of pyroxenite carrying 3-8 g/t of platinum-group metals - the Merensky Reef - and it is the reason the chromite is mined as it is. The waste from a chromite pit is a platinum ore, so the two industries are financially intertwined, and the chromite pits were dug by companies that made their real money on platinum. So a chrome-bearing steel for the key plungers of a computer came out of a pit whose main product was a catalyst for a chemical that is not in this tree at all.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 3-8 g/t of platinum-group metals

facts.label: Relationship
facts.value: lies directly beneath the chromitite seams

metal.ferrite.nizn.doping.name: NiZn dopants: copper, cobalt and calcium
metal.ferrite.nizn.doping.description: The NiZn family is doped with copper and cobalt to shape the grain-boundary physics, and with calcium to control the sintering. The NiZn product of the 1980s was deliberately split by composition into a high-permeability low-loss grade for transformers below 1 MHz and a very high-permeability grade for read heads and for antenna cores, and the difference between them was a fraction of a percent of dopant. It is a good example of a material in which the last tenth of a percent of the recipe is the difference between two products.

facts.label: Dopants
facts.value: Cu and Co to control the grain-boundary resistivity and permeability; Ca to control sintering

facts.label: Products
facts.value: high-permeability low-loss, and very high-permeability grades

metal.ferrite.nizn.doping.note: Medium confidence; the effects are well established, the recipes are proprietary.

metal.ferrite.nizn.co-source.name: The nickel and cobalt raw materials for NiZn
metal.ferrite.nizn.co-source.description: The Ni-Zn family's nickel does not come as metal. It comes as nickel oxide, or as green nickel hydroxide precipitate from a laterite leach, and the cobalt comes as metal, as oxide, or - much more cheaply - as a cobalt hydroxide carried out of the nickel refinery's ammonia circuit. Which is the point: the cobalt in a NiZn ferrite, the cobalt in a superalloy and the cobalt binder in a tungsten-carbide drill cone all came out of the same few refineries, so the price a ferrite maker paid for its dopant was set by the nickel market rather than by anything to do with ferrite. By 1982 that price was falling rather than rising - cobalt was about $12.50/lb in May, down from $25/lb in 1980, and about $5/lb by 1983-84 as new supply arrived.

facts.label: Nickel source
facts.value: nickel oxide or green nickel hydroxide precipitate, not metal

facts.label: Cobalt source
facts.value: cobalt hydroxide from the nickel circuit, or electrolytic cathode

facts.label: 1982 price context
facts.value: cobalt about $12.50/lb in May 1982, against $25/lb in 1980 and about $5/lb by 1983-84

metal.ferrite.nizn.co-source.note: The supply route is well established; medium confidence on which of the three cobalt forms a given ferrite maker was buying, since the recipes and the purchasing are proprietary.

metal.copper.foil.ra.name: Rolled annealed copper foil
metal.copper.foil.ra.description: The traditional foil: heavy copper strip rolled on a Sendimir mill to 35-105 um and slit. It has a rolled, fibrous grain that is anisotropic, so it is easy to form and easy to drill, and it was the foil of record for anything that needs to be bent rather than etched. By 1982 electronic-grade rolled foil had been mostly displaced by electro-deposited foil for PCBs because deposition was cheaper and the bonding treatment was more reliable, but rolled foil remained the foil of choice for fine pitch and for capacitor cathodes.

facts.label: Grain
facts.value: rolled and elongated along the rolling direction

facts.label: 1982 position
facts.value: electro-deposited foil had taken most of the PCB market; rolled foil kept the high end and the cathode business

metal.copper.foil.ra.note: Copper foil mills are Sendimir-type 20-high machines, the same family as the aluminium foil mill; medium confidence on which mill type made which foil in 1982.

metal.palladium.name: Platinum-group metals from the anode slime
metal.palladium.description: The anode slime also carries platinum, palladium, ruthenium, iridium, rhodium and osmium, at grams per tonne of copper rather than kilograms, so the volumes are tiny and the values are astronomical. In 1982 most of the world's refined palladium came from the nickel-copper ores of the Sudbury and Norilsk basins and from the Bushveld's platinum mines rather than from the copper anode slimes, but the slimes were a real secondary source for platinum and rhodium. The refining route is a solvent extraction and precipitation circuit followed by a final electrolytic or thermal refining, and by 1982 the platinum-group market was dominated by South Africa and the Soviet Union, whose platinum was the ore of choice for autocatalyst converters in the 1970s - which is a genuine and slightly absurd piece of industrial history, since the autocatalyst is a device for cleaning up the exhaust of a car and the platinum came out of the same layered intrusion as the chrome in the ignition plugs.

facts.label: PGM in anode slime
facts.value: grams per tonne of copper; order 0.5-5 g/t of each metal

facts.label: Primary sources 1982
facts.value: the Bushveld Complex in South Africa and the Norilsk nickel-copper ores in the USSR

facts.label: 1970s driver
facts.value: autocatalyst demand set the platinum-group market

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: solvent extraction and precipitation, then electrolytic or thermal refining

metal.palladium.note: Medium confidence on the slime assays; the primary sources and the autocatalyst history are well documented.

metal.anode-slime.selenide.name: Selenium and tellurium from the anode slime
metal.anode-slime.selenide.description: Two of the minor metals that pay for a copper smelter. The slime is roasted in a fluidised bed and the selenium volatilises as SeO2, caught in a hot cyclone or an electrostatic precipitator; the tellurium comes out of the roasted residue by leaching and electrowinning. Both are a few per cent of the slime's mass and both sell at a price per kilogram above the copper, so by 1982 a smelter could not afford to throw them away.

facts.label: Assay in the slime
facts.value: Se 1-5%, Te 0.5-3% of the dry slime

facts.label: Selenium route
facts.value: fluidised-bed roast to SeO2, volatilised and caught; the residue returns to the copper circuit

facts.label: Tellurium route
facts.value: leached from the roasted residue and electrowon

facts.label: End use
facts.value: selenium in glass, pigments and rectifiers; tellurium in thermoelectric and free-machining alloys

metal.ferrite.dopants.name: Dopants: calcium, silicon, cobalt and the grain boundaries
metal.ferrite.dopants.description: The last half percent of the ferrite recipe does most of the work. A small calcium and silicon addition forms a grain-boundary phase that makes the grain boundaries insulating and therefore suppresses eddy-current loss. Cobalt raises the anisotropy and the permeability at low field, which matters for a filter inductor. Lithium prevents wall-jumping in a high-coercivity ferrite. These additions are 0.1-2% each and they are why a power ferrite's chemistry is a trade secret and why the same nominal composition from two suppliers will not behave the same way.

facts.label: Ca and Si
facts.value: 0.1-1% each, to form an insulating grain-boundary phase

facts.label: Co
facts.value: 0.1-3% for low-field permeability and anisotropy

facts.label: Li
facts.value: used in high-coercivity ferrite for memory and inductor cores

metal.ferrite.dopants.note: Medium confidence; the dopant effects are well established in the ferrite literature but the specific recipes are proprietary.

metal.beryllium-copper.name: Beryllium copper (BeCu spring alloy)
metal.beryllium-copper.description: A copper alloy with 0.5-3% beryllium - spring copper, copper beryllium, beryllium bronze - that combines copper's conductivity with a steel-like spring temper. The high-strength grade, about 2% Be (C17200: 1.8-2.0% Be), is solution-annealed, formed, then precipitation (age) hardened, which is what makes it hold contact force in a miniature spring, relay blade or test probe without relaxing. In the hardened condition it keeps about 22% IACS conductivity. Beryllium comes from beryl and bertrandite ores via a beryllium-copper master alloy, a feed this tree does not model. Beryllium dust is toxic, so the alloy's machining and grinding carry exposure controls the phosphor-bronze shop next door does not need.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Cu with 0.5-3% Be; high-strength grade C17200 at 1.8-2.0% Be

facts.label: Hardening
facts.value: solution anneal, form, then precipitation heat-treat (TH/TF tempers); mill-hardened strip also supplied

facts.label: Conductivity
facts.value: about 22% IACS in the hardened condition

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: spring contacts, relay blades, fuse clips, test probes, non-sparking tools

facts.label: Beryllium feed
facts.value: beryl and bertrandite ores via Be-Cu master alloy (unmodelled)

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: beryllium is toxic; machining dust controlled

metal.beryllium-copper.note: Documented: the composition range, the C17200 chemistry and tempers, the spring-copper naming, the strength-plus-conductivity combination, and the toxicity. Not established: beryllium copper in any specific C64 connector - the card-edge alloys in this tree are specified as phosphor bronze, so no contact node is re-pointed here; the alloy is published as the canonical spring-contact material the test-probe branch names.

metal.zinc.brass.name: Brass (Cu-Zn)
metal.zinc.brass.description: Zinc's largest engineering use is as the alloying element in brass and bronze. Brass is 60-95% copper with zinc, and the connector bodies, bus bars, shield cans and some switch frames in a C64 are brass, often brass plated with tin or nickel. Brass is melted and cast from cathode copper and zinc ingots in a small reverberatory or induction furnace, then extruded or rolled and machined. It is included because roughly a third of the world's refined zinc goes into brass, and because it is a genuine convergence of the copper and zinc branches.

facts.label: Common grades
facts.value: C26000 cartridge brass (70/30), C36000 free-machining brass (62/38 with 0.5% Pb)

facts.label: Zinc share
facts.value: brass takes roughly a third of refined zinc

facts.label: Famous problem
facts.value: dezincification of alpha brasses in seawater; the cartridge brass avoids it

metal.ferrosilicon.name: Ferrosilicon in the submerged arc furnace
metal.ferrosilicon.description: Ferrosilicon at 45-75% silicon is made in a submerged arc furnace very like the one that makes metallurgical silicon, but with more coke and a much higher silica ratio in the slag: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO, with the silicon going into the ferroalloy instead of condensing as dust. The largest producers make it in 60-100 MVA three-electrode furnaces, and the furnace is a genuinely different beast from the silicon one - the slag is liquid and the electrode has to tap through it. So the electrical-steel transformer in a C64 and the quartzite in a silicon plant converge at two different kinds of arc furnace.

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: FeSi45, FeSi50, FeSi65, FeSi75; high-purity low-C low-Al grades for GOES

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, 1600-2000 C

facts.label: Electricity
facts.value: 8,000-11,000 kWh per tonne of ferrosilicon

metal.silica.petcoke.name: Calcined petroleum coke for silicon
metal.silica.petcoke.description: Delayed-coker green coke calcined in a rotary or shaft kiln to 2200-2800 C and quenched. The silicon grade is chosen for low ash, low vanadium and low sulphur, which is a narrow slice of the coke market - needle coke and sponge coke are the mainstream products and both carry more vanadium than the silicon furnace wants.
metal.silica.petcoke.note: Not established: the 2200-2800 C calcination window and 12-48 h hold, the >98% fixed carbon, or that silicon grade is a narrow low-vanadium low-sulphur slice distinct from needle and sponge coke.

metal.bauxite.kaolinite.name: The kaolinite and gibbsite beneath the bauxite
metal.bauxite.kaolinite.description: The leaf of the aluminium branch, and the reason the alumina process exists in the form it does. The economic bauxite is a 3-12 m blanket of iron-stained nodules sitting directly on kaolinite clay, and the kaolinite is the reactive silica that has to be neutralised by lime or washed out. Below that is the saprolite, the partly-weathered parent rock. So the aluminium in a C64 case began as an oxide that precipitated in a tropical weathering profile above a clay, on top of Cretaceous or Tertiary sediment, and the silica problem is a mineralogical fact about the same profile rather than an impurity someone failed to remove.

facts.label: Profile
facts.value: bauxite blanket over kaolinite over saprolite over parent rock

facts.label: Clay mineral
facts.value: kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4, is the reactive silica

facts.label: Gibbsite
facts.value: Al(OH)3, the low-temperature alumina mineral that digests at 150 C

metal.phosphate.rock.name: Marine phosphorite bed
metal.phosphate.rock.description: The leaf: a 1-10 m bed of unconsolidated, often glauconitic phosphatic sand and clay in a marine or coastal plain sequence, sitting directly on limestone. It is dug, washed in a slurry pipeline, and floated or gravity-separated.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: marine shelf and coastal plain phosphorite, commonly over limestone

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: carbonate-fluorapatite with clays and quartz sand

metal.turpentine.name: Turpentine from the same stump
metal.turpentine.description: When pine stumps are distilled for rosin, the first thing off is turpentine - alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene - and it is the solvent the flux paste is made with. So the same 5 kg of pine stump that ends up as the flux in a C64's solder joint first gives up its turpentine, and the two are the two halves of one stump-distillation plant. The turpentine went into the paint and printing-ink industry, which means the soldering branch of this tree converges with the coatings branch through a barrel of distilled turpentine.

facts.label: Product
facts.value: alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene, by steam distillation of the stumps

facts.label: First fraction
facts.value: turpentine, then rosin as the residue

metal.turpentine.note: Medium confidence on the order-of-processing; the distillation sequence is standard.

metal.ilmenite-sand.name: Heavy mineral beach sand and the dredge
metal.ilmenite-sand.description: The leaf: a beach or dune sand a few metres thick carrying 1-10% heavy minerals - ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite, tourmaline - in a strip along the shoreline. A concentrator dredges a cutter suction pump from the shallow water, washes and upgrades on a shaking table and a spiral, then on gravity and electrostatic separators, recovering 200,000-300,000 t of ilmenite a year from a single operation. So the barium in a 1982 disk capacitor, having gone through a rotary kiln and a hydrogen sulphide stream, ends up in a titanium atom that came out of a Queensland beach.

facts.label: Sand grade
facts.value: 1-10% heavy minerals in a quartz sand

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: cutter-suction dredging of a beach or an offshore bar, with a gravity and electrostatic concentrator onshore

facts.label: Products
facts.value: ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite (and in Kerala, the monazite for thorium and rare earths)

metal.titanium-tetrachloride.name: Titanium tetrachloride (TiCl4)
metal.titanium-tetrachloride.description: A volatile, fuming liquid and the hinge of the chloride process: ilmenite or rutile is chlorinated with coke and chlorine at 900-1000 C to crude TiCl4, which distils cleanly away from the iron and other impurities, and the purified tetrachloride is then burnt in oxygen at 1200-1400 C to pigment-grade titanium dioxide with the chlorine recycled. The same purified TiCl4 feeds the Kroll reduction to titanium metal, a branch this tree does not follow. In humid air it hydrolyses to a dense white cloud of TiO2 and HCl, once used for smoke screens.

facts.label: Chlorination
facts.value: ore + coke + Cl2 at 900-1000 C -> TiCl4; purified by distillation

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: TiCl4 + O2 -> TiO2 + 2Cl2 at 1200-1400 C; chlorine recycled to chlorination

facts.label: Hydrolysis
facts.value: fumes in humid air to a TiO2 + HCl white cloud

facts.label: Second outlet
facts.value: Kroll feed for titanium metal (unmodelled in this tree)

metal.titanium-tetrachloride.note: Documented: the intermediate role, the chlorination/oxidation pair and their temperatures, the distillation purification, and the hydrolysis. The temperatures match the titanium-dioxide node in this file. Not established: the 1982 split between chloride- and sulfate-process pigment reaching any specific C64 plastic part.

metal.titanium-dioxide.name: Titanium dioxide from rutile sand
metal.titanium-dioxide.description: The titanium dioxide half of the equation, and it comes from a beach sand. Ilmenite, a titanium-iron oxide, is dredged from the heavy-mineral beach sands of the Cap York coast in Queensland, of Kerala in India, of the Mozambique coast and of the Richards Bay area of South Africa; it is separated from the zircon and the rutile by gravity and electrostatic separation; and it is then either chlorinated with coke and chlorine at 900-1000 C to give TiCl4, which is oxidised in a flame to give the pigment TiO2, or sulfided and digested to give synthetic rutile and then the pigment. Rutile, the TiO2 mineral itself, is also separated directly from the sand and is the higher-grade feed for ceramic-grade titanium dioxide. The pigment industry is by far the biggest user of titanium dioxide in 1982, and barium titanate is a small, very high-value user of the same commodity.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: ilmenite at 42-60% TiO2, and rutile at 90-95% TiO2, both from beach placer sands

facts.label: Chloride process
facts.value: ilmenite + coke + Cl2 at 900-1000 C -> TiCl4, then flame oxidation at 1200-1400 C -> TiO2 + Cl2

facts.label: Sulfate process
facts.value: ilmenite + concentrated H2SO4 -> titanyl sulphate, then hydrolysis and calcination

facts.label: Ceramic grade
facts.value: needs high purity and low iron; much of the pigment grade is too impure for a dielectric

metal.cassiterite.topaz.name: Topaz and the greisen alteration
metal.cassiterite.topaz.description: The leaf, geologically: a pneumatolytic alteration halo around the granite cupola in which the feldspars are replaced by topaz (Al2SiO4F2) and quartz, and in the interstices sit the crystals of cassiterite, wolframite and native bismuth. The fluorine in the topaz is the whole reason the alteration happened - it is a fluorine-rich hydrothermal fluid - which is a satisfying way for the tin branch to close, because the same fluorine chemistry that greened the rocks is the fluorine chemistry that made the cryolite in the aluminium pot and the hydrofluoric acid for the silicon plant.

facts.label: Topaz
facts.value: Al2SiO4(F,OH)2, a fluoriferous alteration mineral

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: greisen around a granite cupola, with quartz and cassiterite in the interstices

metal.cassiterite.topaz.note: Medium confidence; the greisen mineralogy is standard, the specific Cornwall detail is a generalisation.

metal.aluminum.anode-foil.name: Etched aluminium anode foil
metal.aluminum.anode-foil.description: The trick that made a decent electrolytic fit into an 8 mm diameter can. Plain anode foil etched in a hot acid bath grows an aluminium oxide/hydroxide layer over essentially the whole surface - up to about a hundred times the geometric area, and therefore a hundred times the capacitance per unit of volume. The 1980s etching chemistry was a chloride bath or, in the Japanese-dominated high-end market, a chlorate bath with acetic acid; the etch pits are then hardened with a phosphate or chromate formation treatment and the surface is impregnated with the electrolyte. The chloride ion eats its way into the foil along the grain boundaries and leaves a field of round tunnels 0.1-2 um across; oxidation inside those tunnels is what multiplies the area. A formation step then grows oxide in a controlled taper so the weakest point - the mouth of each pit - is the first to fail if the etch is wrong, which is why a 1982 capacitor that failed early failed as a short circuit and a vent rather than as a slow leak.

facts.label: Surface area gain
facts.value: ~50-100x the geometric area after etching and formation

facts.label: Oxide layer
facts.value: order 0.1-1 um of Al2O3, grown by a DC formation voltage

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: chloride, or chlorate plus acetic acid, at about 60-80 C

facts.label: Formation voltage
facts.value: raised in steps to the working voltage of the finished capacitor, typically 6-25 V for a computer supply rail

facts.label: Etch pit
facts.value: 0.1-2 um tunnels along grain boundaries; oxide breakdown at the pit mouth is the failure mode

metal.aluminum.anode-foil.note: The 1980s high-capacitance anode foil industry was concentrated in Japan and the exact etch chemistry was proprietary, split between the chloride and the chlorate camps. Medium confidence on the bath detail. Some formation treatments used chromate for stability, and hexavalent chromium was already being restricted in the workplace by 1982.

metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.tallow.name: Fatty-acid esters from tallow and palm fat
metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.tallow.description: The ester lubricants are made from animal or vegetable fats - tallow, palm, rapeseed - hydrolysed to fatty acids and re-esterified, on a paraffinic mineral base or a synthetic ester. This is the one place in the aluminium chain where biomass chemistry is genuinely load-bearing: an aluminium rolling lubricant is a soap-and-fatty-acid chemistry, not a petrochemical one. In 1982 tallow was still the dominant base; vegetable ester formulations grew through the 1990s.

facts.label: Feedstocks
facts.value: rendered animal fat, pressed palm oil, rapeseed oil

facts.label: Note
facts.value: crude petroleum was still a common base in the cheaper grades

metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.tallow.note: Medium confidence on the 1982 split between tallow, vegetable and petroleum-based grades.

metal.silica.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N
metal.silica.tcs.description: Colourless fuming liquid, the money molecule of the whole silicon industry. Made by chlorinating impure silicon with hydrogen chloride in a fluidised bed, then purified to 11 nines purely by fractional distillation, because every one of the metal impurities that matter happens to be a chloride with a different boiling point from HSiCl3.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 11N (99.999999999%) after distillation

metal.nickel.limonite-garnierite.name: Limonite and garnierite: the two nickel minerals
metal.nickel.limonite-garnierite.description: The leaf of the nickel branch, and it is a mineral solution rather than a mineral. There is no nickel mineral in a laterite. Nickel substitutes for magnesium in the smectite and kaolinite clays - the mineral is garnierite, which is really a mixture - and it substitutes for iron in the goethite of the limonite, so a limonite laterite's nickel is spread through amorphous iron oxide at a few percent. The two grades of laterite that matter commercially are the high-iron limonite ore and the low-silica saprolite ore, and the difference between them is the grade of the nickel-bearing lattice, which is why the pressure leach was developed for one and not the other.

facts.label: Garnierite
facts.value: (Ni,Mg)3Si2O5(OH)4, nickel substituting for magnesium in a smectite

facts.label: Limonite
facts.value: nickel substituting for iron in amorphous goethite, FeO(OH)

facts.label: Two commercial ores
facts.value: high-iron limonite ore and low-silica saprolite ore

metal.dms.fe-silicon.name: Ferrosilicon powder for dense-media separation
metal.dms.fe-silicon.description: The liquid in a dense-medium separator is ferrosilicon - an alloy of iron and silicon made in exactly the submerged arc furnace described in the electrical-steel and metallurgical-silicon branches of this file. So a 1982 concentrator that separated galena from sphalerite by density was running a slurry of metallurgical silicon, and the silicon branch of this tree reaches a zinc concentrator as well as a power transformer. Silicon really does end up everywhere: 60-90% of all ferrosilicon production goes into the steel and aluminium branches, but the rest goes into heavy-media separation, and it is the sharpest possible illustration of why a tree like this has cross-links.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 15-30% Si, ground to under 100 um

facts.label: Source
facts.value: ferrosilicon, made in a submerged arc furnace

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.2-1 kg of ferrosilicon per tonne of ore processed

metal.dms.fe-silicon.note: Medium confidence on the consumption rate; it varies greatly with the ore.

metal.manganese.nodule-rock.name: Manganese oxide concretions on pelagic clay
metal.manganese.nodule-rock.description: The leaf: millimetre-to-centimetre potato-shaped concretions of Mn-Fe oxide lying unattached in a soft abyssal red clay. The metal has precipitated out of seawater around a nucleus, slowly, over millions of years. It is the most extraordinary leaf in this tree: the manganese in a C64's steel is, in principle, available from the floor of an ocean.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: pelagic abyssal red clay, thousands of metres down

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: 1-10 mm per million years

metal.manganese.nodule-rock.note: Documented: manganese nodules are concretions of iron and manganese oxides on the sea floor built in concentric layers around a nucleus, and the largest deposits lie on abyssal plains at 4,000-6,000 m. Not established: the 1-10 mm per million year growth rate, and the host described specifically as abyssal red clay.

metal.manganese.oxide-phase.name: The oxide and carbonate phases of the ore
metal.manganese.oxide-phase.description: The leaf of the manganese branch's rock: the manganese in a supergene ore is not one mineral but four. Pyrolusite MnO2 is the black, soft, fibrous one; psilomelane is a barium-bearing cryptocrystalline mixture; braunite Mn2O3 is the hard brown one; and rhodochrosite MnCO3 is the pink carbonate in the primary zone. The refractory braunite is the one the smelter hates, because it takes three times the reductant and gives a high slag. Which phase a shipment is made of determines whether it goes to a ferromanganese furnace or to a chemical plant, and the assay is a chemical analysis, not a visual test.

facts.label: Pyrolusite
facts.value: MnO2, black and soft, easily reduced

facts.label: Braunite
facts.value: Mn2O3, hard and refractory, expensive to reduce

facts.label: Rhodochrosite
facts.value: MnCO3, pink, in the primary carbonate zone

metal.cupellation.cupel.name: Bone ash cupel from animal bone
metal.cupellation.cupel.description: Traditional cupels are made of calcined bone - tricalcium phosphate - ground and pressed into a shallow cup with a porous, low-density surface that absorbs the molten litharge. Bone ash is the reason cupellation is called what it is, and by the 1982 industry the major refineries had largely moved to magnesia and alumina cupels for the big furnaces, though bone ash was still in use. So a refinery furnace foot was, historically, a rendering-house product.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: calcined bone ash Ca3(PO4)2, or magnesia or alumina for larger units

metal.cupellation.cupel.note: By 1982 the major refineries were largely on magnesia or alumina cupels; medium confidence that bone ash remained in use anywhere significant.

metal.copper.enamel-resin.name: Polyurethane enamel from a di-isocyanate
metal.copper.enamel-resin.description: The wire enamel is a thermosetting urethane, made from a diol and a di-isocyanate such as toluene di-isocyanate, with a blocked-isocyanate cure so the coating is stable in the coating bath and only reacts in the cure oven. Its advantage over phenolic (vinyl formal, the pre-war standard) and polyester is that it strips cleanly and bonds without a heat gun. So a C64 transformer's insulation is a chemical product of the polyurethane industry, not a distillation product.

facts.label: Former standard
facts.value: vinyl formal (phenolic) enamel, still used for thermal class 180

facts.label: 1982 class
facts.value: polyurethane dominated thermal class 130-155

metal.copper.enamel-resin.note: The chemistry of commercial wire enamels is proprietary; medium confidence on the general description.

metal.copper.wire-lubricant.name: Drawing lubricant: copper sulfonate or oil emulsion
metal.copper.wire-lubricant.description: The die must be lubricated or the copper galls and the die wears out. In the 1980s the standard was a water-based emulsion or a copper-sulfonate-and-fatty-acid concentrate, applied in a die box or as a once-through bath. Lubricant chemistry is also the friction and galling story in the die, which is why the drawing lubricant industry is a small speciality chemical business rather than an oil business.

facts.label: Lubricant
facts.value: copper sulfonate or ammonium sulfonate in a fatty-acid base, or an oil-in-water emulsion

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: order 0.5-5% in the emulsion

metal.copper.wire-lubricant.note: Formulations are proprietary; medium confidence on the general chemistry.

metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.name: The diaphragm and the asbestos inheritance
metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.description: The cell needs the anodic chlorine kept away from the trivalent chromium in the catholyte, and the membrane that does that was, until the 1980s, asbestos cloth - the same asbestos as the chlor-alkali diaphragm cells. So the chromium and chlor-alkali industries of the early twentieth century share a materials problem that was only being dealt with in the 1980s, in both cases by a conversion programme driven by worker exposure rather than by metallurgy. The 1982 answer was a synthetic fibre diaphragm, which worked and cost more.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: asbestos cloth, replaced by synthetic fibre and PTFE-lined designs through the 1980s

metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.note: Low confidence on the specific 1982 chromium cell diaphragm practice; the asbestos overlap with chlor-alkali is real, but the chromium side of it is inferred.

metal.bentonite.name: Bentonite binder from a clay pit
metal.bentonite.description: A sodium bentonite with a high swelling capacity, mined from a montmorillonite clay bed and used as the binder that makes a pellet roll up instead of shatter. In 1982 the world bentonite market was dominated by Wyoming and by Italy and the Balkan sources, and it was also the drilling mud of the oil industry, so the two applications competed for the same tonnage. The particular clay a pelletiser wants is a sodium montmorillonite, which is a specific alteration product of volcanic ash - the leaf of this little branch is a bentonite bed in a Tertiary volcanic sequence.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: sodium montmorillonite, high swelling capacity

facts.label: Dose
facts.value: 2-3% of the pellet mass

metal.bentonite.note: Pellet binder levels are standard; the specific source geology is medium confidence.

metal.coke-breeze.name: Coke breeze: the sinter fuel
metal.coke-breeze.description: The 3-10 mm fraction of coke, screened out at the coke plant, that would be too small for the blast furnace. A steelworks' sinter plant is therefore a consumer of its own coke plant's fines - a neat example of an internal recycling loop in the iron and carbon chain that closes from the coke oven's quench, through the sinter plant, back into the blast furnace's burn.

facts.label: Use
facts.value: 8-12% of the sinter mix as the fuel

metal.coke-breeze.note: The coke reference defines coke breeze as the fraction under 10 mm, so the upper bound is right. Not established: the 3 mm lower bound and the 8-12% of the sinter mix share.

metal.silica.reducer.name: Carbothermal reductant: coke and woodchips
metal.silica.reducer.description: The silicon furnace burns roughly one tonne of high-ash-reduction carbon per three tonnes of silicon, and the recipe is a tight compromise: too much ash and you get slag, too much volatile and the furnace fumes. Producers blend low-ash petroleum coke or anthracite with a proportion of woodchips, because the wood brings in hydrogen and potassium that volatilise out and are quietly useful, and because the porosity of the burnt wood helps the charge breathe. The same class of carbon, at different purity, is the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, ferrosilicon, ferromanganese and ferrochrome branches of this file.

facts.label: Ash target
facts.value: <1% for the reducer, versus the 10-12% typical of foundry coke

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.9-1.1 t of carbon per t of silicon

metal.silica.reducer.note: The consumption ratio varies with furnace design and recovery; treat as order of magnitude.

metal.laterite-terrace.name: The Cretaceous laterite surface
metal.laterite-terrace.description: The leaf, geologically: a flat, deeply weathered surface on Cretaceous sandstone where a tropical lateritic profile has developed over tens of millions of years, with a bauxite horizon at the top, kaolinite below it, and the saprolite and fresh rock beneath. The flatness is the point - it is why the pits are cheap and the ore is shallow - and it is a direct consequence of the rock type and of the extraordinarily long, warm, wet chemical weathering that made it.

facts.label: Profile
facts.value: bauxite, kaolinite, saprolite, fresh Cretaceous sandstone

facts.label: Relief
facts.value: a few metres over tens of kilometres, which is what makes surface mining cheap

metal.laterite-terrace.note: Documented: laterite forms by leaching of parent rock under a humid sub-tropical monsoon climate, leaving the more insoluble iron and aluminium oxides, and its composition depends on the parent rock and depth. Not established: that this is a Cretaceous laterite surface on sandstone with a bauxite horizon over kaolinite over saprolite, and the claim that its flatness over tens of kilometres is what makes surface mining cheap.

metal.gold.contact-jewel.name: Gold-plated contacts: the edge connector and the switches
metal.gold.contact-jewel.description: Two very different gold contacts in the C64. The 62-way edge connector at the rear has gold-flashed fingers - a 35 um copper-alloy finger with 0.1-0.5 um of gold and a nickel underplate, inserted in the board by a wipe in the card guides. The keyboard and the rocker switches use either gold-plated copper-alloy leaf springs or, in the better keys, solid silver or silver-alloy contacts. The gold flash on the edge connector is the only place where gold must survive thousands of insertions, and it does so because the nickel underplate stops the copper from diffusing into the gold and the gold itself never oxidises.

facts.label: Edge connector
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 um gold flash on 1-3 um nickel over a copper-alloy finger

facts.label: Insertion life
facts.value: 50,000-100,000 insertion cycles is a normal target for a gold-flashed card edge

facts.label: Why gold
facts.value: no oxide, no tarnish; noble metal does not form a resistive film

facts.label: Jewel switches
facts.value: some high-end switches used solid gold-alloy leaf springs, but 1982 consumer keyboards mostly used silver-plated or nickel-plated springs

metal.gold.contact-jewel.note: The gold flash thickness and the contact material choice on the actual Commodore keyboard I cannot confirm; these are the standard ranges. Medium confidence on the specifics, high on the metallurgy.

metal.cassiterite.gravel.name: Stanniferous alluvium and laterite
metal.cassiterite.gravel.description: The leaf: unconsolidated stony clay and gravel of a valley floor or a coastal plain, with cassiterite grains scattered through it and concentrated at the base of gravel layers where the wave or the stream action is right. In Malaysia it is a young alluvial fan over limestone; in Bolivia it is not alluvial at all but a hard-rock lode in Ordovician slates and granites, which is why Bolivia's process chain is longer.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: alluvial gravel over limestone (Perak) or residual laterite over a lode (Bolivia, Cornwall)

children.name: Cassiterite lode in the Bolivian and Cornwall tin belt
children.description: For contrast: the tin lodes of the Cordillera Real in Bolivia and of the Cambrian granite cupolas in Cornwall are hydrothermal cassiterite in quartz veins and greisens, and they have to be blasted and milled. Bolivia's Oruro and La Paz districts still supply a fraction of world tin from ore averaging 0.3-1% Sn, with the famous manioc mill and the hydraulic concentrator. Cornwall's industry was by 1982 essentially finished - the last deep mine closed in 1984 - a hundred years after the smelter industry had been moved to the East.

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% Sn in lodes and pipes

facts.label: Cornwall's end
facts.value: Grezmerry closed in 1984, ending Cornish tin mining after 2,500 years

metal.aluminum.mill-scale.name: Mill scale (iron-bearing aluminium oxide)
metal.aluminum.mill-scale.description: Hot rolling oxidises the surface and the scale is knocked off by the descaling rolls. The chips that fall are a mix of alumina and iron oxides pulled in from the ingot surface, and they are the same material the ferroalloy and cement industries fought over - and, ground and magnetically separated, the raw iron oxide for soft ferrites. In 1982 most was dumped.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Al2O3 with 5-30% Fe2O3

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 30-60 kg of scale per tonne of hot-rolled strip

metal.aluminum.mill-scale.note: Iron content varies with ingot surface condition; medium confidence on the range.

metal.zinc-oxide-powder.name: Zinc oxide powder
metal.zinc-oxide-powder.description: Zinc oxide for ceramics was, in 1982, made by burning high-purity zinc in air, by calcining high-purity zinc carbonate, or - for the highest grades - by the vapour-phase oxidation of high-purity zinc metal, which gives spherical sub-micron particles with a very tight size distribution. A varistor powder needs high-purity ZnO because any foreign phase at the grain boundary changes the voltage knee. So the varistor in the C64's power supply starts with 99.99% zinc.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: combustion or calcination; vapour-phase oxidation for the best powder

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: sub-micron for the vapour route

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 2Zn + O2 -> 2ZnO at 400-600 C

metal.zinc-oxide-powder.note: The exact powder route for a given varistor is proprietary; medium confidence. The atmospheric oxidation of zinc metal is the bottom of this branch and is a certainty.

metal.salt-solar-pan.name: Evaporate brine in a solar salt pond
metal.salt-solar-pan.description: A series of shallow ponds, from 2 m down to 30 cm, through which seawater is stepped down in salinity, precipitating gypsum first and then halite. A hectare of pond evaporates tens of thousands of tonnes of salt a year. The leaf is a solar pond on a coastal lagoon.

facts.label: Depth steps
facts.value: 2-5 m intake, 0.3 m evaporator, 0.2 m crystalliser

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 100-200 kg per m2 of pond per year

metal.salt-solar-pan.note: Yields are strongly climate-dependent; medium confidence on the per-hectare figure.

metal.chlor-alkali.name: Chlor-alkali electrolytic cell
metal.chlor-alkali.description: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2. In 1982 almost all of it was a diaphragm cell or a mercury cell. The diaphragm cell - an asbestos-cloth cathode separator - gave low-purity caustic loaded with salt and was steadily displaced through the late 1970s and 1980s by the membrane cell, which delivers 50% NaOH essentially free of salt. Mercury cell caustic went to a short finishing step, causticisation with sodium carbonate, to strip the last mercury; the Hooker Chemical conversion of its Niagara Falls works to membrane in 1984 is the emblematic date.

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 3.0-4.5 V diaphragm, 4-5 V membrane, 4.5-5 V mercury

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: ~2300-2700 kWh per tonne of chlorine

facts.label: 1982 technology split
facts.value: diaphragm dominant, membrane a fast-growing minority, mercury still common

facts.label: Chlorine purity
facts.value: ~98-99% dry, enough for HCl synthesis

children.name: The diaphragm cell and the asbestos problem
children.description: The 1980s chlor-alkali cell was a rectangular steel box, 2-3 m long, with an anode compartment of brine and a cathode compartment of water separated by an asbestos cloth diaphragm deposited on a wire gauze. The diaphragm was cheap, durable and effective, and it was the reason the world's chlor-alkali industry had a mesothelioma problem. The cell voltage was low, 3.0-3.5 V, and the caustic carried 10-15 g/L of salt because the diaphragm let chloride through. The Hooker Chemical conversion at Niagara Falls in 1984 to a membrane cell was the moment the asbestos diaphragm began to disappear from the industry.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: 2-3 m long rectangular steel box, brine anode compartment, water cathode compartment

facts.label: Diaphragm
facts.value: asbestos cloth on a steel gauze

facts.label: Caustic impurity
facts.value: 10-15 g/L of NaCl carried through

facts.label: Transition date
facts.value: Hooker Chemical converted its Niagara Falls works to membrane in 1984

children.note: The Hooker conversion year is a well-documented landmark in the chlor-alkali industry.

children.name: Dechlorination and the brine circuit
children.description: The brine leaving a cell still has hypochlorite in it, because chlorine dissolves in the caustic. It is treated with sodium sulphite and then acidified, the brine is re-saturated with salt and re-purified on a soda ash and barium carbonate cycle, and it goes back to the cell. So a chlor-alkali plant also consumes sodium carbonate and barium carbonate - the latter being, note, the barium carbonate from the barium branch of this file. The barium carbonate is there to remove the sulphate from the brine as barium sulphate, which is filtered off and, until the 1980s, dumped.

facts.label: Dechlorination
facts.value: sodium sulphite, then hydrochloric acid to pH 2-3

facts.label: Sulphate removal
facts.value: barium carbonate -> barium sulphate sludge, filtered and discarded

facts.label: Brine consumption
facts.value: order 0.3-0.6 t of salt per tonne of chlorine

children.note: Medium confidence on the consumption figures; the barium carbonate sulphate removal is standard practice.

children.name: Membrane cell
children.description: The cell type that replaced the mercury cell through the 1980s: a perfluorosulfonate membrane separating the anode and cathode, giving chlorine at 99.5%+ without the mercury the older cell had to manage. The conversion of the world's chlor-alkali from mercury to membrane was one of the largest and fastest industrial changeovers of the decade, and it was driven by mercury emissions - the same environmental logic that removed mercury from the PVC acetylene process.
children.note: The membrane cell commercialised from the late 1970s and displaced mercury cells through the 1980s-90s; the timetable varied by region.

metal.hall-heroult.name: Hall-Heroult electrolysis of alumina in cryolite
metal.hall-heroult.description: The cell is a steel shell the size of a bathtub lined with carbon, containing 300-500 t of molten cryolite at 950-970 C. Alumina dissolves in the melt and is reduced at a carbon cathode; current passes through the anodes, where the oxygen from the alumina burns the carbon away and makes carbon dioxide. The metal pools on the floor and is tapped every day or two. A pot takes 3-6 V at 100-200 kA, which is why a 200,000 t/year smelter is also a 2-3 GW power station.

facts.label: Bath temperature
facts.value: 950-970 C; cryolite alone melts at 1012 C

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 3.5-4.5 V against a theoretical minimum of about 2.1 V

facts.label: Current
facts.value: 100-200 kA per pot; one pot makes 1-3 t of aluminium a day

facts.label: Current efficiency
facts.value: 80-90% in 1980s plants

facts.label: Power
facts.value: 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne of aluminium; 1982-era plants were commonly 15,000-17,000

facts.label: Net reaction
facts.value: 2 Al2O3 + 3 C -> 4 Al + 3 CO2

facts.label: 1980s technology
facts.value: the point feeder and prebaked anode design of 1980, which raised current density to 0.7-0.8 A/cm2, is still the state of the art; no fundamental change since

metal.hall-heroult.note: The ~2.1 V theoretical minimum cell voltage and the ~90% ceiling on current efficiency are why the energy number has barely moved since 1950.

children.name: Carbon pot lining and the cathodic block
children.description: The steel shell is lined first with refractory brick, then with a monolithic carbon lining about 400-600 mm thick made of calcined coke, graphite and hot pitch, rammed in place. A block lining of graphitised carbon blocks is better and was common in newer cells. The lining is deliberately cathodic: the aluminium that seeps into the pores becomes a cathode of itself, and when the cell is finally relined after 3-8 years the spent lining is leached for the metal it swallowed.

facts.label: Lining thickness
facts.value: 400-600 mm monolithic, plus 200-300 mm of brick

facts.label: Lining life
facts.value: 3-8 years

facts.label: Pitch coke after bake-out
facts.value: about 2000-3000 C

facts.label: Metal locked up in a spent lining
facts.value: order 5-15 t of aluminium per pot

children.name: Alumina dredges and the alumina crust
children.description: Alumina fed into the pot floats and solidifies into a chilled crust on the bath surface, which is far more stable than loose powder. Machines called dredges or skimmers break holes in this crust and feed alumina down them at a controlled rate; the classic 1980 design was the dual-feed with pneumatic runners. The holes are also where carbon dust from the anode is skimmed off. A floating crust is good for the pot but insulates the bath, so the balance between a thick stable crust and a cool cell is the operator's whole job.

facts.label: Feed rate
facts.value: order 1-1.5 kg of alumina per kA-hour

children.note: The feed rate is a rule of thumb that varies with cell design; medium confidence.

children.name: Aluminium dross and the skimmings
children.description: Two or three tonnes of dross and sludge per pot per year: oxide, carbon, and aluminium that never reached the cathode. Because aluminium dross burns spectacularly it must be handled under cover, and the smelter had a dross furnace to burn out the aluminium and get it back. The recovered metal is dirty and low grade, and in 1982 it went straight back into the pot - a small but real recycling loop, since remelted aluminium needs only about 5% of the energy of primary metal.

facts.label: Yield loss
facts.value: roughly 2-4% of metal production leaves as dross

facts.label: Remelt saving
facts.value: ~5% of the primary electrolysis energy

children.note: The roughly 5% remelt saving is the widely quoted fraction of primary energy; medium confidence on precision.

metal.cryolite.synthesis.name: Synthetic cryolite from hydrofluoric acid
metal.cryolite.synthesis.description: Because natural cryolite was one mine in Greenland, the industry made its own.
