Sodium carbonate or caustic soda reacts with hydrofluoric acid and aluminium hydroxide at 60-90 C: 6HF + 3Na2CO3 + Al(OH)3 -> 2Na3AlF6 + 3CO2 + 3H2O. So the electrolyte solvent of the aluminium pot is manufactured from fluorspar, caustic soda and alumina - three of this file's other endpoints in one reaction.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 6HF + 3Na2CO3 + Al(OH)3 -> 2Na3AlF6 + 3CO2 + 3H2O

facts.label: Also used for
facts.value: the sodium cryolite is a constituent of the EPA-registered rodenticide and insecticide 'cryolite' - a genuinely different market

metal.bayer.name: Bayer process
metal.bayer.description: A 110-year-old caustic-leach purification that every tonne of aluminium still goes through. Five steps: crush and wash, digest in caustic at pressure, clarify and throw away the red mud, cool and precipitate pure aluminium hydroxide, calcine to alumina. It works because the alumina in bauxite is amphoteric - it dissolves in hot caustic as sodium aluminate - while the iron and titanium oxides are not, and silica is neutralised by lime into a harmless calcium silicate.

facts.label: Steps
facts.value: preparation, digestion, dilution and red-mud separation, precipitation, calcination

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 150-200 C for low-temperature gibbsitic ore; 240-280 C for high-temperature diasporic

facts.label: Lime
facts.value: added during digestion as a desilication reagent

children.name: Caustic digestion in autoclaves
children.description: Bauxite slurry and 150-300 g/L free caustic (as Na2O) are charged into stirred autoclaves and held at temperature for 30-90 minutes. The alumina dissolves as NaAl(OH)4; the iron oxide stays as a red slurry. Older low-temperature plants used a bank of horizontal autoclaves with indirect steam heating; high-temperature plants used vertical autoclaves. The pressure was only 5-15 bar because the vessel was not a modern high-pressure autoclave but a horizontal drum with a vapour space.

facts.label: Free caustic
facts.value: ~150-300 g/L as Na2O

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 140-150 C gibbsitic; 240-280 C diasporic

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: order 5-15 bar gauge, set by the boiling point of the liquor

facts.label: Al2O3 extraction
facts.value: >95% of the available alumina

children.note: Documented: bauxite is heated in a pressure vessel with a sodium hydroxide solution at 150 to 200 C, and the aluminium dissolves as sodium aluminate, primarily Al(OH)4-. Not established, and partly in tension with that reference: the 140-150 C gibbsitic and 240-280 C diasporic split, the 150-300 g/L free caustic as Na2O, the 30-90 min residence and the greater than 95% extraction. The high-temperature Bayer plant for diasporic bauxite is real but is not described in this reference.

children.name: Reactive silica and the lime reaction
children.description: The killer impurity in bauxite is reactive silica - kaolinite clay and opal - which dissolves in the caustic and then reacts with aluminate to form a non-redissolving kaolinite-nepheline hydrate that permanently traps alumina. Two defences. In low-temperature digestion the clay is left undissolved by keeping the caustic concentration high. In high-temperature digestion the reactive silica dissolves, so lime is added and the silica is converted to hydrogrossite; the liquor is then given a short holding period during which the silica precipitates harmlessly. Every tonne of bauxite eats some caustic and some tens of kilos of lime that never come back.

facts.label: Reactive silica penalty
facts.value: order 3-6 kg Na2O and 1-2 kg Al2O3 lost per 1% reactive silica

facts.label: Pre-desilication step
facts.value: removing clay by attrition washing before digestion, standard for high-silica ore

children.note: The penalty range depends strongly on how the silica is mineralogically bound; medium confidence.

children.name: Clarify the liquor and dam the red mud
children.description: The digested slurry is diluted with process water, cooled, and settled in a bank of gravity settlers with mechanical rakes; the red mud bottoms out and is pumped to the mud dam. A large plant produces 100-150 tonnes of red mud per tonne of alumina, which is why every alumina refinery has a mud dam engineered like a tailings facility.

facts.label: Red mud ratio
facts.value: 100-150 t per t of Al2O3 produced

facts.label: Settling time
facts.value: 1-4 hours in a deep cone settler

facts.label: Sodium loss
facts.value: order 5-15 kg Na2O per tonne of alumina goes out with the mud

children.name: Precipitate aluminium hydroxide from the cooled liquor
children.description: The clear caustic aluminate solution is cooled from 100-110 C to 60-80 C and seeded with a few grams per litre of finely ground aluminium hydroxide already in the plant. The seed grows into the supersaturated solution as a hexagonal-plate alumina trihydrate over 24-48 hours, and the mud is filtered and washed. Washing matters twice over: to remove the caustic that would otherwise attack the kiln, and to recover the soda. The mother liquor goes back to digestion, and this recycle loop is what makes the caustic consumption manageable at all.

facts.label: Cooling
facts.value: from about 105 C to 60-80 C

facts.label: Seed
facts.value: 0.5-5 g/L of fine Al(OH)3

facts.label: Product
facts.value: alumina trihydrate, 2-8% soda before washing

children.name: Rotary vacuum filtration and counter-current washing
children.description: The hydrate is filtered on a rotating vacuum drum with cloth- or paper-covered segments, then washed on a multi-stage counter-current filter. By the time the wash water reaches the pregnant liquor the caustic is essentially recovered, so the caustic circuit closes to better than 95%. This single piece of equipment is why alumina refining has the caustic efficiency it does.

facts.label: Filtration rate
facts.value: order 0.3-1.5 kg of hydrate per m2 of filter area per minute

children.note: Filtration rates vary with product particle size; medium confidence on the range.

children.name: Calcine the trihydrate to smelter-grade alumina
children.description: The hydrate goes into a rotary kiln or, more often by 1982, a fluidised-bed calciner, and at 1000-1100 C it gives off its water of crystallisation and recrystallises from gamma through theta to alpha alumina. Alpha alumina is the hard, insoluble, spark-resistant form that will dissolve in cryolite. The rotary kiln burns 400-600 kg of fuel oil or gas equivalent per tonne of alumina and emits a lot of carbon dioxide; the fluidised bed is more efficient and was being adopted through the 1980s.

facts.label: Product form
facts.value: alpha-Al2O3, 99.5%+, with under 1% loss on ignition

facts.label: Water removed
facts.value: 3 H2O per Al2O3, i.e. 34% of the hydrate's mass

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: ~300-600 kg of oil equivalent per tonne of alumina

facts.label: Steam recovery
facts.value: the kiln flue gas is used to generate process steam, standard since the 1970s

children.name: Fluidised-bed calciner
children.description: Hot gas from a multi-flash evaporator is blown through a bed of alumina hydrate on a distributor of alloy nozzles, holding the bed fluid at 1000-1100 C by balancing gas throughput against feed rate. The bed fluidises like a boiling liquid and every grain sees the same temperature, which is exactly why the alpha alumina comes out with a tight particle-size distribution. The 1980s smelter-grade alumina market effectively standardised on this machine.

facts.label: Particle size out
facts.value: roughly 20-100 um, closed-loop ground

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: uniform residence time, so alpha conversion completes in one pass

metal.stainless.cold-work.name: Cold rolling, bright annealing and finishing of stainless
metal.stainless.cold-work.description: Stainless is rolled and formed by the same equipment as mild steel - a Sendimir mill, a continuous annealing line, a Timesaver - but the tooling is different, because austenitic stainless work-hardens violently and needs much more force, and because a bright anneal must be carried out in hydrogen or in a vacuum to avoid discolouration and to avoid needing a thick pickling. A 1982 bright annealing line used hydrogen at 1000-1100 C with dewpoint control, which is a very refined piece of metallurgy for a machine that cost $395.

facts.label: Bright anneal
facts.value: 1000-1100 C in dry hydrogen, or in vacuum

facts.label: Pickling
facts.value: mixed nitric and hydrofluoric acid, or a nitric-sulphuric alternate

facts.label: Work hardening
facts.value: 304 work-hardens to about 1.3 GPa tensile before it must be annealed

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: 20-30% nitric acid, 30 min, at room temperature or 50 C

metal.stainless.cold-work.note: The nitric-hydrofluoric pickle is the classic stainless pickling line; by 1982 lower-HF alternatives were being developed for environmental reasons. Medium confidence on the transition timing.

metal.magnetite.roasting.name: Fluidised-bed roasting of magnetite concentrate
metal.magnetite.roasting.description: The Krivoy Rog and Finnish magnetite concentrates were roasted before magnetic separation and before the blast furnace, because a magnetite concentrate that has been oxidised to hematite sinter is far easier to reduce - hematite is the reducible oxide, magnetite is not. A fluidised bed of concentrate with a magnetite-gangue composition can be held at 700-800 C indefinitely without sintering, and it is the only economical way to oxidise a hundred thousand tonnes of fine concentrate. The plant is a tall rectangular refractory-lined box with a bed of nozzles on the floor and water-cooled walls, and its throughput is enormous.

facts.label: Feed size
facts.value: under 0.1 mm concentrate

facts.label: Product
facts.value: hematite sinter, with the sulphur and the alkalis driven off

metal.magnetite.roasting.note: Medium confidence; the fluidised-bed roast is standard Soviet and Finnish practice but the parameters are plant-specific.

children.name: Oxide pellets and the direct reduction route
children.description: A different branch of the same ore: magnetite concentrate is the only ore that can be reduced to sponge iron directly, without coke, by a hydrogen-nitrogen mixture at 1100-1200 C in a shaft furnace. That is the MIDOR and HYL processes, which by 1982 were the strategic reserve of the steel industry in the oil shock years - a few per cent of world steel but a hedge, and the reason a Soviet or Brazilian or Venezuelan integrated steelworks would spend a decade building an ore-based direct-reduction plant. It is also the only ore that can be shipped as a pellet and reduced at a distant site without smelting.

facts.label: Gas
facts.value: natural gas reformed to H2/N2 at 55-65% H2

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: magnetite or hematite pellets, 8-16 mm

facts.label: 1982 share
facts.value: a small percentage of world steel, but a strategic one after 1973

children.note: Direct reduction was a genuine 1980s strategic technology; medium confidence on the 1982 share.

metal.nickel.drying.name: Dry the laterite before smelting
metal.nickel.drying.description: A laterite arrives at 30-45% moisture and the submerged arc furnace cannot take it wet, because the water costs more steam than the reaction releases. So the dewatered ore is dried in a rotary dryer or - in the Cuban and Philippine operations of the 1980s - in a suspension dryer with the hot flue gas, to below 1-2% moisture, and the drier's exhaust is the source of the dust and the fuel consumption that dominated the cost. Some plants solved the problem differently: the Queensland operations calcined and reduced the ore on the pad and then shipped a nickel oxide, which moved the water problem upstream to the leach.

facts.label: Feed moisture
facts.value: 30-45% from the washing plant

facts.label: Product moisture
facts.value: below 1-2%

facts.label: Alternatives
facts.value: rotary dryer, or a suspension dryer, or on-pad reduction and shipping a nickel oxide

metal.nickel.drying.note: Medium confidence; the alternative routes are well documented for specific operations.

metal.manganese.nodule.name: Abyssal manganese nodule dredge
metal.manganese.nodule.description: The other, entirely different source: polymetallic nodules lying in thousands of square kilometres of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone and the Peru Basin at 4,000-6,000 m depth, containing 30% Mn, 2% Ni, 1% Cu and 25% Fe. Collecting them means a 10,000-tonne ship dragging a pipe across the seabed for 20,000 hours a year. It was never commercial in 1982 - technology trials were running but no mine was producing - and the incentive that eventually made it real was nickel, not manganese. This node is here because the 1980s seabed mining industry was built by exactly the people looking at the ore as a nickel resource, and by 1982 the C64's nickel supply chain and this geological curiosity were the same corporate conversation.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: hydraulic collector on a dragline with a riser to a ship, or a riserless system

facts.label: 1982 status
facts.value: technology demonstration only; no commercial production until decades later

children.name: Why the 1970s nodule trials were abandoned
children.description: By 1982 seabed nodule mining was a real programme with real money behind it, and the money is the interesting part. The incentive was not manganese - the grades were assumed recoverable but nobody had proved it at scale. The incentive was nickel and cobalt, because the strategic metal studies of the 1970s and early 1980s concluded that the West had too little nickel and too little cobalt and that the seabed was the answer. The trials - the French Nodule, the American DOMES and NOAA work, the Japanese and the German programmes - put a collector on the bottom and brought up tonnages. Nothing commercial resulted before the 2000s, largely on legal grounds, but the 1982 assessment was optimistic, and that is a genuine piece of the 1982 story rather than hindsight.

facts.label: Programmes
facts.value: Nodule (France), DOMES and NOAA (United States), and Japanese and German programmes

facts.label: Incentive
facts.value: strategic-mine concern about nickel and cobalt supply, not about manganese

facts.label: 1982 outcome
facts.value: no commercial production; trials demonstrated recovery at the collector only

children.note: Low confidence on the specific programme details and outcomes. The strategic argument of the period is well understood; the individual trials are not.

children.name: The hydraulic collector head
children.description: The machine the whole idea rests on: a manifold of suction nozzles, 10-30 m across, towed along the seabed at 1-3 knots, that lifts the nodules into a riser pipe and up to a ship 4,000-6,000 m above. The 1970s trials worked at the point where the ocean is deepest to learn whether nodules survive being lifted - the attrition of the nodules on the way up turned out to be a genuine engineering problem - and the riserless concepts that would have solved it were still on paper. It is a beautiful illustration of how much of deep-sea mining is really a fluid mechanics problem.

facts.label: Collector
facts.value: 10-30 m manifold of suction nozzles, towed at 1-3 knots

facts.label: Riser
facts.value: several thousand metres of pipe to a surface ship

children.note: Low confidence on the specific dimensions; the general design is standard and the detail is prototype-specific.

metal.die-steel.vacuum.name: Vacuum melting and the purity of tool steel
metal.die-steel.vacuum.description: A tool steel that contains a hundred parts per million of sulphur will embrittle, and one with two hundred ppm of oxygen will pit. So the melt for a die is made in a vacuum induction or a vacuum arc furnace rather than in an air-melted crucible, and the ingot is remelted by the VAR or the EB process - electron beam - which gives a fine equiaxed grain with no inclusions and no segregation. The vacuum arc furnace is a modified version of the vacuum-arc remelting process that the titanium industry invented, and by 1982 the extrusion die industry and the mould industry both bought them.

facts.label: Processes
facts.value: VIM, then VAR or EBCHM remelting

facts.label: Sulphur target
facts.value: below about 0.005% for a good die steel

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: a 2 t extrusion die blank in vacuum-processed SKD61 cost several times a conventionally cast one

metal.die-steel.vacuum.note: Medium confidence; vacuum melting of tool steel is standard practice but the specific purity targets are supplier-specific.

metal.copper.ingot-casting.name: Copper ingot and rod casting
metal.copper.ingot-casting.description: The cathode is melted in an induction furnace or a reverberatory with a controlled sulphur addition, then cast - either continuously into wire rod by the Properzi upcast method or into 250-450 kg ingots for further processing. The 1980s standard route to rod was continuous casting; the alternative, longer route was a DC casting machine feeding a wire rod mill. Melting loses almost nothing because copper does not oxidise appreciably; the real problem is gas absorption.

facts.label: Melting
facts.value: 1150-1250 C, induction or gas-fired reverberatory, under a cover

facts.label: Rod diameters
facts.value: 6.0-8.0 mm for drawing, cast as wire rod

facts.label: Deoxidation
facts.value: phosphorus added as a copper-phosphorus master alloy, 0.01-0.05% residual

children.name: Upcast wire rod line
children.description: In the Properzi upcaster the melt runs out of a horizontal holding furnace into a vertical casting trough behind a steel die that is being drawn upward by a rotating carousel; the trough is water-cooled and the copper solidifies against the moving die face, giving a controlled solidification structure. It makes 6-9 mm rod very cheaply and was standard in the 1980s, though the resulting cast structure needs patenting before drawing.

facts.label: Cast speed
facts.value: order 0.1-0.5 m/s

facts.label: Output
facts.value: single upcaster order 2-6 t/h

children.note: Upcasting was still widely used in the 1980s but continuous casting replaced it from the 1990s; medium confidence on the 1982 split.

metal.copper.ingot-casting.note: Not established: the Properzi upcast route, the 250-450 kg ingot, the 1150-1250 C melt under a cover, the 6.0-8.0 mm wire rod diameters, and the 0.01-0.05% residual phosphorus. The copper refining reference reached in this pass resolves to the general Refining (metallurgy) article, which does not cover rod casting, and there is no Wikipedia article on wire-rod casting.

metal.copper.anode.casting.name: Anode casting and the anode scrap stream
metal.copper.anode.casting.description: About 10-20% of the anode never makes it into a cell - it is broken in handling, or the bars are too thin, or the busbar is corroded away - and it goes back to be remelted and recast. Every tankhouse therefore has a stub and an anode scrap yard and a melt, and the plant's anode book is a mass balance between the smelter's output and the tankhouse's demand. At the end of its life an anode is a thin, perforated, gold-bearing skeleton of iron and lead oxide that goes back to the smelter, so the gold in the anode is in a closed loop with the refinery and the melt is where the loop is closed.

facts.label: Anode stub and scrap
facts.value: 10-20% of the anode mass returns to remelting

facts.label: Busbar
facts.value: a cast copper bar, and the contact point where the anode is electrically connected

metal.copper.anode.casting.note: Medium confidence on the stub and scrap rate; it varies by tankhouse practice.

metal.copper.foil.ed-drum.name: Electro-deposited drum foil
metal.copper.foil.ed-drum.description: A rotating drum cathode, 1-2 m diameter and 1-1.5 m wide, dips into an acid copper sulphate bath and turns; copper plates onto it at 20-100 A/dm2. A scraper peels the foil off at the top of the drum as a continuous 6-18 um web, which is then slit and wound. The deposit is not bulk metal: it is a columnar, sometimes dendritic growth, which is exactly why it etches into foil capacitors so well and why, for PCBs, it needs a bonding treatment before the laminate resin will stick to it.

facts.label: Drum
facts.value: 1-2 m diameter, rotating cathode, 100-500 A/dm2

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: CuSO4/H2SO4 with a brightener and a suppressant; the additive package is proprietary

facts.label: Grain
facts.value: columnar and favourably oriented, unlike rolled foil's rolled structure

children.name: Nodular treatment for PCB foil adhesion
children.description: Bare copper foil will not bond to epoxy; it delaminates. So the foil is treated in a warm sulfuric acid bath with a silicofluoride or a silane - historically sodium silicofluoride, later silanes - which grows a forest of microscopic oxide nodules on the surface. The resin flows into the forest and locks in, and the peel strength goes from a few N/cm to about 20 N/cm. This etching of the foil surface is the single most important step in making a copper-clad laminate, and the silicofluoride comes from the same fluorochemical industry as the hydrofluoric acid in the aluminium and tantalum branches.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: 0.5-2.5% silicofluoride in 15-30% sulfuric acid at 40-70 C

facts.label: Peel strength
facts.value: order 20 N/cm after treatment, versus a few N/cm untreated

facts.label: 1982 practice
facts.value: sodium silicofluoride in sulfuric acid; the chromic-acid treatment was being phased out

children.note: The exact chemistry shifted through the 1980s and the chromate-era process was being abandoned for toxicological reasons; medium confidence.

metal.anode-slime.cupellation.name: Cupellation of the gold-silver dross
metal.anode-slime.cupellation.description: The slime is smelted with lead and flux into a litharge, then the litharge is blown with air in a cupellation furnace. The lead and everything else oxidises and is absorbed by a bone-ash or magnesite cupel, and what is left on the cupel is gold and silver together. This is the oldest refinery process in the book and it was still standard in 1982, because it is simple and it works.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 1100-1200 C in the cupellation furnace

facts.label: Cupel material
facts.value: bone ash (calcium phosphate) or magnesia

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 6-24 h per charge depending on the mass

metal.nickel.electroplating.name: Nickel electroplating and the gold underplate
metal.nickel.electroplating.description: The single most important metallurgical fact about nickel in a 1982 C64: gold plating does not sit on copper. It sits on a nickel underplate of 1-3 um, and the reason is electrochemistry - gold will not plate directly onto copper because the copper dissolves faster than the gold deposits, and a gold-copper diffusion couple makes a brittle, corrosion-prone joint. So the connector fingers and the IC leads get nickel and then a thin gold flash, or electroless nickel - a nickel-phosphorus deposit from a hypophosphite bath - followed by gold. The electroless route was standard in the semiconductor industry of the era and was how the die-attached gold on a hybrid IC was built.

facts.label: Watts bath
facts.value: nickel sulphate plus nickel chloride plus boric acid, 50-60 C, pH 4.0-4.5

facts.label: Voltage and current
facts.value: 3-8 V, 2-8 A/dm2; 15-60 s for a flash

facts.label: Underplate
facts.value: 1-3 um of nickel under 0.05-0.25 um of gold

facts.label: Electroless nickel
facts.value: Ni-P from nickel sulphate and sodium hypophosphite, 3-8% phosphorus, at 85-95 C

metal.nickel.electroplating.note: The Watts bath composition is textbook; the specific underplate thicknesses on Commodore's connectors in 1982 are not something I can confirm. Medium confidence on the specific figures, high on the mechanism.

metal.hydrochloric-acid.synthesis.name: HCl synthesis and absorption
metal.hydrochloric-acid.synthesis.description: Chlorine and hydrogen are fed to a steel burner with a plug of graphite or a water film that quenches the flame - a free gas-phase hydrogen-chlorine reaction is not something you leave unattended. The hot HCl gas is then absorbed in a water scrubber to make the azeotrope, and the acid is pumped out to wherever it is going: the fluidised bed, the pickle line, the tankhouse.

facts.label: Flame temperature
facts.value: >2000 C, quenched below 400 C within milliseconds

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: water scrubber, adiabatic, controlled by a weak-acid bleed

metal.zinc.galvanising.name: Hot-dip galvanising of steel strip
metal.zinc.galvanising.description: Steel sheet, strip or fabric is pickled in hydrochloric acid, fluxed in an ammonium chloride-zinc chloride bath, and dipped in a kettle of molten zinc at 450-470 C. The zinc wets the steel, forms an iron-zinc intermetallic, and the kettle surface is skimmed of dross by a wiper roll. Every galvanising line in the world consumed thousands of tonnes of zinc a year this way, and a big continuous strip line used 50-300 t a day. The C64 itself is not galvanised, but its chassis and any sheet-metal bracket, and much of the world around it, was.

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: 45-85 g/m2 for sheet; 300-600 g/m2 for fabric

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: a continuous strip line uses 50-300 t of zinc a day, of which the dross is a real loss

facts.label: Coating form
facts.value: pure zinc for general use; Zn-Al alloy for high-drip lines; Zn-Ni for automotive sheet

metal.zinc.galvanising.note: Zinc-aluminium and zinc-nickel coated sheet for automotive was a 1980s development, not a 1982 consumer-electronics one.

children.name: Recover the zinc from the galvanising dross
children.description: The iron-rich dross and the bottom ash skinned off a galvanising kettle are picked out, and the metal is recovered in a specialised horizontal crucible furnace, where the dross is heated with a flux and the iron drops out as Fe-Zn hard zinc. The remaining zinc is pumped out. A galvanising line therefore recovers most of its zinc, and in 1982 the galvanising industry was also the main secondary source of zinc, second only to galvanised scrap.

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 70-90% of the dross metal is recovered

children.note: Recovery efficiency varies with dross age; medium confidence.

metal.zinc.die-cast.name: Zamak die-cast alloy and the pressure die-caster
metal.zinc.die-cast.description: Zinc's most interesting product for this tree. A zinc alloy with 4% aluminium and a little copper - Zamak 3 is Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5, Zamak 5 with 5% aluminium for better die-castability - is injected into a steel die at 380-430 C under 20-150 MPa by a cold-chamber machine with 200-800 tonnes of clamping force. It fills the thinnest sections any metal can fill - 0.8 mm walls, and details you could not machine - and it holds a fine surface as cast. The 1982 pressure die-caster was a 350-800 tonne machine, and the seconds per shot multiplied by the shots an hour is the number that set the cost of a key plunger or a case bracket.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: Zamak 3: Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5; Zamak 5: Zn 95 / Al 5 / Cu 0.5

facts.label: Clamp force
facts.value: 200-800 t on a 1982 machine

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 1-5 s per shot; 400-700 shots per hour on a small machine

facts.label: Minimum wall
facts.value: 0.8-1.0 mm, tighter than aluminium

metal.zinc.die-cast.note: Zinc die casting lost share to aluminium and to engineering polymers during the 1980s-90s, and the alloy names (Zamak, ZA, ZA-8) are supplier-dependent. High confidence on the chemistry and the process, medium on the specific alloy for any Commodore part.

children.name: Zinc alloy melting furnace
children.description: The die-caster does not melt its own alloy from primary metal; it buys 10-25 kg alloy ingots of a certified composition and melts them in a thermostatically controlled holding furnace - typically a 100-500 kg crucible furnace with an immersed resistance heater and a lead bath to keep the alloy away from air. A crucible furnace full of molten zinc is the classic source of metal-fume fever among die-casters, because zinc oxide fume is generated wherever the surface is disturbed.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: 100-500 kg crucible, resistance or oil-heated, 380-430 C, held under a cover flux

facts.label: Occupational hazard
facts.value: zinc oxide fume from disturbed surfaces; metal-fume fever

children.note: Furnace design varies widely; medium confidence on capacities.

metal.zinc.electroplate.name: Electrolytic zinc plating of steel
metal.zinc.electroplate.description: For small plated parts - chassis fasteners, brackets, EMI shields - zinc is electroplated rather than dipped. An alkaline cyanide bath, a non-cyanide acid chloride bath, or in the barrel a simple sulphate. The deposit is sacrificial: even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially and protects the steel underneath. A chromate passivation on top gives the characteristic yellow or olive colour and much better corrosion resistance, and by 1982 chromate was already being restricted because of hexavalent chromium.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: alkaline cyanide zincate, or acid chloride, or sulphate

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: 5-25 um for passivated decorative and EMI shielding work

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: yellow or olive chromate conversion coating

metal.zinc.electroplate.note: Trivalent chromium passivation arrived in the 1990s-2000s; hexavalent chromate was the 1982 norm.

metal.lead.cupellation-lead.name: Cupellation of the silver dross to silver and gold
metal.lead.cupellation-lead.description: The dross from the Parkes process is mixed with lead and flux and cast into a 30-50 kg charge, which is placed in a cupellation furnace at 1000-1150 C and blown with air. The lead oxidises to litharge, PbO, which melts at 888 C and is absorbed by the porous cupel, while the silver and gold do not oxidise and stay on the surface. When all the lead is gone the silver is 96-99% pure and the gold is 30-50% of it; the gold is then cupelled again, or electrorefined, to 99.9%. So every lead bullion makes a small pile of very pure silver - a deliberate convergence of the lead and silver branches.

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 30-50 kg of dross with litharge and flux

facts.label: Products
facts.value: silver at 96-99%, gold dore at 30-50% Au

metal.lead.cupellation-lead.note: Points to metal.silver.ingot and metal.gold.ingot in the same tree.

metal.sinter.name: Sinter the fine ore on a travelling grate
metal.sinter.description: Fine iron ore cannot be charged into a blast furnace - it would be blown away or it would pack. So it is sintered: mixed with 8-12% returning sinter fines, 5-7% coke and 10-20% lime, moistened to 6-8%, spread in a 0.7-1.0 m bed on a travelling grate, and ignited. At 1200-1400 C the bed self-fuses into a porous 100-150 mm cake. A modern sinter strand produces 3,000-6,000 t of sinter an hour and consumes about 1 GJ of fuel per tonne. It is the same machine as the lead sinter and the manganese sinter, and it emits a great deal of dust.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 1200-1400 C in the flame front

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 3,000-6,000 t/h per sinter strand

facts.label: Return fines
facts.value: 10-25% of the sinter produced is crushed and recycled

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke breeze or anthracite, ~60-90 MJ per tonne of sinter

facts.label: Gas cleaning
facts.value: cyclones and an electrostatic precipitator; the sinter plant was the biggest single dust emission at a steelworks

metal.pellet.name: Pelletising the concentrate on a disc or a pelletiser
metal.pellet.description: Very fine concentrate - under 45 um - is mixed with 5-8% bentonite binder and 0.5-1% limestone, moistened, and fed to a rotating disc pelletiser or a drum pelletiser where 3-10 mm green pellets are rolled up by capillary action. The green pellets are then fired on a travelling grate at 1200-1350 C in an oxidising atmosphere, which sinters the surface, gives the pellet its compressive strength and, if the furnace is properly controlled, magnetises it - the hematite becomes magnetite, which means the pellet can itself be recovered magnetically, and its reduction in the blast furnace is faster. Pelletising is what made the 1970s and 1980s post-and-tensile steel possible and it is the reason Brazil and Canada have a modern steel industry at all.

facts.label: Pellet
facts.value: 9-16 mm, compressive strength 200-300 daN per pellet

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 2-3% bentonite; the pellet must survive handling from the pellet plant to the furnace

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: pellet capacity became the binding constraint on a new blast furnace's size

metal.electrical-steel.lamination.name: E-E laminations and the stamping
metal.electrical-steel.lamination.description: The 0.3 mm strip is blanked and stamped into E and I shapes - or, in a cheaper 1982 supply, into E-E pairs and then stacked and interlocked - on a 400-800 tonne mechanical or hydraulic press with a compound die that does the whole lamination stack in one stroke. The stamping is heavily lubricated and the edges are deburred and then given a magnetic insulation treatment: a thin epoxy or phenolic varnish, or an 'insulation coating' of an inorganic glassy film, applied so that the laminations do not short-circuit each other. The core of the C64's transformer is about 30-60 stamped laminations, and the number is set by the stack height and the available die.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: 400-800 t, one stroke for the whole stack in a compound die

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: epoxy or phenolic varnish, or an inorganic glassy film; a C-core varnish coat

facts.label: Stacks
facts.value: 30-60 laminations for a small switcher

metal.electrical-steel.lamination.note: The interlocked E-E stamping process was the standard for small transformers in the 1980s; confidence high.

metal.electrical-steel.silicon-source.name: Make the ferrosilicon and add it to the steel
metal.electrical-steel.silicon-source.description: How does 3% silicon get into sheet steel at all? Ferrosilicon is added to the ladle, or - in the parent process - the ore is smelted with silica and coke in a submerged arc furnace to give 45-75% Si ferroalloy, and that alloy is added to the steel in the ladle or in the EAF. So the silicon steel branch intersects the ferrosilicon furnace, which is a carbon-reduction electric furnace just like the ferromanganese and ferrochrome furnaces in this tree, and which ultimately runs on the same metallurgical silicon and quartzite chain as the semiconductors. One of the more satisfying loops in the tree.

facts.label: Ferrosilicon
facts.value: FeSi45 (45% Si) to FeSi75 (75% Si), made in a submerged arc furnace at 1600-2000 C

facts.label: Addition
facts.value: to give 2.5-4.5% Si in the steel

facts.label: Grade for GOES
facts.value: high-purity, low-C, low-Al ferrosilicon is preferred because aluminium oxides in the film kill the magnetic properties

metal.electrical-steel.silicon-source.note: The low-aluminium requirement on silicon steel is well documented in the GOES literature; high confidence.

metal.electrical-steel.casting.name: Continuous casting and the Goss texture formation
metal.electrical-steel.casting.description: Electrical steel is continuously cast, hot rolled, and then given the two anneals that make it grain-oriented. The first, at 800-1100 C, is an ordinary recrystallisation anneal in wet hydrogen; the second, at 1100-1200 C, is the orientation anneal, in which the steel is held just below the Curie point in a magnetic field aligned with the rolling direction so the alpha-iron grains with their [110] axis along the field grow preferentially. The second anneal takes a week or more in a hydrogen atmosphere, which is why GOES costs three or four times what mild sheet costs and why a C64's transformer was one of the most expensive parts in it.

facts.label: First anneal
facts.value: 800-1100 C in wet hydrogen, 1-30 min

facts.label: Orientation anneal
facts.value: 1100-1200 C in dry hydrogen in a 5-10 T field, 10-100 h

facts.label: Grain size
facts.value: 2-10 mm, with the [110] axis parallel to the rolling direction

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: GOES sheet at 0.3-0.35 mm was several times the price of mild sheet

metal.electrical-steel.casting.note: The orientation anneal conditions are well documented; medium confidence on the exact field strength, which varies by producer.

metal.tin.atomisation.name: Air atomisation of tin to powder
metal.tin.atomisation.description: Molten tin at about 1150 C is poured into a launder and a high-pressure air jet at the bottom of a vertical stack sprays it into a fog of droplets that solidify on the way down. It is cheap, it works for metals that do not oxidise much, and it gives a bimodal powder. Under nitrogen it gives the fine, oxide-free powder that solder paste needs. Every particle in the can came out of a slot in a nozzle.

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: 10-25 um for solder-grade powder

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: air, or nitrogen for the low-oxide grade

metal.tin.atomisation.note: The 1980s powder market was real but small relative to solid wire; medium confidence on relative volumes.

metal.bauxite.creek-wash.name: Wash the bauxite in a creek sluice
metal.bauxite.creek-wash.description: The last leaf of the aluminium branch. In the Weipa and Gove deposits on the Cretaceous laterite surface, bauxite is dug in the wet season and the clay is washed out of it in a creek: a 200 m long, 30 m wide sluice excavated along the edge of the terrace, into which the bauxite is tipped and a stream of water is run, and the light clay washes away over a long distance while the pisolitic bauxite nodules, 5-50 mm and iron-stained, stay behind and are recovered by hand or by a mechanical rake. It is a 1980s technology on a Cretaceous rock surface in tropical Queensland, and it is the reason those deposits look the way they do.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: a sluice or creek 200-300 m long, washing the clay out of the nodules

facts.label: Nodule size
facts.value: 5-50 mm pisolite, iron-stained

facts.label: Season
facts.value: worked in the wet season, when there is water to run the sluice

metal.bauxite.creek-wash.note: Medium confidence; the Weipa creek-washing practice is well described in Queensland mining history.

metal.silica.tcs.distillation.name: Fractional distillation of HSiCl3
metal.silica.tcs.distillation.description: Tall, stainless, pressure-rated columns that separate trichlorosilane from its neighbours purely on volatility. The separation is the entire purification strategy: nothing clever happens chemically, the same material is simply re-fractionated until the boron is gone.
metal.silica.tcs.distillation.note: The boron cuts are the hard part: BCl3 boils close to trichlorosilane and boron has a low distribution coefficient, so 1980s plants used tall columns and many theoretical plates.

metal.silica.tcs.fluid-bed-chlorination.name: Fluid-bed chlorination of silicon at ~300 C
metal.silica.tcs.fluid-bed-chlorination.description: Metallurgical silicon is fluidised with nitrogen and metered HCl gas at 290-320 C. Silicon converts to trichlorosilane with hydrogen off; a large fraction of the feed instead goes to silicon tetrachloride, because the oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals push the stoichiometry. The bed is a tall stainless vessel with a distributor plate, and the reaction is exothermic enough that cooling coils matter.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Si + 3HCl -> HSiCl3 + H2, with Si + 4HCl -> SiCl4 + 2H2 as the side reaction

facts.label: Feed requirement
facts.value: ~99% Si with boron below ~20 ppm

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: historically copper or copper chloride; most modern plants run catalyst-free

children.name: Silicon tetrachloride by-product and recycling
children.description: Roughly half to two thirds of the silicon fed to a fluidised-bed chlorinator leaves as SiCl4 instead of HSiCl3, because oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals conspire. SiCl4 boils at 57.6 C and separates easily; it was largely dumped in the 1970s and later re-admitted as a chlorinating agent. The stoichiometric route that lets a plant recycle SiCl4 back into HSiCl3 by adding hydrogen and more silicon is the reason modern plants get the yields they do.

facts.label: 1980s practice
facts.value: a large fraction of by-product SiCl4 was sold as a solvent or to fumed-silica makers; full recycle came later

children.note: The fraction and its fate vary strongly between plants and years; high confidence in the chemistry, medium on the 1982 commercial split.

metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.name: Submerged-arc furnace reduction at 1800-2000 C
metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.description: A three-phase submerged arc furnace drops quartz, coal and woodchips down between graphite electrodes into a molten carbide bath at 1800-2000 C, and carbothermic reduction strips the oxygen off silica. Chemical silicon came to dominate this furnace by the late 1970s because the copper-clad electrode could then be pushed to a much higher current density. The off-gas, silicon monoxide at 400-1000 C, carries the energy away and is what lets the furnace run near-thermoneutral on the electrode side.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO

facts.label: Furnace size
facts.value: 25-75 MVA, 3-6 electrodes, 150-400 t/day of silicon

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: graphite or UHP carbon, consumed at ~1-1.5 t per t of silicon

facts.label: Off-gas
facts.value: SiO-rich gas leaving at 400-1000 C, cleaned in cyclones and baghouses

facts.label: Power
facts.value: order 11,000-13,000 kWh per tonne of silicon from the arc furnace alone

metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.note: The off-gas silicon monoxide chemistry was well understood by the 1980s and was the basis of several recovery processes that were still being commercialised then.

metal.gold.wire-bonding.name: Gold wire bonding of the die
metal.gold.wire-bonding.description: Each die has to be electrically connected to the package. The 1982 method was wire bonding: a 25 um gold or aluminium wire is threaded through a ceramic or carbide capillary, the tip is melted by a discharge or by a heated work holder, and the first weld is made to the die's aluminium pad. The wire is then run out and the second weld is made to the package bond pad, and the wire is cut. A 40-pin chip has 80 of these welds per package, each under a milligram of gold, and the whole thing happens a thousand times a minute. Aluminium bonding wire was already displacing gold on most logic parts by 1982 for cost reasons, but gold remained the default for anything requiring a conductive epoxy or a eutectic die attach.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 20-50 um gold or aluminium

facts.label: Methods
facts.value: thermasonic (ultrasonic plus heat), the 1980s default for gold

facts.label: Bonds per package
facts.value: order 80 for a 40-pin DIP

facts.label: Gold per bond
facts.value: order 0.05-0.3 mg

facts.label: Intermetallic
facts.value: Au-Al intermetallics form in the bond; the purple plague is AuAl2

metal.manganese.sintering.name: Sintering the manganese ore
metal.manganese.sintering.description: Manganese ore is very fine and very friable, so it cannot be blown into a submerged arc furnace as a powder; it is sintered first, on a travelling grate exactly like the lead sinter, to make a 30-50 mm porous cake. The sinter belt at a manganese works is a zinc-works sinter plant or a lead-works sinter plant wearing different clothes, which makes it a nice example of a single machine serving three of the branches in this file.

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: travelling-grate sinter strand, 1100-1300 C in the burn zone

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 30-50 mm cake

metal.manganese.sintering.note: Medium confidence on the sinter temperature range; the process itself is standard.

metal.manganese.deoxidiser.name: Deoxidation and desulphurisation in the steel ladle
metal.manganese.deoxidiser.description: Where the alloy is actually used. During tapping, ferromanganese is added to the steel. Manganese has a higher oxygen affinity than iron, so it combines with the dissolved oxygen to form MnO inclusions - which is the point: the oxygen is now safely tied up in an oxide the steelmaker can float out instead of being trapped as a gas bubble or an oxide stringer. Manganese also lowers the sulphur by forming MnS. The cost is that every kilo of manganese added becomes an inclusion unless the steel is properly deoxidised and the slag properly cleaned, which is why the amount is carefully calculated and why clean, low-inclusion steel is a specific technical achievement.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Mn + [O] -> MnO, and Mn + [S] -> MnS

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.5 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: during tapping or in the ladle, before the degasser

children.name: Aluminium and silicon deoxidation
children.description: The last step in the ladle is the one that actually decides the steel's quality. Manganese ties up the bulk of the dissolved oxygen as MnO inclusions, and then a calculated addition of aluminium - 0.5-2 kg per tonne - ties up the rest as Al2O3. Those inclusions have to go, and in a well-run plant they are floated out in the ladle or removed later by degassing and filtering. Manganese is what makes the aluminium deoxidation work: without manganese in solution, aluminium would oxidise preferentially as Al2O3 straight out of the bath and never reach the steel.

facts.label: Sequence
facts.value: Si, then Mn, then Al - the order matters

facts.label: Aluminium
facts.value: 0.5-2 kg per tonne, for a final soluble oxygen of 2-5 ppm

facts.label: Result
facts.value: fine Al2O3 inclusions dispersed in a MnS-bearing matrix

children.note: Medium confidence; the sequence is standard practice in aluminium-killed steel.

children.name: Removing the inclusions: degassing and filtration
children.description: A modern low-sulphur steel has few MnS inclusions but a lot of fine Al2O3, and that is a different problem: fine alumina does not float out, so it has to be filtered. A 1980s plate mill that wanted clean, formable sheet for deep drawing or for tinplating ran a ladle through a vacuum degasser to flush hydrogen and nitrogen and then through a ceramic foam filter in the ladle, or poured through a tundish filter. This is the technology that made the C64's chassis panel and the tinplate base material reproducible rather than lucky.

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: <10 mbar, 10-25 min, with argon stirring

facts.label: Filter
facts.value: ceramic foam, 0.4-1.0 mm pore, in the ladle or the tundish

facts.label: Target
facts.value: total oxygen below 20 ppm and sulphur below 0.005% for ultra-clean steel

children.note: The filtration step is a genuine 1980s development; medium confidence on the specific purity targets.

metal.cassiterite.alluvial.name: Alluvial cassiterite gravel: dredging and panning
metal.cassiterite.alluvial.description: Tin gravel is a beach or stream deposit: pebbles and clay with a few grams of cassiterite per tonne. The classical recovery is the sluice and the jig, where a stream of water over an inclined riffled box stratifies by density and the heavy mineral stays behind. The Kinta Valley in Perak, Malaysia, was dredged on an enormous scale from the 1900s through the 1980s by suction dredges working a 100 m wide alluvial fan at 30-100 m depth, pumping gravel through a 3-6 inch suction pipe to a floating washing plant and a jig. Off Thailand and Indonesia it was offshore and shallow-sea dredging. Gravel is essentially quarried from a sea floor.

facts.label: Dredge
facts.value: cutter-suction dredge, 100-300 mm gravel, 200-500 L/s

facts.label: Recovery route
facts.value: sluice box, jig, then a shaking table and a magnetic separator

facts.label: 1982s shift
facts.value: the Kinta dredging era was ending and hard-rock and residual mining was taking over as the Malaysian industry

metal.aluminum.blending.name: Alloying to 3003, 6063 or A13
metal.aluminum.blending.description: The rolling mill is not a refinery. It melts primary ingot, remelted can scrap and dross recovery in a reverberatory or an induction furnace, adds the alloying elements as lumps of master alloy, degasses with a rotating argon lance to strip hydrogen, and skims the dross. Manganese for 3003, magnesium and silicon for 6063, silicon for the A13 casting alloy. So the C64's case metal is partly recycled metal, and its chemistry is set in a small furnace rather than a pot.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: oil- or gas-fired reverberatory melting furnace of 100-300 t, or an induction furnace

facts.label: Degassing
facts.value: rotating argon or nitrogen lance, or a chlorine-salt flux
~1.0-1.2% Mn, balance aluminium

facts.label: A13 (casting)
facts.value: ~11-13% Si, the standard 1980s die-casting alloy

metal.aluminum.blending.note: The specific alloy used for the Commodore case is not something I can confirm; 6063 and 1050 are the plausible candidates. Medium confidence.

metal.aluminum.dc-casting.name: DC casting to a rolling ingot
metal.aluminum.dc-casting.description: Molten aluminium at 700-750 C is poured into a steel mould that is being withdrawn by a hydraulic jack at a controlled few millimetres per second, so the metal freezes progressively behind a solidification front instead of all at once. The front is water-cooled and the emerging surface is squirted with a water mist to control its shape. This produces a big flat rectangular billet - typically 500-1000 mm wide, 600 mm thick, 5-25 t - with a fine equiaxed chill zone at the surface. Because it is a continuous process, a 1980s smelter and a modern one produce ingots of essentially identical shape.

facts.label: Ingot mass
facts.value: 5-30 t, most often 10-25 t

facts.label: Section
facts.value: 0.5-1.0 m wide by 0.5-0.8 m thick, 1-6 m long

facts.label: Ingot temperature
facts.value: 720-750 C at the mould

facts.label: Chill zone
facts.value: 10-25 mm of fine equiaxed surface grains, which helps the ingot survive rolling without cracking

facts.label: Homogenisation
facts.value: a follow-up soak of 6-24 h at 450-600 C to dissolve Al-Zn-Mg clusters

children.name: Homogenising soak
children.description: A long hold in a gas- or electrically-heated pit furnace, typically 12-24 h at 450-600 C, whose only job is to let the alloying elements diffuse evenly. Without it a slab rolled on one edge behaves differently from the same slab rolled on the other and the foil tears. It also rounds the dendritic structure into equiaxed grains, which is what makes the achievable surface quality possible.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 6-24 h depending on section

children.note: Typical range; specific alloy timetables vary by producer.

metal.aluminum.hot-rolling.name: Hot rolling to 2-6 mm
metal.aluminum.hot-rolling.description: The ingot is preheated to 300-400 C for wide slab or 450-550 C for narrower, thicker slab, and a reversing hot mill takes it down to 2-6 mm in one or two passes. Aluminium's rolling window is famously narrow - too cold and it tears at the edges, too hot and the ingot surface oxidises and scales - so a 1980s reversing hot mill had two or three stands and quite tight control. Scale is removed with hot descaling rolls, which presses a rolled-in oxide pattern into the surface that later helps the lubricant out of the pores.

facts.label: Reheat temperature
facts.value: 300-400 C for wide slab, up to 450-550 C

facts.label: Exit thickness
facts.value: 2-6 mm

facts.label: Reduction per pass
facts.value: order 3-8 mm per pass, about a 30% reduction limit

facts.label: Descaling
facts.value: hot descaler rolls force water under the oxide scale and knock it off

metal.aluminum.hot-rolling.note: Documented in general terms only: hot rolling is done above the recrystallization temperature and starts from ingots, slabs, blooms and billets, with the finishing temperature set above the recrystallization point. Not established for aluminium: the 300-400 C and 450-550 C preheat ranges, the 2-6 mm exit thickness, the 30% per-pass reduction limit and the hot descaler roll practice. The rolling reference is the general Rolling (metalworking) article and carries no aluminium-specific figures.

metal.silica.polysilicon.deposition.name: Siemens deposition on UHF-heated rods
metal.silica.polysilicon.deposition.description: Trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow over silicon rods held just below their melting point by radio-frequency induction, and silicon atoms drop out as polycrystalline growth. Rod temperature is the whole ballgame: too cold and you get powder, too hot and you get liquid droplets that fall into the bed. Two temperature measurement methods were in use - an optical pyrometer sighted on a blackened patch of rod, and a movable thermocouple in the gas stream - and calibrating that pyrometer was a plant secret worth millions.

facts.label: Induction frequency
facts.value: 200-500 kHz historically, multi-MHz later

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 100-200 kWh per kg of polysilicon across the whole chlorosilane route

facts.label: Deposition rate
facts.value: single-digit micrometres per hour per rod in 1980s reactors

children.name: Doped vs undoped polysilicon
children.description: Two grades were produced side by side in the same plant. UNdoped polysilicon went to the crystal puller for Czochralski ingots. Heavily doped material - p-type with boron or phosphorus, n-type with phosphorus or arsenic - went to subcollector plugs, to doped polysilicon films in later processes, and, most importantly, to the heavily doped epi and subcollector wafers that the NMOS logic was built on. In 1982 the dopant was dosed into the trichlorosilane stream as phosphine or the corresponding trichloride.

facts.label: Target resistivity
facts.value: 0.005-0.02 ohm-cm for a doped polysilicon film; subcollector 0.1 ohm-cm

facts.label: Dopant sources
facts.value: PH3 for both polarities in older practice; AsH3 for n-type

children.note: Not established: which dopant gas a given 1982 Taiwanese polysilicon plant used; the specific pairing is medium confidence.

children.name: Crushing, flaking and acid etching of the rod
children.description: The deposited rod is sawn with a slurry-impregnated circular saw, then the pieces are fractured and leached in hot hydrochloric-nitric acid to strip near-surface contamination from the seed end. What the puller wants is small pieces with clean fracture faces, because every surface is a chance to recontaminate. Rod ends were also ground back and reused as seed.
children.note: The etch chemistry varied plant to plant and was rarely published; described here from general practice.

facts.label: Chunk size
facts.value: 5-30 kg per sawn rod segment in 1980s practice

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: a hot HCl/HF polish removes the saw damage and the surface boron before the chunk is charged to the puller

metal.refractory-ladle.name: The refractory ladle lining
metal.refractory-ladle.description: The AOD vessel is lined with magnesia or with magnesia-carbon, and the slag at pH 5 or higher eats a basic lining - which is why a stainless ladle lining is more expensive and more carefully maintained than a mild steel one. The lining is a consumable of its own, replaced every few hundred heats. So the chromium branch reaches the bottom not only in an ore body but in a sea of magnesia sand, and the magnesia is from seawater or from a magnesite mine.

facts.label: Lining
facts.value: magnesia or magnesia-carbon brick, 200-300 mm

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: dead-burnt magnesite (MgCO3) or seawater magnesia (Mg(OH)2)

metal.refractory-ladle.note: Medium confidence; the magnesia supply chain is well documented but is not part of this subsystem's requested scope.

metal.copper.patenting.name: Patenting: annealing the rod before drawing
metal.copper.patenting.description: Copper work-hardens fast: a few percent of reduction raises the tensile strength enormously and the wire simply snaps in the die. So the rod is heated - in steam, in air, or in a fluidised bed - to about 200-350 C, which recrystallises the elongated drawing structure back to equiaxed grains, and then quenched. The black oxide that air patenting leaves is actually helpful, because it stops the wire rusting in the draw bin. Patenting is the cheapest trick in the whole wire business.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 200-350 C in steam, or a fluidised bed at up to about 400 C

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: recrystallisation: copper goes from about 60-70 kg/mm2 work-hardened to 35-45 kg/mm2 annealed

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: steam or air - air leaves a useful black oxide; inert gas only for fine wire

metal.copper.multiwire-drawing.name: Multiwire drawing through diamond dies
metal.copper.multiwire-drawing.description: Since the 1960s the industry stopped drawing one wire at a time and started drawing 7-19 wires simultaneously through a cone of dies, so the die size needed for a 0.2 mm wire is much larger and lasts much longer. The dies are natural diamond - or, as synthetic diamond tooling matured through the 1980s, polycrystalline diamond compact - set in a steel holder with a hardened steel casing. Drawing to 0.15 mm means the copper has been elongated by a factor of order 1600, which is why magnet wire is made only from low-oxygen, low-sulphur electrolytic cathode and never from cast copper.

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: 7-19 wires per pass through coned dies

facts.label: Die material
facts.value: natural diamond or synthetic PCD in a steel holder

facts.label: Total reduction to 0.2 mm
facts.value: from 8 mm, a total elongation of order 1.6 x 10^3

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: needed above about 1-2 mm drawn diameter

metal.copper.enamelling.name: Enamelling and cure of magnet wire
metal.copper.enamelling.description: The drawn wire is passed through a die and coated with liquid polyurethane enamel in a continuous length of 10-20 coats, each flash-dried, then cured in a vertical oven at 150-220 C for up to an hour. The result is a wire whose insulation survives a 155 C winding temperature and whose dielectric strength is 5-10 kV between turns. Enamelling is a chemical coating line rather than a metallurgy process, but the wire underneath it is this branch's problem.

facts.label: Coats
facts.value: 10-20 flash-dried coats for a 15-40 um build

facts.label: Cure temperature
facts.value: 150-220 C, up to about 1 h

facts.label: Dielectric strength
facts.value: 5-10 kV across the enamel

children.name: The enamelling line and the cure oven
children.description: A magnet-wire enamelling line is a 20-40 m long machine: a pay-off, a bunch of dies applying 10-20 coats with flash-off between them, a vertical cure oven 8-15 m tall, a capstan, a take-up. The cure oven is gas or electric at 150-220 C with the wire passing through it in a helix, and it is the cure schedule and not the coating that decides the wire's class. A class 155 wire needs a full hour at temperature; a class 130 wire can get away with less. In 1982 the whole world's magnet wire was made on lines of exactly this design, whether the wire came from Japan, France or the United States.

facts.label: Coats
facts.value: 10-20, each flash-dried

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 150-220 C, up to about 1 h

facts.label: Speed
facts.value: 60-300 m/min depending on the wire gauge

children.note: Medium confidence on the speed range; it is strongly gauge-dependent.

metal.ferrite.gap-scrape.name: Cutting the air gap in the centre leg
metal.ferrite.gap-scrape.description: An ungapped ferrite E core has a very high inductance and would not regulate a switch-mode supply; the switcher's magnetising current would be wrong and the whole design fails. So the gap is made deliberately, and on a 1982 E core it was cut with a carbide-tipped scraper - literally a hand blade run along the face of the centre leg - to 0.2-1.0 mm. Cutting rather than inserting a gap material keeps the inductance high and spreads the gap's fringing over an area, and it does it with a machine a ferrite buyer can operate. The tolerance of that hand cut is what sets the inductance tolerance, and the whole thing is one of the more beautiful pieces of 1980s manufacturing: a blade and a number.

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 0.2-1.0 mm, cut with a carbide scraper

facts.label: Why cut
facts.value: spreads the fringing flux over an area and keeps the inductance high

facts.label: Control
facts.value: the gap sets the inductance, so the transformer builder measured it and often adjusted it per core

metal.ferrite.gap-scrape.note: Medium confidence; the scraper-gap technique is very widely documented for small E and EE cores of that era.

metal.fluorspar.vein.name: Fluorite vein in limestone
metal.fluorspar.vein.description: The leaf: a purple, green or white vein of CaF2 a few centimetres to a few metres thick in a fractured carbonate host, in a limestone hill.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: limestone with fluorite veining

metal.nickel.peridotite.name: Serpentinised peridotite
metal.nickel.peridotite.description: The leaf: an ultramafic igneous rock, mostly olivine, now largely converted to serpentine, that has been chemically weathered for tens of millions of years in a warm wet climate. The nickel is in the clay and in the limonite, not in a crystal. Cuba, New Caledonia and the Philippines all have large serpentinite bodies, and that is why the island arcs of the Pacific are the nickel map.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: serpentinised peridotite / dunite, weathered to garnierite-bearing laterite

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: tropical weathering profile, tens of metres thick, on an ultramafic body

metal.quartzite.rock.name: Quartz sandstone protolith (metaquartzite)
metal.quartzite.rock.description: The rock as a geologist would name it: a quartz-rich sandstone or siltstone, now a hard white metaquartzite of interlocking quartz grains with the bedding picked out by iron oxides. Some of the Norwegian material is a hydrothermal replacement body in a metasedimentary sequence. Either way the leaf of the silicon chain is a sedimentary or metamorphic rock exposed at the surface and dug out of a hillside.

facts.label: Rock type
facts.value: metaquartzite / quartzite; SiO2 >95% by definition

metal.quartzite.rock.note: The rock is right but one figure is not: quartzite is not defined as SiO2 >95%. The British Geological Survey classification quoted in the quartzite reference requires at least 80% quartz by volume. Not established from the references fetched: the claim that some Norwegian material is a hydrothermal replacement body in a metasedimentary sequence.

metal.banded-iron-formation.name: Banded iron formation: a chemical precipitate from seawater
metal.banded-iron-formation.description: The leaf of the whole iron and steel branch, and one of the great ones. Around 2.0-1.8 billion years ago, the oceans contained dissolved ferrous iron and oxygen appeared in the atmosphere as a result of an earlier generation of photosynthetic organisms. Wherever the oxygen-rich surface water sank and met the anoxic iron-rich deep water, the iron oxidised and precipitated, as a jelly of iron oxide that settled as a chemical mud. It compacted into alternating silica and iron bands, and it is that banding which gives the rock its name and which makes the high-grade hematite ore bodies on the Hamersley Range the size they are. So the iron in a C64 chassis began, two billion years ago, as an oxide precipitating out of an ocean.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: 2.0-1.8 Ga, the Great Oxidation Event interval

facts.label: Lithology
facts.value: alternating magnetite and chert (BIF), later metamorphosed to hematite

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: a marine chemical precipitate on a continental shelf

metal.sphalerite.massive-sulphide.name: Massive sulphide in a sedimentary basin
metal.sphalerite.massive-sulphide.description: The leaf: a lens-shaped body of fine-grained sulphide - sphalerite, galena, pyrite, with chalcopyrite and arsenopyrite - conformable with the bedding of a marine shale or carbonate, and sitting at a specific stratigraphic horizon. The Red Dog deposit is exactly this: a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin. The ore is not in a vein you can see from the surface; it is a stratigraphic layer you have to know is there.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: sediment-hosted massive sulphide lens in fine-grained clastic sediment

metal.sphalerite.host.name: The host basin and its caprock
metal.sphalerite.host.description: The final leaf of the zinc chain is not a rock but a structure: a sedimentary basin with a metal-bearing horizon in it. The Red Dog deposit is a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin on the Tukarakka Peninsula; Broken Hill is a metamorphosed, deformed massive sulphide in a sequence of Proterozoic metasediments. In both cases the orebody sits at a specific stratigraphic level, and the mine is a series of ramps and stopes chasing a bedding-parallel body a few metres thick. So the zinc in a C64's die-cast key plunger came out of a bed that happens to lie a kilometre beneath a river delta.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: sediment-hosted massive sulphide at a specific horizon in a basin

facts.label: Ore thickness
facts.value: 5-25 m of ore under hundreds of metres of host rock

metal.chromite.layered.name: Layered norite of the Bushveld Complex
metal.chromite.layered.description: The leaf: a 2 km thick layered mafic intrusion with a spectacularly regular magmatic stratification - a metre-scale layering of plagioclase and pyroxene laid down by a magma chamber over about a million years - with the chromite concentrating into a single thin seam at one horizon. It is the single most chromium-rich geological structure on Earth.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: layered norite, pyroxenite and anorthosite with a chromitite seam

facts.label: Age
facts.value: about 2.05 billion years

metal.galena.rock.name: Galenite replacement in carbonate rock
metal.galena.rock.description: The leaf: galena crystals and veins in a fossiliferous limestone - literally the remains of a Carboniferous sea floor. The Tri-State district is one of the great fossil-mineral coincidences of industrial history: a lead-bearing limestone under a farm field.

facts.label: Host rock
facts.value: Mississippian limestone and dolomite

facts.label: Form
facts.value: replacement bodies and veins along bedding and fractures

metal.bauxite.laterite.name: Lateritic bauxite profile
metal.bauxite.laterite.description: The leaf: a 3-12 m pisolitic blanket of iron-stained bauxite nodules sitting on a Cretaceous or Tertiary lateritic surface above a kaolinitic clay. Guinea's deposits are the classic tropical pisolite; the Australian Weipa and Gove ores are flat-lying terrace deposits on Cretaceous sediments. Either way the rock outcrops at the surface and is dug, not tunnelled.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 3-12 m of economic bauxite over kaolinite

metal.bauxite.laterite.note: Documented: laterite forms in hot wet tropical areas, is a source of aluminium ore, and consists largely of clay minerals and the hydroxides gibbsite, boehmite and diaspore so that it resembles bauxite. Not established: the pisolitic texture, the 3-12 m blanket thickness, and the description of the Australian Weipa and Gove ores as flat-lying terrace deposits on Cretaceous sediments.

metal.cassiterite.greisen.name: Greisen and quartz vein
metal.cassiterite.greisen.description: The leaf for the hard-rock route: a pneumatolytic alteration halo of topaz-bearing greisen and milky quartz with cassiterite disseminated through it, around a granite cupola. It is a rock, it is in a hillside, and it is drilled.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: greisen and quartz vein in a granite cupploa

metal.nickel.ore-washing.name: The laterite washing and screening plant
metal.nickel.ore-washing.description: The laterite arrives from a bucket-wheel excavator as a slurry, and it goes through a log washer, a scrubber, a screen tower and a series of hydrocyclones, and the -0.5 mm fraction is rejected outright as low-grade clay. The coarse fraction is dewatered on a screen and stacked in a concrete bin. In the Cuban and Philippine operations the stacked ore was then leached in place on a pad, in the Queensland operations it was dried in a rotary dryer and shipped to a furnace. The whole plant exists because the ore is a soft, wet, variable, low-grade bulk material, and the plants are mostly about handling water.

facts.label: Rejection
facts.value: the -0.5 mm clay fraction is discarded, and it is often 20-40% of the feed

facts.label: Dewatering
facts.value: screens, cyclones, and a large thickener

facts.label: Moisture in the dried ore
facts.value: reduced to below 1-2% before any furnace

metal.nickel.ore-washing.note: Medium confidence; the flowsheet is well documented for Cuban and Philippine operations.

metal.hematite.crushing.name: Crushing, screening and the lump/fines split
metal.hematite.crushing.description: The ore is crushed in a gyratory and then on a screen, and the product is split three ways: lump ore above 6.3 mm that goes straight into the blast furnace, fines below 6.3 mm that must be sintered or pelletised, and a reject stream of the banded iron formation that is too low grade to smelt. The lump/fines split is a commercial decision rather than a metallurgical one: in 1982 the steelmakers wanted as much direct-shipping lump as possible because it avoided the sintering plant's capital and its fuel.

facts.label: Lump
facts.value: above 6.3 mm, direct to the blast furnace

facts.label: Fines
facts.value: below 6.3 mm, to the sinter strand or the pellet plant

facts.label: Rejects
facts.value: the banded iron formation itself, at 30-45% Fe, often stockpiled

metal.hematite.crushing.note: Not established: the 6.3 mm lump/fines split point, the three-way split with a reject stream, the 30-45% Fe reject grade, and the 1982 steelmaker preference for direct-shipping lump. The iron ore reference distinguishes direct-shipping ore at over about 60% Fe from ore needing beneficiation but gives no size cut-off.

metal.sphalerite.mill.name: Zinc concentrator: differential flotation
metal.sphalerite.mill.description: The ore is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground to 50-100 um in a ball or autogenous mill, and floated in stages. The classic circuit is differential: copper and lead sulphides are floated first with a stronger collector and a higher pH, and then the sphalerite is floated from the tailings with a weaker collector at a lower pH, with copper sulphate added as an activator because sphalerite does not float on its own. That gives a 50-60% Zn concentrate at 85-92% recovery. The Red Dog and Sullivan concentrators were among the largest in the world and are the reason those two mines could be mines at all.

facts.label: Circuit
facts.value: Cu-Pb bulk float first, then Zn float from the tailings

facts.label: Activator
facts.value: copper sulphate, 0.1-1 kg/t

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 85-92% to a 50-60% Zn concentrate

metal.sphalerite.mill.note: Medium confidence on the specific additive dosages; the circuit configuration is standard.

children.name: Dense-media separation of galena from sphalerite
children.description: Galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 are separable on a shaking table or, much faster, in a dense-medium separator using a ferrosilicon or magnetite suspension at a cut density of about 3.0-3.5. The lead concentrate and the zinc concentrate are thereby split before flotation, which lets the flotation plant be small. Dense-medium separation of a polymetallic ore is one of the great quiet successes of twentieth-century mineral processing.

facts.label: Medium
facts.value: ferrosilicon or magnetite in water at 2.5-3.5 specific gravity

facts.label: Cut density
facts.value: 3.0-3.5 separates galena from sphalerite

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: 100-500 t/h on a modern separator

children.note: The cut densities and throughputs are class values; medium confidence.

metal.manganese.washing-plant.name: Scrubber, sluice and jig beneficiation
metal.manganese.washing-plant.description: Groote Eylandt and the South African operations do not smelt the raw lump: they wash it. The ore is dumped on a heap, a high-pressure water monitor scrubs off the fines and the clay, and the coarse goes over a sluice and a jig where the density difference between the manganese minerals (4.5-5.1) and the iron formation (5.0-5.3 but with a very different mineralogy) and the waste gangue separates the product. That is why a 30% Mn ore can make a 40% Mn product at low cost: the operation is a placer operation with a shovel in it.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: scrubbing with water monitors, sluice boxes and jigs

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 30-40% Mn, and the fines go to the sinter belt

metal.manganese.washing-plant.note: The scrubbing and jigging flowsheet is well documented for Groote Eylandt; medium confidence on the exact recoveries.

metal.chromite.bench.name: Following a seam: the narrow-bench problem
metal.chromite.bench.description: A normal open pit advances in benches 15 m high and 100-200 m wide, with haul roads on every bench. A chromite seam is 1-6 m thick, so the pit has to advance along the seam instead, and the benches are 100-200 m high with a 5-10 m working width and a haul road cut into the wall. The consequence is a bench width of a few tens of metres where a truck needs twenty, so the ore is either hauled a long way or handled by a shovel that strips the ore off the face and tips it down to a loading point on the bench floor. That is why the Bushveld pits look nothing like an iron ore pit even though they move similar tonnages, and it is a nice demonstration that mining cost is a function of geometry before it is a function of the rock.

facts.label: Bench
facts.value: 100-200 m high with a 5-10 m working width

facts.label: Advance
facts.value: along the seam, not across it

facts.label: Truck requirement
facts.value: order 20 m of road width, more than the seam provides

metal.chromite.bench.note: Medium confidence; the geometry argument is sound and the specific figures are representative of the Bushveld pits.

metal.galena.sorting.name: Hand picking and gravity sorting
metal.galena.sorting.description: The Tri-State district's ore was a 3-6% lead limestone that could not be selectively mined and could not be concentrated, so the technique was brute force: the rock was shot down, the lead-bearing rock was picked out of the face by hand by a face worker, and then the cars were run over a sorting table or a picking table where a sorter took out the visibly lead-coloured lumps from the limestone. In 1930 the Tri-State had about 15,000 sorters - a third of them children - and that is what made the district the largest lead producer on Earth. It is a labour technique rather than a machine, and it is a genuine leaf of the tree.

facts.label: Recovery by sorting
facts.value: a face worker and a car sorter could double the mill feed grade

facts.label: Sorters
facts.value: order 15,000 sorters at the peak of the Tri-State, a third of them children

facts.label: Why it stopped
facts.value: the ore got deeper and thinner, and the labour became uneconomic; the district closed in the 1960s-70s

metal.galena.sorting.note: Medium confidence; the Tri-State hand-sorting era is well documented in the labour history literature.

children.name: The sorting table
children.description: A sloping table with a light on it and a raised lip, worked by two or three people, one on each side. Galena is bright and heavy and galena-bearing limestone is dark and light, so the visual contrast is real, and the sorter's job is to lift out the dark lumps at perhaps 2-4 tonnes per shift. It is the lowest-skill, lowest-pay, highest-volume job in the lead industry, and it is where a great many Missouri families started.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: order 2-4 t of rock sorted per person per shift

children.note: Medium confidence; sorting rates are anecdotal and vary enormously with the ore.

metal.bauxite.beneficiation.name: Bauxite crushing, washing and drying
metal.bauxite.beneficiation.description: The Bayer plant does not want a 300 mm boulder and it certainly does not want the clay. The run-of-mine ore is crushed in a gyratory or a jaw crusher to 25-50 mm, and then - in the wet-grinding route that became standard for high-temperature bauxite - it is ground in a ball mill in a rod or a wet scrubber to a slurry, and that slurry is screened and washed to remove the clay, which is called 'desilication by attrition washing'. The under-0.5 mm clay is discarded as tailings, and it is often 15-30% of the mass. What goes into the digestor is a 40-50% solids slurry of 25-50 mm lumps with the reactive silica taken out, and the moisture matters because every kilo of water into the autoclave is a kilo of steam wasted.

facts.label: Crushing
facts.value: to 25-50 mm in a gyratory or jaw crusher

facts.label: Desilication by washing
facts.value: the -0.5 mm clay fraction is removed, often 15-30% of the mass

facts.label: Feed to the digestor
facts.value: a 40-50% solids slurry

facts.label: Direct-feed route
facts.value: the older route, in which crushed ore went to the digestor unwashed, is still used on low-silica ore

metal.bauxite.beneficiation.note: Medium confidence on the mass fractions removed by washing; they are strongly ore-dependent.

metal.magnetite.separators.name: Magnetic separation and the taconite concentrator
metal.magnetite.separators.description: The separator is a rotating drum 1-2.5 m in diameter with a 4-10 pole magnet of 400-1,200 gauss at the drum surface, or a high-gradient can of ferrite pole pieces that achieves 10,000-20,000 gauss on the tips. Slurry flows past and the magnetic grains are held to the drum and carried around until they fall off the other side. With the magnetoferrite in the drum the recovery of a 30-45 um magnetite grain is above 95%. A taconite concentrator at 20-40 Mt a year is one of the largest single streams of water and solids in the world, and the tailings are a billion-tonne deposit in their own right.

facts.label: Drum separator
facts.value: 1-2.5 m diameter, 400-1200 gauss at the surface; high-gradient types to 20,000 gauss

facts.label: Grind
facts.value: 30-45 um before separation

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 65-70% Fe, 2-4% silica

metal.magnetite.separators.note: Separator field strengths and grind targets are standard class values; medium confidence.

children.name: Ferrite magnets in the separator
children.description: A short and important cross-link: the permanent magnet inside a magnetic separator is a ferrite - barium ferrite or strontium ferrite, sintered like the power ferrites but with a different composition and without the permeability requirement. So the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace contains ferrite magnets, and the ferrite branch of this file is the same powder metallurgy.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 or BaFe12O19, sintered; remanence ~0.3-0.4 T

facts.label: In 1982
